content.content:
# PRD Template

## Essential Spine *(almost always present)*

```markdown
---
title: {Product Name}
created: {YYYY-MM-DD}
updated: {YYYY-MM-DD}
---

# PRD: {Product Name}
*Working title — confirm.*

## 0. Document Purpose
[1 paragraph: who this PRD is for (PM, stakeholders, downstream workflow owners), how it's structured (Glossary-anchored vocabulary, features grouped with FRs nested, assumptions tagged inline and indexed). If UX work or other inputs already exist, name them here and reference where they live — this PRD builds on them, it does not duplicate.]

## 1. Vision
[2-3 paragraphs: what this is, what it does for the user, why it matters. Compelling enough to stand alone.]

## 2. Target User

### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done
[Bulleted. Emotional, social, functional, contextual — whichever apply. Even "this is for me as the builder" is a valid framing for a hobby project.]

### 2.2 Non-Users (v1) *(add when the audience boundary is non-obvious)*
[Who this is explicitly not for in v1.]

### 2.3 Key User Journeys
*Named-persona narratives the product enables. Numbered globally as UJ-1 through UJ-N. FRs reference journeys by ID inline ("realizes UJ-3"); SMs may also cross-reference. If a UX doc already exists, mirror its UJ IDs here and point to the source.*

**Default shape:** a named scene with entry state, path, climax, and resolution. Each beat forces specificity the team would otherwise leave implicit — auth assumptions, screen order, what tells the user value landed. Read together as a short narrative; the example below shows the form.

- **UJ-1. {One-line title — persona doing the thing.}**
  - **Persona + context:** one line, grounded enough to explain the *why*.
  - **Entry state:** authenticated? which surface? coming from where?
  - **Path:** 3-5 concrete beats — taps, screens, decisions.
  - **Climax:** the moment value is delivered and how the user knows.
  - **Resolution:** state they're left in, what's next.
  - **Edge case** *(optional)*: one real failure mode and what the user does next.

  *Written out, that becomes:*
  > **UJ-3. Priya checks the trip damage before she's even home.**
  > Priya, budgeting on a single income with a new baby, finishes a grocery run and gets in the car. Already authenticated via biometric on a previous session. She opens the app, taps the FAB camera, and scans the receipt. The app OCRs the total and shows a single-screen overlay: this trip $84.20, weekly cap $250, $172.10 remaining, three days left in the week. She closes the app and drives home. **Edge case:** if she scanned a receipt earlier today, the app asks whether this replaces or adds to that trip before counting it against the cap.

- **UJ-2. ...**

**Scope dial:**
- **Lighter** — hobby/solo, library/CLI, or when the UJ is essentially a JTBD restated: a single sentence works (`{Persona}, {context}, {what they do and why}.`).
- **Heavier** — auth, multi-device handoff, complex navigation, or anything feeding downstream UX/architecture: add a numbered Flow, an Edge cases list, and a capability → FR mapping (`The system must {capability}. → FR-N`).

## 3. Glossary
*Downstream workflows and readers must use these terms exactly. FRs, UJs, and SMs use Glossary terms verbatim; introducing a synonym anywhere in the PRD is a discipline violation. If §4 introduces a new domain noun, add it to the Glossary in the same pass.*

- **Term** — Definition. Relationships to other Glossary terms. Cardinality where relevant.
- **Term** — ...

[Every domain noun the rest of the document uses. Defined once. No synonyms anywhere else in the PRD.]

## 4. Features
*Each subsection is a coherent feature: behavioral description first, FRs nested under it, optional feature-specific NFRs and notes. FRs are numbered globally (FR-1 through FR-N) so downstream artifacts have stable references even if features get reorganized. Reference user journeys by ID inline ("realizes UJ-2") where the chain matters.*

### 4.1 {Feature Name}
**Description:** [Behavioral narrative — how this feature works, who uses it, the user experience, edge cases. Realizes UJ-X, UJ-Y. Use Glossary terms exactly. Embed inline `[ASSUMPTION: ...]` tags where you inferred without confirmation.]

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-1: {Short capability name}

[Actor] can [capability] [under conditions]. Realizes UJ-X.

**Consequences (testable):**
- {Specific testable condition, e.g. "System returns HTTP 429 when request rate exceeds 100/sec per merchant."}
- {Another testable condition.}

**Out of Scope:** *(optional — what this FR explicitly does NOT cover)*
- {bound}

#### FR-2: ...

**Feature-specific NFRs:** *(only if any apply uniquely to this feature)*
- Performance / security / accessibility / etc. specific to this feature.

**Notes:** *(optional — open questions specific to this feature, `[NOTE FOR PM]` callouts)*

### 4.2 {Feature Name}
...

## 5. Non-Goals (Explicit)
[Bulleted. What this product is *not* and what it will *not* do in v1. Does outsized work for downstream readers and workflows — prevents the "let me also add this nearby thing" failure mode at every level (epic, ticket, code). Inline `[NON-GOAL for MVP]` callouts within §4 Features cover deferred items within features; this section captures the broader "we are not building X / we are not becoming Y" statements.]

## 6. MVP Scope

### 6.1 In Scope
[Bulleted, crisp.]

### 6.2 Out of Scope for MVP
[Bulleted. Each item with a one-line reason if the reason matters. Mark items deferred to v2/v3 explicitly. Add `[NOTE FOR PM]` callouts where a deferred item is emotionally load-bearing — flags it for revisit if timeline permits.]

## 7. Success Metrics

*Each SM cross-references the FR(s) it validates. Counter-metrics counterbalance specific primary or secondary metrics.*

**Primary**
- **SM-1**: Metric — definition, target. Validates FR-X, FR-Y.

**Secondary**
- **SM-2**: Metric — definition, target. Validates FR-Z.

**Counter-metrics (do not optimize)**
- **SM-C1**: Metric — why this should *not* be optimized. Counterbalances SM-1.

[Length scales with stakes. Hobby/utility PRD: a single sentence may be enough ("Success: I use this weekly and don't abandon it after a month"). Public launch / enterprise: full quantitative breakdown with measurement methods. Counter-metrics are as load-bearing as primary metrics — they prevent the architect from optimizing the wrong thing and the dev from gaming the wrong target.]

## 8. Open Questions
[Numbered. Things still unknown — they become future tickets or follow-up research, not silent gaps.]

## 9. Assumptions Index
*Every `[ASSUMPTION]` from the document, surfaced for explicit confirmation:*
- Inline assumption from §X.Y — short description.
- ...
```

---

## Adapt-In Menu *(add the clusters the product calls for)*

### Cross-cutting quality and shape *(most non-trivial PRDs)*
- **Cross-Cutting NFRs** — system-wide non-functional requirements not tied to a single feature (performance, security, reliability, observability). Add when system-wide quality attributes are meaningful.
- **Constraints and Guardrails** — Safety, Privacy, Cost. Subsection per cluster. Add when any of these are real concerns.
- **Why Now** — add when timing is load-bearing (a market shift, a technology enabler, a regulatory deadline). Drop when timing is incidental.

### Consumer / branded products
- **Aesthetic and Tone** — visual references, anti-references, voice/tone for any product-generated text.
- **Information Architecture** — top-level surfaces, navigation, screens.
- **Monetization** — free vs. paid, pricing assumptions, ads policy.
- **Platform** — web, mobile, PWA, native, v1 vs. v2+.

### Enterprise initiatives
- **Stakeholders and Approvals** — who must sign off, at what stage.
- **Risk and Mitigations** — operational, security, business, reputational risk register.
- **ROI / Business Case** — quantified benefit, cost, payback period.
- **Operational Requirements** — SLAs, RTO/RPO, support tier, on-call expectations.
- **Integration and Dependencies** — SSO, existing enterprise systems, data sources, downstream consumers.
- **Rollout and Change Management** — phased rollout plan, training, internal communication.
- **Data Governance** — residency, sovereignty, classification, retention.
- **Audit Trail / Decision Provenance** — formal documentation requirements for regulated environments.

### Regulated domains
- **Compliance and Regulatory** — HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR, SOX, SOC 2, Section 508 / WCAG 2.1 AA, FedRAMP, etc. — whichever apply. If any item needs depth, add a `[NOTE FOR PM]` callout to revisit or move to an addendum.

### Developer products (libraries, APIs, CLIs, SDKs)
- **API Contracts / Public Surface** — endpoint shapes, breaking change policy.
- **Versioning and Deprecation Policy**.
- **Performance Budgets** — latency, throughput, resource use.
- **Language / Runtime Targets and Dependency Policy**.

### Embedded / hardware
- **Hardware Constraints** — memory, power, form factor.
- **Deployment and Update Mechanism** — OTA, manual, image-based.
- **Environmental and Reliability Requirements**.

### Small-scope all-inclusive *(use when scope is 1-2 stories' worth and the user wants a single captured artifact — chosen during the Right-skill check in Discovery)*
- **Stories** — story-level specs listed inline at the end of the doc. Each story: *"As a [persona], I can [action] [under conditions]. Acceptance: [testable criteria]."* Numbered Story-1, Story-2, ... for reference. Pair with very lean §1 Vision, §2 Target User (often just JTBD + one UJ), §3 Glossary (handful of terms), §4 Features (often a single feature), §6 MVP Scope (in/out very tight). The whole doc fits on a page or two and captures intent + implementable stories in one place. If the user doesn't want the captured artifact at all, `bmad-build` is the better path — this cluster is only for "I want a doc *and* the stories."

content.content:
usage: memlog.py [-h] {init,append,set} ...

memlog — an append-only memory log: LLM-optimal working memory for a skill.

A memlog is the dense, chronological record of everything that mattered in a piece of
work — every item the user generated or accepted — kept minimal like human memory: only
what's important, never bloated. It persists ACROSS sessions, so a fresh session can

Hi Sherif 👋 — I'm set up to help you build a PRD.

**`_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01/`**

It persists — you can stop and pick this back up any time.

Two things before we dive in:

- At any point you can call **`bmad-party-mode`** for multi-agent perspectives, or **`bmad-advanced-elicitation`** to go deeper on a specific section.
- If a PRD isn't actually what you want: a game → **BMad GDS**; just build it → **`bmad-build`**; a one-pager → **`bmad-product-brief`**; pressure-test the idea first → **`bmad-prfaq`**; an agent/skill → **`bmad-workflow-builder`**.

---

### Brain dump — your turn

**Tell me about what you want to build.** Don't organize it. Ramble. Half-formed is fine — the messy version is more useful to me than a tidy summary.

Whatever comes to mind: what it is, who it's for, why it's bugging you enough to build it, what it should feel like, what you already know is hard about it.

**And — any existing inputs you want me to read?** Product brief, research notes, customer transcripts, competitive analysis, a prior PRD draft, design docs, Slack threads you pasted somewhere. Paths or pasted text both work; long documents are fine, I'll have subagents extract from them rather than reading them wholesale.

Then: **anything else?** — the thing you almost forgot usually matters.

---
title: Ledgerleaf
status: draft
created: 2026-10-01
updated: 2026-10-01
---

# PRD: Ledgerleaf
*Working title — confirm.*

> **Draft in progress.** Sections are written as they are worked. §0 Document Purpose is
> written last, once the final structure is settled.

## 1. Vision

Ledgerleaf is a budgeting app for two-person households that treats **mine**, **yours**, and
**ours** as three genuinely separate piles of money rather than one merged pot with labels on
it. Each partner keeps a personal ledger; the household keeps a shared one; money moves
between them by explicit transfer. At the end of each month Ledgerleaf computes who owes whom
on shared spending — under whatever split the couple agreed to, whether that is even, scaled
to income, or set per category — so the month closes with a single transfer instead of an
argument. Every closed month is kept as a record, so a disagreement about what was agreed is
settled by looking it up rather than by memory.

It is privacy-first by construction, not by policy. Ledgerleaf never asks for a bank
credential and never will. Transactions are entered by hand or imported from CSV/OFX files the
user already has. Data lives on the partners' own devices and syncs between them end-to-end
encrypted, so there is no readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to
mine or sell. Everything exports to CSV at any time, because a product that asks for trust
should be easy to leave.

The point is to retire the household accountant. Today one partner owns the spreadsheet,
maintains it, and resents it, while the other never opens it; bank-linked apps solve the effort
problem by exposing every transaction to both partners and monetising the data behind their
backs. Ledgerleaf takes the opposite trade — a little manual effort in exchange for fairness
and privacy. Six months in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant: the partner who never
opened the spreadsheet checks "can we afford this" before a big purchase on their own, settle-up
takes five minutes, and neither person feels surveilled by the other.

## 2. Target User

Two-adult households, roughly 25-45, both partners employed, with at least one irregular income
source — freelance, tips, or commission. They already share some expenses and deliberately keep
others separate.

**Primary — the spreadsheet keeper.** Owns and maintains the shared budget today. Competent with
it, and resents being the household's accountant. Does the imports, the categorising, and the
month-end reconciliation, and carries the social cost of raising it.

**Secondary — the partner who doesn't open it.** Not disengaged about money, just not willing to
operate someone else's spreadsheet. Wants a ten-second answer to "can we afford this" and to not
be surprised at month end.

### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done

- Keep personal and shared money genuinely separate without running two systems.
- Know in seconds whether a purchase fits, without opening a spreadsheet or doing arithmetic.
- Close out shared spending at month end without reconstructing who paid for what.
- Stop being the household accountant — or stop feeling managed by one.
- Spend personal money without feeling watched by a partner.
- Settle a disagreement about a past month by pointing at a record, not by recalling it.
- Budget against income that is not the same number every month.
- Use a money app without handing over bank credentials or becoming the product.

### 2.2 Non-Users (v1)

- **Solo budgeters.** The entire model is two-party; a single user has nothing to settle.
- **Households of more than two adults.** Roommate groups, multi-generational households.
- **People who want everything categorised automatically.** Ledgerleaf trades effort for privacy;
  that trade is the product, and it is the wrong trade for them.
- **Net-worth and investment trackers.** Ledgerleaf budgets cash flow; it does not track assets.

## 3. Glossary
*Seeded from the user's own vocabulary — to confirm and extend as Features are worked.
Downstream readers and workflows must use these terms exactly; no synonyms elsewhere in this PRD.*

- **Household** — the unit of account: exactly two Partners in v1. Owns three Ledgers.
- **Partner** — one of the two adults in a Household. Each has their own device(s).
- **Ledger** — a named pile of money holding Transactions. Exactly three per Household:
  two Personal Ledgers (one per Partner) and one Shared Ledger.
- **Personal Ledger** — a Partner's own money. One per Partner. *(Visibility boundary TBD.)*
- **Shared Ledger** — the Household's joint money. One per Household, visible to both Partners.
- **Transaction** — a single dated money movement in one Ledger, with amount, category, and note.
- **Transfer** — an explicit Transaction pair moving money between two Ledgers of the same Household.
- **Envelope** — a per-category budget allocation for a Period, with a balance that can roll over.
- **Rollover** — carrying an Envelope's unspent balance into the next Period.
- **Period** — a calendar month. The unit over which Envelopes are funded and Settle-Up runs.
- **Split Rule** — how a shared-category cost is divided between Partners: even, income-proportional,
  or a custom per-category ratio.
- **Settle-Up** — the end-of-Period computation of the net amount one Partner owes the other,
  derived from Shared Ledger spending and the applicable Split Rules.
- **Settlement** — the closed, immutable record of one Period's Settle-Up, retained as history.
EOF
echo written && wc -l "$WS/prd.md"

# PRD: Ledgerleaf
*Working title — confirm.*

> **Draft in progress.** Sections are written as they are worked. §0 Document Purpose is
> written last, once the final structure is settled.

## 1. Vision

Ledgerleaf is a budgeting app for two-person households that treats **mine**, **yours**, and
**ours** as three genuinely separate piles of money rather than one merged pot with labels on
it. Each partner keeps a personal ledger; the household keeps a shared one; money moves
between them by explicit transfer. At the end of each month Ledgerleaf computes who owes whom
on shared spending — under whatever split the couple agreed to, whether that is even, scaled
to income, or set per category — so the month closes with a single transfer instead of an
argument. Every closed month is kept as a record, so a disagreement about what was agreed is
settled by looking it up rather than by memory.

It is privacy-first by construction, not by policy. Ledgerleaf never asks for a bank
credential and never will. Transactions are entered by hand or imported from CSV/OFX files the
user already has. Data lives on the partners' own devices and syncs between them end-to-end
encrypted, so there is no readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to
mine or sell. Everything exports to CSV at any time, because a product that asks for trust
should be easy to leave.

The point is to retire the household accountant. Today one partner owns the spreadsheet,
maintains it, and resents it, while the other never opens it; bank-linked apps solve the effort
problem by exposing every transaction to both partners and monetising the data behind their
backs. Ledgerleaf takes the opposite trade — a little manual effort in exchange for fairness
and privacy. Six months in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant: the partner who never
opened the spreadsheet checks "can we afford this" before a big purchase on their own, settle-up
takes five minutes, and neither person feels surveilled by the other.

## 2. Target User

Two-adult households, roughly 25-45, both partners employed, with at least one irregular income
source — freelance, tips, or commission. They already share some expenses and deliberately keep
others separate.

**Primary — the spreadsheet keeper.** Owns and maintains the shared budget today. Competent with
it, and resents being the household's accountant. Does the imports, the categorising, and the
month-end reconciliation, and carries the social cost of raising it.

**Secondary — the partner who doesn't open it.** Not disengaged about money, just not willing to
operate someone else's spreadsheet. Wants a ten-second answer to "can we afford this" and to not
be surprised at month end.

### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done

- Keep personal and shared money genuinely separate without running two systems.
- Know in seconds whether a purchase fits, without opening a spreadsheet or doing arithmetic.
- Close out shared spending at month end without reconstructing who paid for what.
- Stop being the household accountant — or stop feeling managed by one.
- Spend personal money without feeling watched by a partner.
- Settle a disagreement about a past month by pointing at a record, not by recalling it.
- Budget against income that is not the same number every month.
- Use a money app without handing over bank credentials or becoming the product.

### 2.2 Non-Users (v1)

- **Solo budgeters.** The entire model is two-party; a single user has nothing to settle.
- **Households of more than two adults.** Roommate groups, multi-generational households.
- **People who want everything categorised automatically.** Ledgerleaf trades effort for privacy;
  that trade is the product, and it is the wrong trade for them.
- **Net-worth and investment trackers.** Ledgerleaf budgets cash flow; it does not track assets.

## 3. Glossary
*Seeded from the user's own vocabulary — to confirm and extend as Features are worked.
Downstream readers and workflows must use these terms exactly; no synonyms elsewhere in this PRD.*

- **Household** — the unit of account: exactly two Partners in v1. Owns three Ledgers.
- **Partner** — one of the two adults in a Household. Each has their own device(s).
- **Ledger** — a named pile of money holding Transactions. Exactly three per Household:
  two Personal Ledgers (one per Partner) and one Shared Ledger.
- **Personal Ledger** — a Partner's own money. One per Partner. *(Visibility boundary TBD.)*
- **Shared Ledger** — the Household's joint money. One per Household, visible to both Partners.
- **Transaction** — a single dated money movement in one Ledger, with amount, category, and note.
- **Transfer** — an explicit Transaction pair moving money between two Ledgers of the same Household.
- **Envelope** — a per-category budget allocation for a Period, with a balance that can roll over.
- **Rollover** — carrying an Envelope's unspent balance into the next Period.
- **Period** — a calendar month. The unit over which Envelopes are funded and Settle-Up runs.
- **Split Rule** — how a shared-category cost is divided between Partners: even, income-proportional,
  or a custom per-category ratio.
- **Settle-Up** — the end-of-Period computation of the net amount one Partner owes the other,
  derived from Shared Ledger spending and the applicable Split Rules.
- **Settlement** — the closed, immutable record of one Period's Settle-Up, retained as history.
EOF

Drafted and written to `prd.md` — §1 Vision, §2 Target User (+ JTBD, Non-Users), and a seeded §3 Glossary. Here's the Vision for you to confirm or redirect:

> **Ledgerleaf** is a budgeting app for two-person households that treats **mine**, **yours**, and **ours** as three genuinely separate piles of money rather than one merged pot with labels on it. Each partner keeps a personal ledger; the household keeps a shared one; money moves between them by explicit transfer. At the end of each month Ledgerleaf computes who owes whom on shared spending — under whatever split the couple agreed to — so the month closes with a single transfer instead of an argument. Every closed month is kept as a record, so a disagreement about what was agreed is settled by looking it up rather than by memory.
>
> It is privacy-first **by construction, not by policy**. Ledgerleaf never asks for a bank credential and never will. [...] there is no readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to mine or sell. Everything exports to CSV at any time, because a product that asks for trust should be easy to leave.
>
> The point is to **retire the household accountant**. [...] Ledgerleaf takes the opposite trade — a little manual effort in exchange for fairness and privacy. Six months in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant.

Two notes on what I did with your material:

- I folded **settle-up history** into paragraph 1 rather than treating it as a bolt-on — it reads as part of the core promise ("the argument is *over*"), not a feature you'd list separately.
- "Privacy-first by construction, not by policy" is my phrasing of your point. It's a claim the product has to actually honour, so flag it if it overreaches.

I also seeded a **Glossary** from your own vocabulary — Household, Partner, Ledger, Personal/Shared Ledger, Transaction, Transfer, Envelope, Rollover, Period, Split Rule, Settle-Up, Settlement. Skim it when you get a chance; renaming a term now is cheap and renaming it after the FRs are written is not.

---

## The thing I need before we can touch Features

You said: *"Both feel their personal spending is **private-ish**, not surveilled."*

**"Private-ish" is load-bearing and undefined**, and almost everything downstream hangs off it — the data model, what syncs between devices, what settle-up can show its work on, and honestly the trust proposition itself. I'm not going to pick for you. So:

**Sam and Alex are a Ledgerleaf household.** Sam opens the app and navigates toward Alex's personal ledger. **Walk me through what's on screen.** Nothing at all? A balance and no detail? Categories but not merchants? Everything, and "private" just means *nobody outside the household* sees it?

Two follow-ons in the same cluster, because they're the same question wearing different hats:

- **Income-proportional split needs to know both incomes.** Does Sam see what Alex earns — the number, a ratio, or nothing beyond "the split came out 58/42"?
- **Settle-up has to show its work** or nobody trusts it. If a shared expense was paid from Alex's personal money, Sam has to see *that* transaction to verify the math. Does the shared/personal boundary leak at exactly the moment the product is supposed to be building trust?

Answer however it comes out — I'll structure it. If your honest answer is "I don't know yet," say so and we'll walk the consequences of each end of the range instead.

*(Parked in the addendum, not forgotten: your desktop web app needs the decryption key in a browser while "keys never leave the devices." The crypto is architecture's problem — but **how the keeper authorises that browser** is a user-visible flow we'll need when we hit the import feature.)*

input.command:
WS=_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01 && cat >> "$WS/prd.md" <<'EOF'

## 4. Privacy Model
*Cross-cutting. Defines what each Partner can see of the other's money. Every FR that touches
visibility references this section rather than restating it.*

**Default — Personal Ledgers are private at the transaction level.** A Partner opening the
other's Personal Ledger sees nothing: no Transactions, no categories, and no balance total. The
absence is complete; there is no aggregate that hints at the detail.

**Disclosure is per-Transaction and owner-initiated.** A Transaction in a Personal Ledger becomes
visible to the other Partner in exactly two cases:

1. The owner explicitly tags it as shared.
2. It is the funding side of a shared expense — the owner paid a Shared Ledger cost from personal
   money.

In both cases exactly one Transaction is disclosed, carrying merchant, amount, and date. Nothing
else about the Personal Ledger — its balance, its other Transactions, its categories — is revealed
or inferable from the disclosure.

**Income is never disclosed; only its ratio is.** Each Partner enters their own income. It is
stored encrypted. An income-proportional Split Rule derives a ratio from the two figures, and only
that ratio and the resulting percentages (e.g. "58/42") are shared.

> `[NOTE FOR PM]` **The ratio leaks the income.** A Partner who knows their own income and sees
> "58/42" can solve for the other's figure exactly. As written, "income is never disclosed" holds
> literally but not in effect, and the PRD should not make a privacy promise the arithmetic
> breaks. Unresolved — see Open Questions.

**Settle-Up is the one place the boundary opens, deliberately.** Settle-Up shows its work: every
shared-category Transaction with who paid, plus any funded-from-personal Transactions as described
above. Without this, the computation is unverifiable and the product's central promise fails. The
Settle-Up surface states in plain words what is being disclosed and why, at the moment of
disclosure — the opening is never silent.
EOF

new = """- **Entry** — one real-world payment or receipt, recorded once. An Entry has a Payer and produces
  one or more Transactions. *(New term — introduced to model a single card payment split across
  Ledgers. Confirm the name.)*
- **Payer** — the Partner whose own money funded an Entry.
- **Transaction** — a single dated money movement in one Ledger, with amount, category, and note.
  Belongs to exactly one Entry.
"""
assert anchor in t
p.write_text(t.replace(anchor, new, 1))

cat >> "$WS/prd.md" <<'EOF'

## 5. Features

### 5.1 Ledgers & Transactions

**Description.** The spine of the product: three Ledgers per Household, and the act of putting
money into them. Recording a purchase is the single most repeated thing anyone does in
Ledgerleaf, so it is built for the hallway and the supermarket car park — one hand, under
fifteen seconds, no confirmation dialog standing between the user and being done.

The awkward case is the common one: one card payment covering both household and personal
spending. Ledgerleaf models this as a single **Entry** — one real-world payment, with one
**Payer** — that produces one or more **Transactions** across Ledgers. The payment is recorded
once and never double-counted, while each Ledger sees only its own share. When the Payer funded a
Shared Ledger cost from personal money, that is the funding-side disclosure described in §4, and
it surfaces at Settle-Up rather than in the other Partner's day-to-day view.

Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit **Transfer** — to fund shared Envelopes at the start
of a Period, or to reimburse. Transfers are never edited. A mistaken Transfer is corrected by a new,
opposite Transfer, so the history stays append-only and nobody can quietly rewrite what happened.
That property is load-bearing for the product's promise (§1): a Settlement nobody can retroactively
alter is the thing that ends the argument.

Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2 *(journeys captured later — IDs reserved)*.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-1: Quick-add an Entry

A Partner can record an Entry from the Household's primary surface in a single flow, supplying
amount and merchant, with the Ledger and category pre-filled from the most recent Entry.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The quick-add control is reachable in one tap from the app's default screen.
- Amount and merchant are the only required fields; Ledger and category are pre-filled and editable.
- The pre-filled Ledger is the one used by that Partner's most recent Entry.
- A single-Ledger Entry completes in under 15 seconds for a one-handed user, measured from tapping
  quick-add to the entry being committed.
- No confirmation dialog is presented at any point in the flow.

#### FR-2: Split an Entry across Ledgers

A Partner can allocate a single Entry across more than one Ledger, assigning an amount and a
category to each allocation.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Splitting is reachable from within the quick-add flow without discarding entered values.
- The sum of allocations must equal the Entry amount; the flow cannot be committed otherwise, and
  the shortfall or excess is shown.
- Each allocation carries its own category drawn from the Household category set.
- An Entry may allocate across any combination of the Household's three Ledgers.
- The Entry is counted once in reporting and export; allocations never double-count the payment.

#### FR-3: Record the Payer of an Entry

Every Entry records which Partner's money funded it, independently of which Ledgers the Entry
allocates to.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Payer defaults to the Partner recording the Entry and is editable within the flow.
- Where a Shared Ledger allocation has a Payer whose own money funded it, that allocation is marked
  as a funding-side disclosure and becomes visible to the other Partner at Settle-Up per §4,
  carrying merchant, amount, and date only.
- A funding-side disclosure reveals no other Transaction, balance, or category from the Payer's
  Personal Ledger.

#### FR-4: Undo a just-recorded Entry

A Partner can reverse an Entry immediately after recording it, without navigating away.

**Consequences (testable):**
- An undo affordance is presented for 10 seconds after an Entry is committed.
- Undo removes the Entry and all of its allocations.
- After the undo window closes, the affordance is dismissed and the Entry stands.

#### FR-5: Transfer between Ledgers

A Partner can move money between two Ledgers of their Household by recording a Transfer.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Transfer requires amount, from-Ledger, and to-Ledger; a note is optional. No other field is
  collected.
- A Transfer debits the from-Ledger and credits the to-Ledger by the same amount in one atomic act.
- Transfers into a Shared Envelope are reflected in that Envelope's available balance (see §5.3).

#### FR-6: Reverse a Transfer

A Partner can correct a mistaken Transfer by recording an opposite Transfer; Transfers are never
edited in place.

**Consequences (testable):**
- No edit or delete affordance is offered on a committed Transfer.
- A reverse action pre-fills an opposite Transfer with the original amount and Ledgers swapped.
- Both the original and the reversing Transfer remain in history and in export.

#### FR-7: Manage the Household category set

A Partner can rename, add, and archive categories in the single category set shared by all three of
the Household's Ledgers.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A new Household is created with a starter set of approximately 15 categories.
- A category can be renamed; existing Transactions follow the rename and are not re-categorised.
- A category can be archived; archived categories are unavailable for new Transactions and remain
  attached to historical ones.
- Categories cannot be deleted while any Transaction references them.
- Changes to the category set apply to the Household and are visible to both Partners.

#### FR-8: Hide categories from a Personal Ledger view

A Partner can hide categories from their own Personal Ledger view without removing them from the
Household category set.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Hiding is scoped to the hiding Partner's own view of their own Personal Ledger.
- A hidden category remains available in the Shared Ledger and in the other Partner's views.
- Hiding does not alter, move, or conceal any existing Transaction.

**Notes:**
- `[NOTE FOR PM]` Correcting an Entry after the 10-second undo window is undefined. See Open Questions.
- `[NOTE FOR PM]` The §4 "owner tags a Transaction as shared" disclosure route has no flow yet.
  See Open Questions.
EOF
echo appended && grep -c '^#### FR-' "$WS/prd.md"

+## 5. Features
+### 5.1 Ledgers & Transactions
+**Description.** The spine of the product: three Ledgers per Household, and the act of putting
+money into them. Recording a purchase is the single most repeated thing anyone does in
+Ledgerleaf, so it is built for the hallway and the supermarket car park — one hand, under
+fifteen seconds, no confirmation dialog standing between the user and being done.
+The awkward case is the common one: one card payment covering both household and personal
+spending. Ledgerleaf models this as a single **Entry** — one real-world payment, with one
+**Payer** — that produces one or more **Transactions** across Ledgers. The payment is recorded
+once and never double-counted, while each Ledger sees only its own share. When the Payer funded a
+Shared Ledger cost from personal money, that is the funding-side disclosure described in §4, and
+it surfaces at Settle-Up rather than in the other Partner's day-to-day view.
+Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit **Transfer** — to fund shared Envelopes at the start
+of a Period, or to reimburse. Transfers are never edited. A mistaken Transfer is corrected by a new,
+opposite Transfer, so the history stays append-only and nobody can quietly rewrite what happened.
+That property is load-bearing for the product's promise (§1): a Settlement nobody can retroactively
+alter is the thing that ends the argument.
+Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2 *(journeys captured later — IDs reserved)*.
+**Functional Requirements:**
+#### FR-1: Quick-add an Entry
+A Partner can record an Entry from the Household's primary surface in a single flow, supplying
+amount and merchant, with the Ledger and category pre-filled from the most recent Entry.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- The quick-add control is reachable in one tap from the app's default screen.
+- Amount and merchant are the only required fields; Ledger and category are pre-filled and editable.
+- The pre-filled Ledger is the one used by that Partner's most recent Entry.
+- A single-Ledger Entry completes in under 15 seconds for a one-handed user, measured from tapping
+  quick-add to the entry being committed.
+- No confirmation dialog is presented at any point in the flow.
+#### FR-2: Split an Entry across Ledgers
+A Partner can allocate a single Entry across more than one Ledger, assigning an amount and a
+category to each allocation.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Splitting is reachable from within the quick-add flow without discarding entered values.
+- The sum of allocations must equal the Entry amount; the flow cannot be committed otherwise, and
+  the shortfall or excess is shown.
+- Each allocation carries its own category drawn from the Household category set.
+- An Entry may allocate across any combination of the Household's three Ledgers.
+- The Entry is counted once in reporting and export; allocations never double-count the payment.
+#### FR-3: Record the Payer of an Entry
+Every Entry records which Partner's money funded it, independently of which Ledgers the Entry
+allocates to.

content.text:
**§5.1 written — FR-1 through FR-8.** The one place I had to invent rather than transcribe:

Your split-purchase story broke the Glossary. `Transaction` was defined as "a single dated money movement in **one** Ledger," but Alex's £62 is one card payment landing in two. So I added two nouns:

- **Entry** — one real-world payment, recorded once, with a **Payer**, producing one or more Transactions across Ledgers.
- **Payer** — the Partner whose own money funded it.

That keeps "the payment is counted once" enforceable (FR-2) and makes the funding-side disclosure fall out of the model instead of being a special case bolted on. **Confirm the names — `Entry` is the weakest part, and renaming costs nothing right now.**

Also made your "never edited, only reversed" explicit as FR-6, and wrote into the feature description *why* it's there — append-only history is what makes a Settlement un-rewritable, which is what ends the argument. It's a trust property, not a data-hygiene preference.

---

### Two gaps your story didn't cover — both flagged `[NOTE FOR PM]`

**1. Correcting an Entry after the 10 seconds are up.** You gave transfers a clean rule (reverse, never edit) but regular entries only got an undo toast. So: Alex typos £620 instead of £62, notices at bedtime. What happens? The honest options pull in different directions — strict append-only is consistent with the transfer rule and keeps the history bulletproof, but asking a consumer to "reverse and re-enter" for a typo is harsh. There may also be a distinction worth drawing between a *personal* transaction (nobody else's business, let them edit) and anything that has already hit settle-up (frozen). Your call.

**2. "Tag a transaction as shared" has no flow.** §4 names two disclosure routes. Alex's story only exercises one — the split, which puts the shared part straight into Ours at entry time. Does the *other* route — a transaction that's already sitting in a personal ledger, later marked shared — actually exist? If so, what's it for: retroactively catching something you forgot? And does it *move* to the Shared Ledger or stay personal and get counted at settle-up? If it doesn't exist, I'd rather delete it from §4 than carry an unimplemented promise.

---

### 5.5 — Settle-Up & Settlement History

The product's climax, and the most decision-dense thing in the document.

**It's the 1st of November. Narrate the close of October** — for both partners, since they probably don't experience it the same way. Who initiates, what's on screen, what does each person actually do, and where does it end? Carry it all the way through to money actually moving.

Then the parts that usually only surface when someone argues:

- **Disagreement.** Sam looks at the list and says "that £40 wasn't groceries for us, that was your work lunch." What does the product let Sam *do*? Is there a dispute mechanism, or is the answer "talk to each other, then one of you edits it"?
- **Closing.** Does a Settlement require both partners to accept, or can one person close the month? What makes it immutable — and is the *actual transfer* of money part of the close, or does the app just say "Alex owes Sam £137" and get out of the way?
- **The late transaction.** A receipt from 28 October gets entered on 3 November, after the close. Where does it go?

*(Written out of document order — features 5.2 through 5.4 follow. FR IDs are assigned in the order

**Description.** The moment the product earns its keep. From the 1st of a Period onward, either

Shared Ledger Transaction, who paid it, the Split Rule applied, the funded-from-personal ones marked
as such, and one number at the bottom — *"Alex owes Sam 137.00"*. This is the surface where the
privacy boundary deliberately opens, and per §4 it says so in plain words, where the user is looking.

Settle-Up is two-sided by design, because a number one person computed alone is exactly the
spreadsheet problem Ledgerleaf exists to retire. The initiator **Proposes**; the other Partner is
notified, reviews the same statement, and **Accepts**. Acceptance is always of the exact list on
screen — if anything underneath changes, the proposal is withdrawn and re-proposed automatically,
so nobody ever accepts a number that has since moved. On both accepts the Settlement is **sealed**:
immutable, retained in Settlement History with a hash of its contents.

Ledgerleaf does not move money, and does not want to. It says who owes whom and then gets out of
the way; the Partners pay each other however they already do. When that happens, the app offers to
record it as a Transfer. **The Settlement closes on both accepts, not on payment** — the agreement
and the money are separate acts, and conflating them would let an unpaid debt hold the next month
hostage.

There is no dispute mechanism in v1, deliberately. Disagreement is a conversation between two people
who live together, not a workflow. Tapping any line offers **ask about this**, which attaches a note
to that Transaction for the other Partner; whoever entered it then edits it while the Period is
still open, and the proposal re-forms around the corrected figure. The product carries the question;
the couple settles it.

Settled Periods are never reopened. A Transaction dated inside a sealed Period but entered after it
closed lands in the current Period, flagged with its true date, and settles there.

Realizes UJ-3, UJ-4 *(journeys captured later — IDs reserved)*.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-12: Configure Split Rules

A Household can set how shared costs divide between Partners, as a default and per category.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Household default Split Rule is one of: even, income-proportional, or a custom ratio.
- Any category can carry a Split Rule overriding the Household default.
- Selecting income-proportional presents the §4 disclosure statement that it reveals relative income
  before it can be applied.
- Each Partner enters their own income; neither figure is transmitted to the other Partner.
- A change to a Split Rule applies to the open Period onward and never alters a sealed Settlement.

#### FR-13: Open the Settle-Up statement for a closed Period

Either Partner can open Settle-Up for a Period from its first day onward.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Settle-Up for a Period is available from the first day of the following Period.
- The statement lists every Shared Ledger Transaction in the Period with date, merchant, amount,
  category, Payer, and the Split Rule applied.
- Funded-from-personal Transactions are visually marked as such.
- The statement resolves to a single net figure naming the owing Partner and the amount.
- The statement states, in plain language and on the statement itself, what is being disclosed and why.

#### FR-14: Propose a Settlement

A Partner can propose the statement to the other Partner for acceptance.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Proposing notifies the other Partner.
- A proposal is bound to the exact contents of the statement at the moment it was proposed.
- Either Partner may be the initiator; the role is not fixed to one Partner.

#### FR-15: Accept a Settlement

The non-initiating Partner can accept the proposed statement, sealing it.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The accepting Partner sees the same statement the initiator proposed, line for line.
- A Settlement seals only when both Partners have accepted.
- On sealing, the Settlement becomes immutable and is written to Settlement History with a hash of
  its contents.
- Every Transaction drawn into a sealed Settlement becomes frozen per FR-9.

#### FR-16: Auto-withdraw a proposal on change

A proposal is withdrawn and re-formed whenever the data beneath it changes.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Any change to a Transaction, Split Rule, or category affecting the Period withdraws an outstanding
  proposal.
- A withdrawn proposal is re-proposed automatically against the updated statement.
- Both Partners are notified that the proposal changed and why.
- No acceptance ever carries over from a withdrawn proposal to its replacement.

#### FR-17: Ask about a line

A Partner can attach a question to any Transaction on the statement.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Ask-about is available from any line of the Settle-Up statement.
- The note is attached to that Transaction and the other Partner is notified.
- Asking does not block, reject, or alter the proposal.
- Notes are visible to both Partners on the Transaction and are retained in Settlement History.

#### FR-18: Record the settling Transfer

After a Settlement is sealed, a Partner can record the real-world payment as a Transfer.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Ledgerleaf initiates no payment and holds no payment credential.
- A sealed Settlement offers to record a Transfer pre-filled with the settled amount and Partners.
- Recording the Transfer is optional and may be done at any time after sealing.
- A Settlement's sealed state is unaffected by whether its Transfer was recorded.

#### FR-19: Review Settlement History

Either Partner can read any sealed Settlement from any past Period.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Every sealed Settlement is retained for the life of the Household.
- A historical Settlement renders the statement as it was sealed, including Payers, Split Rules
  applied, and any attached notes.
- A historical Settlement displays its content hash.
- No affordance edits, deletes, or reopens a sealed Settlement.
- Settlement History is included in CSV export (§5.7).

#### FR-20: Place a back-dated Transaction

A Transaction dated within a sealed Period but entered after it sealed is carried into the open
Period.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The Transaction is recorded in the open Period and settles there.
- The Transaction retains and displays its true date, flagged as dated outside the Period.
- No sealed Period is reopened, recomputed, or amended.

#### FR-21: Correct a sealed Entry by adjustment

A Partner can correct an error inside a sealed Settlement by recording an offsetting adjustment in
the open Period.

**Consequences (testable):**
- An adjustment is a Shared Ledger Transaction referencing the Settlement and Transaction it corrects.
- An adjustment settles in the Period it was recorded in, not the one it corrects.
- The original sealed Settlement is unchanged, and both figures remain visible in history.
EOF

content.text:
**§5.5 written — FR-12 through FR-21.** (FR IDs run in the order we're working, not document order; I've noted in the doc that they get renumbered once all features exist. Nothing downstream references them yet, so it's free.)

The line I wrote that I want you to check, because it's a product philosophy and not just a requirement:

> There is no dispute mechanism in v1, **deliberately**. Disagreement is a conversation between two people who live together, not a workflow. [...] The product carries the question; the couple settles it.

And on keeping the close separate from the payment, I gave your decision a reason it can be defended with: *conflating them would let an unpaid debt hold the next month hostage.* Correct me if your reasoning was different.

---

## The one thing that worries me about 5.5

**Nothing seals without partner #2 tapping Accept.**

Partner #2 is, by your own definition, the person who never opened the spreadsheet. You've put your product's central ceremony behind their active participation. That's defensible — two-sidedness *is* the point, and a number one person computed alone is the thing you're fleeing. But it means the failure you're trying to design out is now the failure that jams the mechanism.

Three sharp edges, and FR-16 makes the first two worse:

- **The stall.** Sam proposes on 1 November. Alex doesn't open the app. What is true on 15 November? Is October just... open, indefinitely? Does anything nudge, escalate, expire, or auto-accept?
- **Can November close if October never sealed?** If settlements must seal in order, one unresponsive month blocks the product forever. If they can seal out of order, what does "Alex owes Sam" even mean when two months are outstanding?
- **Notification fatigue, self-inflicted.** FR-16 auto-withdraws and re-proposes on *any* change. The keeper tidying October's data across three evenings re-pings Alex six times. You will train the exact person you need to respond to ignore your notifications. Worth a debounce, a quiet window, or restricting re-propose to material changes — but that's a product call, so I'm leaving FR-16 as you specified it and flagging this rather than quietly softening it.

**None of these need answering now** — they're logged and I'll carry them into Open Questions. But the first two are phase-blockers in my view: architecture can't model period state without knowing whether periods can seal out of order.

---

### 5.2 — Household Setup & Pairing

Which lands us neatly on the same theme.

**Sam has installed Ledgerleaf, paid, and wants Alex in.** Narrate it — from Sam's first launch to the moment the household is genuinely two-sided. What does Sam do, what does Alex *receive*, and what does Alex have to do before they're useful?

The parts that tend to bite:

- **The cold-start gap.** Between "Sam installed it" and "Alex accepted" — is Ledgerleaf usable, degraded, or inert? Can Sam enter a month of transactions solo and have them be there when Alex joins?
- **Paying.** One subscription per household or per person? Who's billed, and what happens to the household if that person stops paying?
- **The browser.** You parked this earlier and now it's due: the desktop web app needs the key, but keys never leave devices. What does Sam actually *do* to get a browser session working — and is that per-session or once?

#### FR-22: Remind on a stalled proposal

An outstanding proposal prompts the Partner it is waiting on, without ever resolving itself.

**Consequences (testable):**
- One reminder is sent to the non-accepting Partner 7 days after the proposal, and a second at 14 days.
- No further reminders are sent after the second.
- A proposal never auto-accepts and never expires.
- The Period remains open and is labelled as waiting on the named Partner, to both Partners.

#### FR-23: Seal Periods in order

Settlements seal oldest first; a later Period cannot be proposed while an earlier one is unsealed.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Period cannot be proposed while any earlier Period is unsealed.
- A Period with an unsealed predecessor remains fully usable: Entries, imports, Transfers, and
  Envelope activity all continue normally.
- The blocking Period is named where the later Period's Settle-Up would otherwise be offered.

#### FR-24: Carry an unsealed Period forward

Both Partners can agree to merge an unsealed Period into the following one and settle them together.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Carry-forward is offered on a Period that has an outstanding or unproposed Settle-Up.
- Carry-forward requires both Partners to accept, like any Settlement.
- The resulting Settlement covers every Period merged into it and names them.
- Carried Periods produce no separate Settlement of their own and are marked as carried in history.
- Carry-forward may chain, merging more than two Periods.

### 5.2 Household Setup & Pairing

**Description.** Ledgerleaf is worth nothing as a single-player app, so pairing is not onboarding
plumbing — it is the feature on which the product's stated success metric rests. The failure mode is
known by name: the partner who never opened the spreadsheet never opens this either.

One Partner creates the Household and subscribes; billing is one subscription per Household through
the app store. They can then use Ledgerleaf fully alone — entering and importing a whole Period of
Transactions — so the product is useful before it is two-sided and nobody has to sell their partner
on an empty app. That solo work syncs across when the second Partner joins, and the first Partner's
Personal Ledger stays private from the first day, exactly as §4 describes; nothing becomes visible in
retrospect because a second person arrived.

Pairing is deliberately physical. An invite produces a QR code and a one-time link valid for 24 hours;
the key exchange runs device-to-device, and both phones must display the same short verification code
before anyone joins. A pairing that cannot be verified does not complete. The joining Partner sets
their own passcode or biometric — each Partner holds their own device credentials, and neither can
unlock the other's phone into the app.

The desktop web app is reached the same way. The browser shows a QR code, the Partner scans it from
the phone, and the phone hands that browser session its keys. The session is per-browser and
short-lived — it expires after 12 hours idle or when the tab closes — and the phone can revoke it at
any moment. Each Partner authorises their own browser, and a browser session sees only what that
Partner can see; the web surface is not a back door around §4.

Realizes UJ-5 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-25: Create a Household and subscribe

A Partner can create a Household and start its subscription.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Creating a Household provisions its three Ledgers and the starter category set (FR-7).
- A Household carries exactly one subscription, billed to the creating Partner through the platform
  app store.
- A Household supports exactly two Partners.

#### FR-26: Degrade a Household on lapsed subscription

A Household whose subscription lapses becomes read-only rather than inaccessible.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A lapsed subscription starts a 30-day grace period during which the Household functions normally.
- After the grace period the Household is read-only for both Partners: no new Entries, Transfers,
  proposals, or Settlements.
- Export (§5.7) remains available in full while read-only.
- Restoring the subscription restores write access without data loss.

#### FR-27: Invite the second Partner

A Partner can invite one other person to join their Household.

**Consequences (testable):**
- An invite presents both a QR code and a one-time link.
- An invite is valid for 24 hours and for a single use.
- An invite that is used, expired, or revoked cannot be reused.
- A Household already holding two Partners cannot issue an invite.

#### FR-28: Pair devices with verified key exchange

Joining a Household exchanges keys device-to-device and requires both Partners to confirm a matching
verification code.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Key material is exchanged between the two devices; no server holds a readable copy.
- Both devices display a short verification code during pairing.
- Pairing completes only when both Partners confirm the codes match.
- A mismatch or declined confirmation aborts pairing, and the invite is consumed.
- The joining Partner sets their own device passcode or biometric, independent of the inviter's.

#### FR-29: Use a Household solo before pairing

The founding Partner can use Ledgerleaf fully before a second Partner joins.

**Consequences (testable):**
- All Entry, import, Transfer, and Envelope capability is available with one Partner.
- Work done solo syncs to the second Partner on joining.
- The founding Partner's Personal Ledger Transactions remain private on joining, per §4; none become
  visible retroactively.
- Settle-Up cannot be proposed until a second Partner has joined.

#### FR-30: Onboard the joining Partner

The second Partner reaches a useful state immediately on joining.

**Consequences (testable):**
- On first run the joining Partner sees the Shared Ledger and their own, empty, Personal Ledger.
- The joining Partner is prompted to enter their income for the Split Rule as their first action.
- The joining Partner can skip the income prompt and supply it later; income is required only to
  apply an income-proportional Split Rule.
- The joining Partner sees no Transaction, balance, or category from the other Partner's Personal
  Ledger.

#### FR-31: Authorise a browser session

A Partner can grant a desktop browser temporary access to their view of the Household.

**Consequences (testable):**
- The web app presents a QR code to an unauthorised browser.
- Scanning it from the phone app under Settings grants that browser session its keys, delivered
  encrypted.
- A session expires after 12 hours idle, and on closing the tab.
- A browser session exposes only what the authorising Partner can see; it is not a route around §4.
- Each Partner authorises their own browser sessions independently.

#### FR-32: Revoke a browser session

A Partner can end an authorised browser session from their phone at any time.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Active sessions are listed in the phone app with their start time.
- Revoking a session ends its access without waiting for expiry.
- A revoked session cannot be resumed and must be re-authorised by QR.
EOF

content.text:
**§5.2 written — FR-25 through FR-32** — plus the three 5.5 edges closed as FR-22 (reminders), FR-23 (seal in order), FR-24 (carry forward), and FR-16 relaxed to material-changes-only with daily notification batching.

Transport details went to the addendum: key-exchange protocol, what the verification code actually defeats, how browser keys live for a session, and **what the Settlement content hash covers and proves to whom** — the PRD promises it's displayed, which is a claim architecture has to make good on.

---

## Two things 5.2 surfaced that I don't think you've decided

**1. Sam's lapsed card makes Alex's private ledger read-only.**

FR-26 as you specified it: one subscription, billed to Sam, lapse → *both* partners read-only. So Alex's own personal ledger — the one Sam is constitutionally forbidden from seeing — freezes because of Sam's expired card. In a product whose pitch is **fairness** and **not being dependent on the partner who owns the system**, that's the spreadsheet problem wearing a new hat. Alex has no agency over their own data.

And the obvious fix is genuinely hard: app-store subscriptions are bound to an Apple/Google account, so "Alex takes over billing" isn't a settings toggle. I'd rather you decide this than have me pick. **Live with it, or is there a floor — e.g. a lapsed household stays read-only for shared data but each partner keeps writing their own personal ledger?**

**2. The household ends. Nothing in the PRD knows that.**

You're building a two-person financial app for couples. Couples break up. Right now the document has no concept of dissolution: no way to remove a partner, split the data, or stop syncing. Three distinct questions, and they're not all equal:

- **Mundane:** can a household be dissolved, and does each partner walk away with a usable copy?
- **Who keeps settlement history?** It's immutable, jointly accepted, and may be the only record of who paid what — which is exactly the thing people want during a separation.
- **The one I'd push you hardest on:** a privacy-first money app for couples, with device pairing and sync, has a safety surface. Someone may need to leave *quickly and unilaterally* — revoke their partner's access to shared data, stop syncing, take their ledger and go, without the other party's cooperation. FR-28 requires *both* partners to confirm a pairing. Does anything let one partner end it alone?

"Out of scope for v1" is a legitimate answer to all three — but it should be an **explicit non-goal you chose**, not a gap. The third one I'd want written down either way, even if the v1 answer is just "delete the app and export your data," because a reviewer will ask.

---

### 5.3 — Envelope Budgeting

**It's the 1st. Sam sits down to set up the month's budget.** Walk me through it — what Sam is looking at, what Sam decides, and what the household's envelopes look like when Sam's done.

Then the one you planted in your own persona and haven't cashed yet:

- **Irregular income.** You defined your user as "at least one irregular income source." Envelope budgeting classically assumes you know what's coming in. Alex freelances — some months £1,800, some months £5,000, and in March they don't know until the 20th. **What does Ledgerleaf do with that?** Does Sam budget against last month's actual, a conservative floor, nothing at all until money lands? This is the hardest unsolved thing in the product, and you picked the persona on purpose — so I suspect you have a view.
- **Rollover and ours.** Do all three ledgers have envelopes, or only Ours? And when a shared envelope rolls over with £40 left, whose £40 is that at settle-up?

cat >> "$WS/prd.md" <<'EOF'

#### FR-33: Dissolve a Household unilaterally

Either Partner can end the Household alone and immediately.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Dissolution requires the action of one Partner only; the other's consent is neither sought nor required.
- Dissolution takes effect immediately on the acting Partner's device and is not reversible.
- Sync of the Shared Ledger between the two devices stops; neither Partner receives the other's
  subsequent changes.
- The remaining Partner is informed that the Household was dissolved, and is given no reason, no
  attribution, and no further detail.
- No notification, record, or export discloses where either Partner was when they acted.

#### FR-34: Retain data through dissolution

Each Partner keeps a usable copy of everything they could see.

**Consequences (testable):**
- After dissolution each Partner can export the Shared Ledger as it stood, their own Personal Ledger,
  and all sealed Settlements, as CSV.
- Each Partner's Personal Ledger remains private to them through and after dissolution.
- Sealed Settlements remain intact and readable in both Partners' exports.
- Ledgerleaf divides no balances, allocates no assets, and proposes no final reckoning.

### 5.3 Envelope Budgeting

**Description.** Envelopes are how a Household decides what money is *for* before it is spent, and
they are what makes §5.6 answerable in ten seconds. On the 1st, a Partner opens **This month** and
sees the envelope list: category, planned amount, rolled-over amount, spent, and left. Setting up a
month is mostly not a decision — **copy last month** is one tap and is the path most months take.

Envelopes exist on the Shared Ledger and on each Partner's own Personal Ledger. Personal envelopes
are private to their owner under §4 in exactly the way personal Transactions are: the other Partner
sees no personal envelope, its planned amount, or its balance.

Irregular income is handled by refusing to pretend. The Household sets a conservative **Floor** —
defaulting to the lowest of the last six months of income, each Partner entering their own — and
envelopes are funded against the Floor. Income arriving above the Floor does not get budgeted in
advance; it lands in the **Unallocated Pool** and is assigned when it exists, never before. A
freelancer's good month is not a promise, and Ledgerleaf will not spend it until it has arrived.

Rollover is chosen per envelope: carry the unspent balance forward, or reset to zero. A Shared
envelope that rolls over keeps its balance in Ours, owned by the Household, and is never attributed
to either Partner at Settle-Up — Settle-Up compares what each Partner *paid* against their share of
what was *spent*, and balances do not enter into it.

Realizes UJ-6 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.

#### FR-35: View the Period's envelopes

A Partner can see the state of every envelope they are entitled to see for the open Period.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Each envelope displays category, planned amount, rolled-over amount, spent, and remaining.
- Shared envelopes are visible to both Partners.
- A Partner's Personal Ledger envelopes are visible only to that Partner, per §4.
- The view is scoped to one Period.

#### FR-36: Create and fund envelopes

A Partner can create an envelope against a category and set its planned amount for the Period.

**Consequences (testable):**
- An envelope is created against a category from the Household category set (FR-7).
- A Ledger holds at most one envelope per category per Period.
- Shared envelopes may be created or changed by either Partner.
- A Personal Ledger envelope may be created or changed only by its owner.
- Total planned across Shared envelopes may exceed the Floor; the shortfall is shown rather than blocked.

#### FR-37: Copy the previous Period's envelopes

A Partner can populate the open Period from the one before it in a single action.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Copy carries each envelope's category and planned amount forward.
- Copy carries no spent amounts.
- Copying is available for Shared envelopes and, separately, for the acting Partner's own Personal
  envelopes.
- Copy over an already-populated Period is offered only as an explicit replace.

#### FR-38: Set per-envelope rollover

Each envelope carries its own rollover behaviour.

**Consequences (testable):**
- An envelope is set either to roll its remaining balance into the next Period or to reset to zero.
- Rollover behaviour is per envelope, not per Ledger or per Household.
- A rolled-over Shared envelope balance remains in the Shared Ledger, owned by the Household.
- A rolled-over balance is excluded from Settle-Up and is attributed to neither Partner.

#### FR-39: Set the Household income Floor

The Household sets the conservative income figure that envelopes are funded against.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Each Partner enters their own income history; the Floor defaults to the lowest of the last six
  months of combined income.
- The Floor is editable by either Partner. `[ASSUMPTION: either Partner may change the Floor, since
  it governs shared budgeting. Confirm — it may warrant both Partners' agreement.]`
- Individual income figures are never disclosed to the other Partner, per §4; only the Floor and any

- Changing the Floor affects the open Period onward and never a sealed Settlement.

#### FR-40: Hold above-Floor income in the Unallocated Pool

Income above the Floor is not budgeted until it has arrived.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Income recorded above the Floor accrues to the Unallocated Pool rather than to any envelope.
- The Unallocated Pool is not committed to any category and is shown as unassigned.
- No envelope can be funded from income that has not been recorded.
- `[ASSUMPTION: the Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool visible to both Partners, and each
  Personal Ledger has its own, private to its owner. Confirm.]`

#### FR-41: Assign from the Unallocated Pool

A Partner can move money from the Unallocated Pool into envelopes once it exists.

**Consequences (testable):**
- Assignment moves an amount from the Pool to a named envelope in the same Ledger.
- Assignment cannot exceed the Pool's balance.
- Shared Pool assignment is available to either Partner; a Personal Pool only to its owner.
- An unassigned Pool balance carries into the next Period rather than lapsing.
