+sees no personal envelope, its planned amount, or its balance.
+Irregular income is handled by refusing to pretend. The Household sets a conservative **Floor** —
+defaulting to the lowest of the last six months of income, each Partner entering their own — and
+envelopes are funded against the Floor. Income arriving above the Floor does not get budgeted in
+advance; it lands in the **Unallocated Pool** and is assigned when it exists, never before. A
+freelancer's good month is not a promise, and Ledgerleaf will not spend it until it has arrived.
+Rollover is chosen per envelope: carry the unspent balance forward, or reset to zero. A Shared
+envelope that rolls over keeps its balance in Ours, owned by the Household, and is never attributed
+to either Partner at Settle-Up — Settle-Up compares what each Partner *paid* against their share of
+what was *spent*, and balances do not enter into it.
+Realizes UJ-6 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.
+**Functional Requirements:**
+#### FR-35: View the Period's envelopes
+A Partner can see the state of every envelope they are entitled to see for the open Period.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Each envelope displays category, planned amount, rolled-over amount, spent, and remaining.
+- Shared envelopes are visible to both Partners.
+- A Partner's Personal Ledger envelopes are visible only to that Partner, per §4.
+- The view is scoped to one Period.
+#### FR-36: Create and fund envelopes
+A Partner can create an envelope against a category and set its planned amount for the Period.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- An envelope is created against a category from the Household category set (FR-7).
+- A Ledger holds at most one envelope per category per Period.
+- Shared envelopes may be created or changed by either Partner.
+- A Personal Ledger envelope may be created or changed only by its owner.
+- Total planned across Shared envelopes may exceed the Floor; the shortfall is shown rather than blocked.
+#### FR-37: Copy the previous Period's envelopes
+A Partner can populate the open Period from the one before it in a single action.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Copy carries each envelope's category and planned amount forward.
+- Copy carries no spent amounts.
+- Copying is available for Shared envelopes and, separately, for the acting Partner's own Personal
+  envelopes.
+- Copy over an already-populated Period is offered only as an explicit replace.
+#### FR-38: Set per-envelope rollover
+Each envelope carries its own rollover behaviour.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- An envelope is set either to roll its remaining balance into the next Period or to reset to zero.
+- Rollover behaviour is per envelope, not per Ledger or per Household.
+- A rolled-over Shared envelope balance remains in the Shared Ledger, owned by the Household.
+- A rolled-over balance is excluded from Settle-Up and is attributed to neither Partner.
+#### FR-39: Set the Household income Floor
+The Household sets the conservative income figure that envelopes are funded against.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Each Partner enters their own income history; the Floor defaults to the lowest of the last six
+  months of combined income.
+- The Floor is editable by either Partner. `[ASSUMPTION: either Partner may change the Floor, since
+  it governs shared budgeting. Confirm — it may warrant both Partners' agreement.]`
+- Individual income figures are never disclosed to the other Partner, per §4; only the Floor and any
+  derived ratio are shared.
+- Changing the Floor affects the open Period onward and never a sealed Settlement.
+#### FR-40: Hold above-Floor income in the Unallocated Pool
+Income above the Floor is not budgeted until it has arrived.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Income recorded above the Floor accrues to the Unallocated Pool rather than to any envelope.
+- The Unallocated Pool is not committed to any category and is shown as unassigned.
+- No envelope can be funded from income that has not been recorded.
+- `[ASSUMPTION: the Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool visible to both Partners, and each
+  Personal Ledger has its own, private to its owner. Confirm.]`
+#### FR-41: Assign from the Unallocated Pool
+A Partner can move money from the Unallocated Pool into envelopes once it exists.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Assignment moves an amount from the Pool to a named envelope in the same Ledger.
+- Assignment cannot exceed the Pool's balance.
+- Shared Pool assignment is available to either Partner; a Personal Pool only to its owner.
+- An unassigned Pool balance carries into the next Period rather than lapsing.
+### 5.4 Statement Import
+*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*
+**Description.** Ledgerleaf will never ask for a bank credential, so the bridge between a bank and a
+Ledger is a file the Partner already has the right to download. Import accepts CSV and OFX. It is a
+desk activity — reconciling a month of rows is miserable on a phone — so it lives on the desktop web
+surface. `[ASSUMPTION: import is desktop-web only in v1 and is not offered on the phone. Confirm;
+phone-side import is a plausible v1 inclusion.]`
+Import is staged, never silent. A file is parsed into a review list, and nothing reaches a Ledger
+until the Partner commits it. Rows land by default in the importing Partner's own Personal Ledger —
+a bank statement is one person's account, and §4 says that is private — and the Partner then marks
+individual rows as shared via FR-10, which is precisely the retroactive catch-up path that FR-10
+exists for. `[ASSUMPTION: default destination is the importer's Personal Ledger, with per-row
+reassignment to any Ledger during review.]`
+Banks disagree about everything, so CSV column mapping is per source and remembered. OFX carries its
+own structure and needs no mapping. `[ASSUMPTION: saved mappings are named by the Partner and reused
+on subsequent imports from the same bank.]`
+Duplicates are the failure that destroys trust in an import, and overlapping statement downloads make
+them routine. Ledgerleaf flags likely duplicates rather than deciding alone. `[ASSUMPTION: a row is
+flagged as a likely duplicate when an existing Transaction shares its amount and falls within a few
+days of its date; the Partner confirms or dismisses each flag, and nothing is auto-discarded.]`
+Realizes UJ-7 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.
+**Functional Requirements:**
+#### FR-42: Import a CSV or OFX file
+A Partner can load a statement file into a staged review list.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- CSV and OFX are accepted; no other format is.
+- No bank credential is requested, stored, or transmitted at any point.
+- Import is available on the desktop web surface to an authorised browser session (FR-31).
+- A file that cannot be parsed is rejected with the reason, and nothing is staged.
+#### FR-43: Map CSV columns to fields
+A Partner can tell Ledgerleaf which columns of a CSV mean what.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Date, amount, and description can each be mapped to a column.
+- A mapping can be saved under a name and reapplied to later imports.
+- A saved mapping is applied automatically when a file's header matches it.
+- OFX files require no mapping.
+#### FR-44: Review staged rows before committing
+Nothing enters a Ledger until the Partner commits it.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Staged rows are listed with date, amount, description, and destination Ledger and category.
+- Each row's destination Ledger and category can be changed before commit.
+- Rows can be excluded individually.
+- Abandoning a review discards the staged rows and changes no Ledger.
+- Committing creates one Entry per committed row, with the importing Partner as Payer.
+#### FR-45: Flag likely duplicates
+Re-importing an overlapping statement does not silently double-count.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- A staged row matching an existing Transaction on amount and within a small date window is flagged.
+- A flagged row is shown alongside the Transaction it may duplicate.
+- No flagged row is discarded automatically; the Partner confirms or dismisses each.
+- Dismissing a flag commits the row normally.
+#### FR-46: Default imported rows to the importer's Personal Ledger
+Imported rows are private until their owner says otherwise.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Committed rows default to the importing Partner's own Personal Ledger.
+- Imported Personal Ledger Transactions are invisible to the other Partner per §4.
+- A row can be reassigned to the Shared Ledger during review, or marked shared afterwards via FR-10.
+### 5.6 Can We Afford It
+*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*
+**Description.** This feature is the whole of the secondary Partner's relationship with Ledgerleaf.
+They are standing in a shop. They have a number in their head. They want to know whether it fits,
+and they want to know in ten seconds without being lectured.
+So it is one tap from opening the app, it takes an amount and a category, and it answers from the
+relevant envelope's remaining balance. `[ASSUMPTION: the check is reachable from the app's default
+screen without navigating into a Ledger.]`
+It reports rather than rules. Ledgerleaf shows what the envelope has left and what would remain after
+the purchase; it does not render a verdict. `[ASSUMPTION: no yes/no judgement is displayed. A product
+built to retire the household accountant should not install a new one — but this is a design call,
+so confirm.]` The decision stays with the person holding the card.
+Visibility follows §4 without exception: checking against a Shared envelope is available to both
+Partners, checking against a Personal envelope only to its owner. `[ASSUMPTION: the check reads only
+envelope balances and ignores both the Unallocated Pool and any outstanding Settlement debt, which
+would otherwise leak settle-up state into a glance.]`
+Realizes UJ-2 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.
+**Functional Requirements:**
+#### FR-47: Check an amount against an envelope
+A Partner can test a prospective purchase against the envelope that would fund it.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- The check is reachable in one tap from the app's default screen.
+- It takes an amount and a category and requires nothing else.
+- It reports the envelope's remaining balance and the balance that would remain after the amount.
+- It displays no approval, refusal, or other verdict.
+- It records nothing; running a check creates no Entry and leaves no trace for the other Partner.
+#### FR-48: Scope the check to visible envelopes
+The check obeys the privacy boundary.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Shared envelopes are checkable by both Partners.
+- A Personal Ledger envelope is checkable only by its owner.
+- A check against a Shared envelope reveals no Personal Ledger state of either Partner.
+- The check draws on envelope balances only, and not on the Unallocated Pool or any unsettled amount.
+### 5.7 Data Ownership & Recovery
+*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*
+**Description.** Ledgerleaf asks for trust, so it is built to be easy to leave. Everything a Partner
+can see, they can export as CSV, at any time, without asking anyone — including while the Household
+is read-only on a lapsed subscription, and including after dissolution. A product that holds data
+hostage has not earned the privacy claim in §1.
+The hard edge of end-to-end encryption is recovery. Keys live on devices; the operator holds nothing
+readable and therefore can restore nothing. `[ASSUMPTION: a Partner who loses their only device can
+recover the Shared Ledger by re-pairing with the other Partner's device, but their own Personal
+Ledger is unrecoverable unless they hold a second device or an export. This is a severe consequence
+with real product surface and is not yet decided — see Open Questions.]`
+`[ASSUMPTION: v1 supports one device per Partner, plus browser sessions. Multi-device for a single
+Partner — phone and tablet — is not in v1. Confirm; this assumption also decides whether the recovery
+story above has an answer.]`
+Realizes UJ-8 *(journey captured later — ID reserved)*.
+**Functional Requirements:**
+#### FR-49: Export everything to CSV
+A Partner can export the full contents of what they can see.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Export covers the Shared Ledger, the exporting Partner's own Personal Ledger, all envelopes they
+  can see, the category set, and all sealed Settlements.
+- Export never includes any part of the other Partner's Personal Ledger.
+- Export is available at any time, without the other Partner's involvement or knowledge.
+- Export remains available while the Household is read-only (FR-26) and after dissolution (FR-34).
+- Exported Settlements carry their content hash.
+#### FR-50: Recover a Household on a replacement device
+A Partner who loses a device can return to their Household.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- A replacement device re-pairs through the verification flow of FR-28.
+- Re-pairing restores the Shared Ledger from the other Partner's device.
+- The operator cannot restore any data, and the product states this plainly before it is relied on.
+- `[ASSUMPTION: the lost device's Personal Ledger is not recoverable through re-pairing. The product
+  must say so before a Partner depends on it, and may need to prompt for periodic export as the only
+  mitigation available. Unresolved — see Open Questions.]`
+#### FR-51: Delete a Household and its data
+A Partner can remove Ledgerleaf's copy of their data.
+**Consequences (testable):**
+- Deletion removes the Household's data from the acting Partner's device.
+- Deletion is offered only after an export has been taken or explicitly declined.
+- Deletion does not reach the other Partner's device; each Partner deletes their own copy.

content.text:
Drafted. **FR-1 → FR-51**, all seven features now exist. `prd.md` is ~895 lines.

**§5.3** is yours verbatim — the Floor / Unallocated Pool mechanism is the strongest idea in the document, and I said why in the prose: *"A freelancer's good month is not a promise, and Ledgerleaf will not spend it until it has arrived."* It's also the thing that makes 5.6 answerable, so I wired that dependency explicitly.

**Also applied:** FR-26 corrected (shared data freezes, personal ledgers keep writing), 5.2 renamed to *Household Setup, Pairing & Dissolution*, dissolution added as FR-33/34 with the safety framing — *"This is a safety requirement before it is a convenience one: a person who needs to leave must be able to, now, and without asking."*

---

### The assumptions worth your attention

Eleven are tagged in-doc and indexed in the memlog. Four actually matter:

**1. Device loss destroys a personal ledger. ⚠️**
> `[ASSUMPTION]` A Partner who loses their only device recovers the Shared Ledger by re-pairing, but their own Personal Ledger is unrecoverable unless they hold a second device or an export.

This falls straight out of E2EE — you hold nothing readable, so you can restore nothing — and it is the single worst user outcome in the product. Phone in a canal, two years of personal finances gone. **It's also coupled to the next one:** if a partner can have a phone *and* a tablet, the problem mostly evaporates. If v1 is one device per partner, your only mitigation is nagging people to export. I've assumed one-device-per-partner and flagged both as unresolved.

**2. "Can we afford it" gives no verdict.** I assumed it shows *"£140 left, £78 after this"* and refuses to say yes or no — reasoning that a product built to retire the household accountant shouldn't install a new one that tuts at you. That's a real design opinion I inserted; overrule it freely.

**3. Import is desktop-only.** You said the web app is "for import and settle-up only," which tells me where import *lives* but not whether the phone also has it. I assumed not.

**4. Imported rows land in the importer's personal ledger by default.** A bank statement is one person's account, so §4 says it's private — and the partner then marks rows shared via FR-10. This made FR-10 and import click together nicely, but it's an inference.

Smaller ones: either partner can change the Floor (should it need both?); dedupe matches on amount within a date window; one Unallocated Pool per ledger.

---

### Carrying on

Next batch, same way — I'll draft and you react:

- **Cross-Cutting NFRs** · **Constraints & Guardrails** (safety, privacy, cost) · **Aesthetic & Tone** · **Information Architecture** · **Platform** · **Monetization**
- **Non-Goals** · **MVP Scope** · **Success Metrics** with counter-metrics
- **§2.3 User Journeys** — I'll build these from the scenes you already narrated (Alex's £62, the 1 November close, Sam pairing Alex) rather than inventing new ones
- **Open Questions** · **Assumptions Index** · **§0 Document Purpose**

Then we hit **Finalize**: memlog audit, input reconciliation, reviewer gate, open-item triage, and polish.

One thing I'd like before I draft Success Metrics — it's the section where guessing is least useful. You gave me *1,000 paying households in 12 months* and *6-month retention above 60%*. **Is there a number for partner-#2 activation?** Your entire retention thesis rests on it, and it's the one metric that would tell you early whether Ledgerleaf is working or whether you've built a nicer spreadsheet for one person. If you don't have one, say so and I'll draft a candidate for you to shoot at.

# Validate

The Validate intent playbook. Standalone — this intent critiques an existing PRD without changing it and ends after the user has seen the report; it does not run Finalize. The synthesis pipeline below is also reused for mid-session report requests during Create/Update.

## Orient

Source-extract against `.memlog.md`, any original inputs, and the PRD/addendum themselves. Delegate to subagents per PRD Discipline → "Extract, don't ingest" (in SKILL.md); the parent assembles from extracts.

## Run the Reviewer Gate

Run the Reviewer Gate (see SKILL.md) against `prd.md` (and `addendum.md` if present). The rubric walker is the default entry in the gate menu; under Validate intent it additionally runs the synthesis pipeline below. The Finalize discipline pass during Create/Update does NOT render a report — findings stay in-conversation.

## Rubric-walker pipeline

The rubric walker is the primary review entry. Spawn it as a subagent with this prompt:

> You are validating a PRD against the quality rubric at `{workflow.validation_checklist_template}`. Read the full rubric first, then read `prd.md` (and `addendum.md` if present). Form a judgment per dimension — *strong / adequate / thin / broken* — and write findings only where they add information. Cite specific PRD locations and quote phrases. Severity ranks impact on the PRD's usefulness, not how easy the fix is. Write your review to `{doc_workspace}/review-rubric.md` in the format the rubric specifies. Return ONLY a compact summary (overall verdict, dimension verdicts, finding counts by severity, file path).

The Reviewer Gate may also dispatch additional reviewers from `{workflow.finalize_reviewers}` (adversarial-general by default) and any ad-hoc reviewers the parent judges warranted. Each writes its review to `{doc_workspace}/review-{slug}.md` and returns a compact summary. Run in parallel.

## Synthesis pipeline

Once every selected reviewer has returned, the parent synthesizes one consolidated report. **Do not skip this step under Validate intent** — it produces the persistent artifact the user opens.

### Inputs

- `{doc_workspace}/review-rubric.md` — primary, structured by the seven dimensions
- Zero or more `{doc_workspace}/review-{slug}.md` files — extra reviewers (adversarial, etc.)
- `{workflow.validation_report_template}` — the HTML skeleton

### What the synthesis pass does

1. Read every reviewer file in `{doc_workspace}/review-*.md`.
2. Fill the HTML skeleton:
   - **Header.** PRD name, path. Grade derived from the rubric verdicts and severity counts: *Excellent* = all dimensions strong/adequate, no high/critical findings · *Good* = ≤1 thin dimension, no critical findings · *Fair* = multiple thin dimensions or any high finding · *Poor* = any broken dimension or any critical finding. Set the matching `grade-excellent | grade-good | grade-fair | grade-poor` class.
   - **Synthesis block.** Lift the rubric's *Overall verdict* paragraph as the lead; if adversarial or ad-hoc reviewers materially shift the picture, add a second paragraph that names what they surfaced.
   - **Dimension summary cards.** One per dimension that was assessed. Colored verdict text. Skip dimensions the rubric marked n/a for this PRD (e.g. downstream usability for a standalone PRD).
   - **Dimension sections.** One `<section class="dimension">` per assessed dimension, in rubric order. `<details open>` for *thin* and *broken*; closed for *strong* and *adequate*. Each contains the dimension judgment (the prose from review-rubric.md) and the findings list.
   - **Reviewer sections.** One `<section class="reviewer-section">` per extra reviewer that ran. The source file path goes in the `<span class="reviewer-source">`. Closed by default. Adversarial findings keep their adversarial voice — do not soften.
   - **Mechanical notes.** Bullet list from the rubric's "Mechanical notes" section. Skip the block if empty.
   - **Footer.** Rubric path, ISO timestamp.
3. Write the filled HTML to `{doc_workspace}/validation-report.html`.
4. Write the markdown twin to `{doc_workspace}/validation-report.md` (same content, grouped by severity rather than by dimension — see format below; this is the canonical form for downstream re-reading).
5. Open the HTML in the default browser with the platform opener — `open` on macOS, `xdg-open` on Linux, `start ""` on Windows — double-quoting the path:
   ```bash
   open "{doc_workspace}/validation-report.html"
   ```
   If the command fails, don't retry with another opener: tell the user the file path and move on. Skip the open step in headless mode (see `references/headless.md`).

### Markdown twin format

```markdown
# Validation Report — {prd_name}

- **PRD:** `{prd_path}`
- **Rubric:** `{rubric_path}`
- **Run at:** {ISO timestamp}
- **Grade:** {Excellent | Good | Fair | Poor}

## Overall verdict
{synthesis paragraphs}

## Dimension verdicts
- Decision-readiness — {verdict}
- Substance over theater — {verdict}
- (etc. for each assessed dimension)

## Findings by severity

### Critical (n)
**[Dimension or Reviewer]** — Title (§ location)
{Note}
Fix: {suggested fix}

### High (n)
...

### Medium (n)
...

### Low (n)
...

## Mechanical notes
- {bullet}

## Reviewer files
- `review-rubric.md`
- `review-adversarial-general.md` (if present)
- (etc.)
```

Re-running validation overwrites the consolidated report in place. The individual `review-*.md` files are preserved so the user can drill in.

## Close

Surface artifact paths; the rendered HTML/markdown is the persistent artifact. Always offer to roll findings into an Update.

WS=_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01 && cat >> "$WS/prd.md" <<'EOF'

#### FR-52: Pair a second device for one Partner

A Partner can run Ledgerleaf on a second device of their own.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Partner can pair at most one additional device to their own identity in the Household.
- A Partner's second device carries a full copy of everything that Partner can see, including their
  Personal Ledger.
- Pairing a second device uses the verification flow of FR-15 and does not involve the other Partner.
- A Partner's second device is invisible to the other Partner and discloses nothing under §4.
- Either of a Partner's devices can unpair the other.

## 6. Platform

Phone-first, native, with a deliberately narrow desktop surface.

- **iOS and Android native applications** are the product. Each Partner uses their own phone.
- **A Partner may pair one additional personal device** — a tablet or second phone (FR-52).
- **A desktop web application** exists only for Statement Import (§5.4) and Settle-Up (§5.5), the two
  tasks that are genuinely worse on a phone. It is reached through a per-session browser
  authorisation (FR-18) and holds no standing access.
- **No other surface ships in v1.** No tablet-specific layout, no watch app, no public API.

`[ASSUMPTION: no minimum OS versions are specified yet. Architecture should set them, since the
cryptographic and secure-storage primitives available will constrain the floor.]`

## 7. Information Architecture
*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — the IA below is inferred from the features and the two personas, not
specified by the product owner. It is a starting position for UX, not a settled design.*

The phone app's shape follows from a hard asymmetry: one Partner does bookkeeping, the other wants a
ten-second answer. A navigation built around ledgers would serve the first and lose the second. So
the default screen is not a ledger.

**Top-level surfaces (phone):**

1. **Today** *(default)* — quick-add (FR-1) and the affordability check (FR-47), both one tap. A
   compact summary of the open Period beneath them. The secondary Partner may never navigate past
   this screen, and that is a success condition, not a failure.
2. **This month** — the envelope list (FR-22) for Ours and for the Partner's own Personal Ledger.
3. **Ledgers** — Ours and Mine. The other Partner's Personal Ledger is not a destination; it does not
   appear in navigation, because under §4 there is nothing there to show.
4. **Settle up** — the open Period's statement, proposal state, and Settlement History (§5.5).
   Surfaces a waiting-on indicator rather than a silent absence (FR-44).
5. **Settings** — Household, Split Rules, categories, devices and browser sessions, subscription,
   export, dissolution.

**Desktop web** carries two destinations only: **Import** and **Settle up**.

`[ASSUMPTION: "Ledgers" shows Ours and Mine as peers rather than nesting Mine under a profile.
The three-piles concept is the product's central metaphor and the IA should probably state it.]`

## 8. Aesthetic & Tone
*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — inferred from the product's stated purpose and from decisions already
made (no verdicts, no dispute workflow, no reason given on dissolution). Not specified directly.*

Ledgerleaf handles two things people are raw about: money, and their relationship. Every word it
says is said into that. The governing rule is that **the product reports and never judges** — it is
already how FR-47 works, and it should be how everything works.

- **Voice: plain, specific, unexcited.** Numbers and facts. "£140 left in Groceries." Not "You're
  doing great!" and not "Careful — you're close to your limit."
- **Never scold, never congratulate.** No streaks, no badges, no scores, no celebration animations,
  no red. A product that gamifies a couple's money becomes a third voice in the argument.
- **Never editorialise between Partners.** Ledgerleaf states what was spent and who paid. It does
  not characterise anyone's spending, flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault. At
  Settle-Up it presents arithmetic, not a case.
- **Say what is being disclosed, where it is being disclosed.** The §4 opening at Settle-Up is
  stated in plain language on that screen (FR-35). Privacy copy belongs at the moment of exposure,
  not in a policy nobody opens.
- **Silence is a feature.** Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44),
  one batched proposal change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10). Nothing else
  may notify.

**Anti-references:** budgeting apps that shame; aggregators that congratulate you on your own money;
anything with a mascot.

## 9. Cross-Cutting Non-Functional Requirements

**NFR-1 — Offline by default.** Every capability except sync, pairing, and browser authorisation
works with no network. The device holds the authoritative copy; connectivity is how two devices
agree, not how the app functions.

**NFR-2 — Entry speed.** Recording a single-Ledger Entry completes in under 15 seconds one-handed
(FR-1). This is a product-defining budget, not an aspiration: it is what replaces the spreadsheet.

**NFR-3 — Launch to usable.** `[ASSUMPTION: the app reaches the Today screen, interactive, within 2
seconds on mid-range hardware. The affordability check is a standing-in-a-shop interaction and a slow
launch destroys it.]`

**NFR-4 — Sync convergence.** `[ASSUMPTION: changes propagate to a Partner's other devices and to the
other Partner within 60 seconds when both are online, and converge without data loss after any period
offline. Conflict semantics are an architecture decision — see addendum.]`

**NFR-5 — No readable server-side copy.** No service operated by Ledgerleaf can read Household
financial content. This is a design constraint on every component, not a property of one.

**NFR-6 — History integrity.** Transfers and sealed Settlements are append-only (FR-6, FR-37). No
code path edits or deletes them, and export reproduces them faithfully.

**NFR-7 — Accessibility.** `[ASSUMPTION: WCAG 2.1 AA for the web surface; platform accessibility
conventions on mobile — dynamic type, screen-reader labelling on every control, and no colour-only
meaning. Primary actions sit within one-handed thumb reach.]`

**NFR-8 — Export completeness.** An export is a faithful, complete substitute for the app's own
record of everything the exporting Partner can see (FR-49). It is tested as such.

**NFR-9 — Currency and locale.** `[ASSUMPTION: a Household operates in a single currency, chosen at
creation. Multi-currency is not in v1. The persona includes freelancers, who are disproportionately
likely to be paid in another currency — confirm.]`

## 10. Constraints and Guardrails

### 10.1 Safety

The product is used by two people in a relationship, and relationships are not uniformly safe.

- **Unilateral exit, always.** Either Partner can dissolve the Household alone and immediately
  (FR-20). No consent, notice period, or cooling-off stands between a person and leaving.
- **No location data anywhere in the product.** Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
  transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input.
- **No reason, no attribution on dissolution.** The remaining Partner learns only that the Household
  ended (FR-20).
- **No activity surveillance.** Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked at,
  where they were, or what they checked. The affordability check records nothing (FR-47).
- **Disclosure is never retroactive.** Nothing a Partner did privately becomes visible later because
  of a change in Household state — not on joining (FR-16), not on dissolution (FR-21).

### 10.2 Privacy

- **No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or transmitted.** Permanent, not a v1 scope line.
- **No readable server-side copy of Household content** (NFR-5).
- **No sale, brokerage, or sharing of user data, in any form, ever.** No advertising.
- **No third-party analytics with access to financial content.** `[ASSUMPTION: product analytics, if
  any, are limited to non-content signals. See Open Questions — this collides with §14.]`
- **Privacy is stated where it is exercised**, not only in a policy document (§8).

### 10.3 Cost

Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive that.

- **Marginal server cost per Household must be near zero.** Content is opaque to the operator, so the
  service relays and stores ciphertext; it does not compute over user data.
- **No per-Household server-side computation.** Settle-Up, budgeting, and import all run on-device.
- **Operational load must suit a solo founder.** `[ASSUMPTION: no on-call rotation, no support SLA,
  and no component whose failure requires a human within hours.]`

## 11. Monetization

- **One subscription per Household**, billed through the platform app store to the Partner who created
  it (FR-12). The second Partner pays nothing and needs no payment method.
- **A few US dollars per month.** `[ASSUMPTION: exact price, and whether an annual plan exists, are
  undecided.]`
- **Lapse degrades, never locks out.** Shared data goes read-only after a 30-day grace period; each
  Partner keeps writing their own Personal Ledger, and export stays available in full (FR-13).
- **Export is never gated.** Not by subscription state, not by dissolution. A product whose pitch is
  trust cannot hold data for ransom.
- **No advertising, no data monetisation, no free tier subsidised by either** (§10.2).
- `[ASSUMPTION: a free trial exists before the first charge, but its length and whether it requires
  pairing are undecided.]`

## 12. Non-Goals (Explicit)

Ledgerleaf is not becoming these things, and v1 does not partially build toward them.

- **Not a bank aggregator.** No credential linking, ever — this is the product's identity, not a
  roadmap item.
- **Not a net-worth or investment tracker.** It budgets cash flow. No assets, no portfolios, no
  balances beyond the Ledgers themselves.
- **Not a payment rail.** Ledgerleaf states who owes whom and records what the Partners did about it.
  It never moves money and holds no payment credential (FR-40).
- **Not a dispute resolution system.** Disagreement is a conversation between two people who live
  together. The product carries the question (FR-39) and nothing more.
- **Not a separation or asset-division tool.** A Household can end (FR-20, FR-21); nothing divides
  balances, proposes a final reckoning, or adjudicates.
- **Not a group-expense app.** Exactly two Partners. Not roommates, not families, not three adults.
- **Not a bill-pay, tax, or allowance product.**
- **Not a zero-effort product.** Manual effort is the price of the privacy guarantee, charged openly.

## 13. MVP Scope

### 13.1 In Scope

- Three Ledgers per Household with Entries, splits, Payer attribution, and Transfers (§5.1).
- The §4 Privacy Model in full, including the deliberate Settle-Up opening.
- Household creation, subscription, invite, verified device pairing, second-device pairing, solo
  cold-start use, and unilateral dissolution (§5.2).
- Envelope budgeting with per-envelope rollover, the income Floor, and the Unallocated Pool (§5.3).
- CSV and OFX import on desktop web, with saved mappings, staged review, and duplicate flagging (§5.4).
- Two-sided Settle-Up with proposal and acceptance, sealed Settlements with content hashes, Settlement
  History, in-order sealing, carry-forward, and back-dated handling (§5.5).
- The affordability check (§5.6).
- Full CSV export, device recovery, and deletion (§5.7).
- iOS and Android native apps; desktop web limited to Import and Settle-Up.

### 13.2 Out of Scope for MVP

- **Bank linking** — permanent non-goal, not a deferral (§12).
- **Receipt OCR** — the product owner has flagged it as a possible later addition. `[NOTE FOR PM:
  this is the one deferred item that was raised unprompted and may be emotionally load-bearing.
  Revisit if timeline permits.]`
- **Automatic categorisation** — deferred; the manual trade is deliberate for v1 (§12).
- **Multi-currency Households** — deferred (NFR-9), and questionable given the freelancer persona.
- **More than two personal devices per Partner** — v1 allows one additional device (FR-52).
- **Tablet-specific layouts, watch app, public API** — deferred (§6).

#### FR-52: Pair a second device for one Partner

A Partner can run Ledgerleaf on a second device of their own.

**Consequences (testable):**
- A Partner can pair at most one additional device to their own identity in the Household.
- A Partner's second device carries a full copy of everything that Partner can see, including their
  Personal Ledger.
- Pairing a second device uses the verification flow of FR-15 and does not involve the other Partner.
- A Partner's second device is invisible to the other Partner and discloses nothing under §4.
- Either of a Partner's devices can unpair the other.

Phone-first, native, with a deliberately narrow desktop surface.

- **iOS and Android native applications** are the product. Each Partner uses their own phone.
- **A Partner may pair one additional personal device** — a tablet or second phone (FR-52).
- **A desktop web application** exists only for Statement Import (§5.4) and Settle-Up (§5.5), the two
  tasks that are genuinely worse on a phone. It is reached through a per-session browser
  authorisation (FR-18) and holds no standing access.
- **No other surface ships in v1.** No tablet-specific layout, no watch app, no public API.

`[ASSUMPTION: no minimum OS versions are specified yet. Architecture should set them, since the
cryptographic and secure-storage primitives available will constrain the floor.]`

*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — the IA below is inferred from the features and the two personas, not
specified by the product owner. It is a starting position for UX, not a settled design.*

The phone app's shape follows from a hard asymmetry: one Partner does bookkeeping, the other wants a
ten-second answer. A navigation built around ledgers would serve the first and lose the second. So
the default screen is not a ledger.

**Top-level surfaces (phone):**

1. **Today** *(default)* — quick-add (FR-1) and the affordability check (FR-47), both one tap. A
   compact summary of the open Period beneath them. The secondary Partner may never navigate past
   this screen, and that is a success condition, not a failure.
2. **This month** — the envelope list (FR-22) for Ours and for the Partner's own Personal Ledger.
3. **Ledgers** — Ours and Mine. The other Partner's Personal Ledger is not a destination; it does not
   appear in navigation, because under §4 there is nothing there to show.
4. **Settle up** — the open Period's statement, proposal state, and Settlement History (§5.5).
   Surfaces a waiting-on indicator rather than a silent absence (FR-44).
5. **Settings** — Household, Split Rules, categories, devices and browser sessions, subscription,
   export, dissolution.

**Desktop web** carries two destinations only: **Import** and **Settle up**.

`[ASSUMPTION: "Ledgers" shows Ours and Mine as peers rather than nesting Mine under a profile.
The three-piles concept is the product's central metaphor and the IA should probably state it.]`

## 8. Aesthetic & Tone
*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — inferred from the product's stated purpose and from decisions already
made (no verdicts, no dispute workflow, no reason given on dissolution). Not specified directly.*

Ledgerleaf handles two things people are raw about: money, and their relationship. Every word it
says is said into that. The governing rule is that **the product reports and never judges** — it is
already how FR-47 works, and it should be how everything works.

- **Voice: plain, specific, unexcited.** Numbers and facts. "£140 left in Groceries." Not "You're
  doing great!" and not "Careful — you're close to your limit."
- **Never scold, never congratulate.** No streaks, no badges, no scores, no celebration animations,
  no red. A product that gamifies a couple's money becomes a third voice in the argument.
- **Never editorialise between Partners.** Ledgerleaf states what was spent and who paid. It does
  not characterise anyone's spending, flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault. At
  Settle-Up it presents arithmetic, not a case.
- **Say what is being disclosed, where it is being disclosed.** The §4 opening at Settle-Up is
  stated in plain language on that screen (FR-35). Privacy copy belongs at the moment of exposure,
  not in a policy nobody opens.
- **Silence is a feature.** Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44),
  one batched proposal change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10). Nothing else
  may notify.

**Anti-references:** budgeting apps that shame; aggregators that congratulate you on your own money;
anything with a mascot.

**NFR-1 — Offline by default.** Every capability except sync, pairing, and browser authorisation
works with no network. The device holds the authoritative copy; connectivity is how two devices
agree, not how the app functions.

### 10.1 Safety

The product is used by two people in a relationship, and relationships are not uniformly safe.

- **Unilateral exit, always.** Either Partner can dissolve the Household alone and immediately
  (FR-20). No consent, notice period, or cooling-off stands between a person and leaving.
- **No location data anywhere in the product.** Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
  transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input.
- **No reason, no attribution on dissolution.** The remaining Partner learns only that the Household
  ended (FR-20).
- **No activity surveillance.** Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked at,
  where they were, or what they checked. The affordability check records nothing (FR-47).
- **Disclosure is never retroactive.** Nothing a Partner did privately becomes visible later because
  of a change in Household state — not on joining (FR-16), not on dissolution (FR-21).

### 10.2 Privacy

- **No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or transmitted.** Permanent, not a v1 scope line.
- **No readable server-side copy of Household content** (NFR-5).

- **No third-party analytics with access to financial content.** `[ASSUMPTION: product analytics, if
  any, are limited to non-content signals. See Open Questions — this collides with §14.]`
- **Privacy is stated where it is exercised**, not only in a policy document (§8).

Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive that.

- **Marginal server cost per Household must be near zero.** Content is opaque to the operator, so the
  service relays and stores ciphertext; it does not compute over user data.
- **No per-Household server-side computation.** Settle-Up, budgeting, and import all run on-device.
- **Operational load must suit a solo founder.** `[ASSUMPTION: no on-call rotation, no support SLA,
  and no component whose failure requires a human within hours.]`

- **A few US dollars per month.** `[ASSUMPTION: exact price, and whether an annual plan exists, are
  undecided.]`
- **Lapse degrades, never locks out.** Shared data goes read-only after a 30-day grace period; each
  Partner keeps writing their own Personal Ledger, and export stays available in full (FR-13).

  trust cannot hold data for ransom.
- **No advertising, no data monetisation, no free tier subsidised by either** (§10.2).

- **Not a net-worth or investment tracker.** It budgets cash flow. No assets, no portfolios, no
  balances beyond the Ledgers themselves.
- **Not a payment rail.** Ledgerleaf states who owes whom and records what the Partners did about it.
  It never moves money and holds no payment credential (FR-40).
- **Not a dispute resolution system.** Disagreement is a conversation between two people who live

- **Not a separation or asset-division tool.** A Household can end (FR-20, FR-21); nothing divides

- **Not a group-expense app.** Exactly two Partners. Not roommates, not families, not three adults.
- **Not a bill-pay, tax, or allowance product.**
- **Not a zero-effort product.** Manual effort is the price of the privacy guarantee, charged openly.

+   this screen, and that is a success condition, not a failure.
+2. **This month** — the envelope list (FR-22) for Ours and for the Partner's own Personal Ledger.
+3. **Ledgers** — Ours and Mine. The other Partner's Personal Ledger is not a destination; it does not
+   appear in navigation, because under §4 there is nothing there to show.
+4. **Settle up** — the open Period's statement, proposal state, and Settlement History (§5.5).
+   Surfaces a waiting-on indicator rather than a silent absence (FR-44).
+5. **Settings** — Household, Split Rules, categories, devices and browser sessions, subscription,
+   export, dissolution.
+**Desktop web** carries two destinations only: **Import** and **Settle up**.
+`[ASSUMPTION: "Ledgers" shows Ours and Mine as peers rather than nesting Mine under a profile.
+The three-piles concept is the product's central metaphor and the IA should probably state it.]`
+## 8. Aesthetic & Tone
+*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — inferred from the product's stated purpose and from decisions already
+made (no verdicts, no dispute workflow, no reason given on dissolution). Not specified directly.*
+Ledgerleaf handles two things people are raw about: money, and their relationship. Every word it
+says is said into that. The governing rule is that **the product reports and never judges** — it is
+already how FR-47 works, and it should be how everything works.
+- **Voice: plain, specific, unexcited.** Numbers and facts. "£140 left in Groceries." Not "You're
+  doing great!" and not "Careful — you're close to your limit."
+- **Never scold, never congratulate.** No streaks, no badges, no scores, no celebration animations,
+  no red. A product that gamifies a couple's money becomes a third voice in the argument.
+- **Never editorialise between Partners.** Ledgerleaf states what was spent and who paid. It does
+  not characterise anyone's spending, flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault. At
+  Settle-Up it presents arithmetic, not a case.
+- **Say what is being disclosed, where it is being disclosed.** The §4 opening at Settle-Up is
+  stated in plain language on that screen (FR-35). Privacy copy belongs at the moment of exposure,
+  not in a policy nobody opens.
+- **Silence is a feature.** Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44),
+  one batched proposal change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10). Nothing else
+  may notify.
+**Anti-references:** budgeting apps that shame; aggregators that congratulate you on your own money;
+anything with a mascot.
+## 9. Cross-Cutting Non-Functional Requirements
+**NFR-1 — Offline by default.** Every capability except sync, pairing, and browser authorisation
+works with no network. The device holds the authoritative copy; connectivity is how two devices
+agree, not how the app functions.
+**NFR-2 — Entry speed.** Recording a single-Ledger Entry completes in under 15 seconds one-handed
+(FR-1). This is a product-defining budget, not an aspiration: it is what replaces the spreadsheet.
+**NFR-3 — Launch to usable.** `[ASSUMPTION: the app reaches the Today screen, interactive, within 2
+seconds on mid-range hardware. The affordability check is a standing-in-a-shop interaction and a slow
+launch destroys it.]`
+**NFR-4 — Sync convergence.** `[ASSUMPTION: changes propagate to a Partner's other devices and to the
+other Partner within 60 seconds when both are online, and converge without data loss after any period
+offline. Conflict semantics are an architecture decision — see addendum.]`
+**NFR-5 — No readable server-side copy.** No service operated by Ledgerleaf can read Household
+financial content. This is a design constraint on every component, not a property of one.
+**NFR-6 — History integrity.** Transfers and sealed Settlements are append-only (FR-6, FR-37). No
+code path edits or deletes them, and export reproduces them faithfully.
+**NFR-7 — Accessibility.** `[ASSUMPTION: WCAG 2.1 AA for the web surface; platform accessibility
+conventions on mobile — dynamic type, screen-reader labelling on every control, and no colour-only
+meaning. Primary actions sit within one-handed thumb reach.]`
+**NFR-8 — Export completeness.** An export is a faithful, complete substitute for the app's own
+record of everything the exporting Partner can see (FR-49). It is tested as such.
+**NFR-9 — Currency and locale.** `[ASSUMPTION: a Household operates in a single currency, chosen at
+creation. Multi-currency is not in v1. The persona includes freelancers, who are disproportionately
+likely to be paid in another currency — confirm.]`
+## 10. Constraints and Guardrails
+### 10.1 Safety
+The product is used by two people in a relationship, and relationships are not uniformly safe.
+- **Unilateral exit, always.** Either Partner can dissolve the Household alone and immediately
+  (FR-20). No consent, notice period, or cooling-off stands between a person and leaving.
+- **No location data anywhere in the product.** Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
+  transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input.
+- **No reason, no attribution on dissolution.** The remaining Partner learns only that the Household
+  ended (FR-20).
+- **No activity surveillance.** Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked at,
+  where they were, or what they checked. The affordability check records nothing (FR-47).
+- **Disclosure is never retroactive.** Nothing a Partner did privately becomes visible later because
+  of a change in Household state — not on joining (FR-16), not on dissolution (FR-21).
+### 10.2 Privacy
+- **No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or transmitted.** Permanent, not a v1 scope line.
+- **No readable server-side copy of Household content** (NFR-5).
+- **No sale, brokerage, or sharing of user data, in any form, ever.** No advertising.
+- **No third-party analytics with access to financial content.** `[ASSUMPTION: product analytics, if
+  any, are limited to non-content signals. See Open Questions — this collides with §14.]`
+- **Privacy is stated where it is exercised**, not only in a policy document (§8).
+Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive that.
+- **Marginal server cost per Household must be near zero.** Content is opaque to the operator, so the
+  service relays and stores ciphertext; it does not compute over user data.
+- **No per-Household server-side computation.** Settle-Up, budgeting, and import all run on-device.
+- **Operational load must suit a solo founder.** `[ASSUMPTION: no on-call rotation, no support SLA,
+  and no component whose failure requires a human within hours.]`
+## 11. Monetization
+- **One subscription per Household**, billed through the platform app store to the Partner who created
+  it (FR-12). The second Partner pays nothing and needs no payment method.
+- **A few US dollars per month.** `[ASSUMPTION: exact price, and whether an annual plan exists, are
+  undecided.]`
+- **Lapse degrades, never locks out.** Shared data goes read-only after a 30-day grace period; each
+  Partner keeps writing their own Personal Ledger, and export stays available in full (FR-13).
+- **Export is never gated.** Not by subscription state, not by dissolution. A product whose pitch is
+  trust cannot hold data for ransom.
+- **No advertising, no data monetisation, no free tier subsidised by either** (§10.2).
+- `[ASSUMPTION: a free trial exists before the first charge, but its length and whether it requires
+  pairing are undecided.]`
+## 12. Non-Goals (Explicit)
+Ledgerleaf is not becoming these things, and v1 does not partially build toward them.
+- **Not a bank aggregator.** No credential linking, ever — this is the product's identity, not a
+  roadmap item.
+- **Not a net-worth or investment tracker.** It budgets cash flow. No assets, no portfolios, no
+  balances beyond the Ledgers themselves.
+- **Not a payment rail.** Ledgerleaf states who owes whom and records what the Partners did about it.
+  It never moves money and holds no payment credential (FR-40).
+- **Not a dispute resolution system.** Disagreement is a conversation between two people who live
+  together. The product carries the question (FR-39) and nothing more.
+- **Not a separation or asset-division tool.** A Household can end (FR-20, FR-21); nothing divides
+  balances, proposes a final reckoning, or adjudicates.
+- **Not a group-expense app.** Exactly two Partners. Not roommates, not families, not three adults.
+- **Not a bill-pay, tax, or allowance product.**
+- **Not a zero-effort product.** Manual effort is the price of the privacy guarantee, charged openly.
+## 13. MVP Scope
+### 13.1 In Scope
+- Three Ledgers per Household with Entries, splits, Payer attribution, and Transfers (§5.1).
+- The §4 Privacy Model in full, including the deliberate Settle-Up opening.
+- Household creation, subscription, invite, verified device pairing, second-device pairing, solo
+  cold-start use, and unilateral dissolution (§5.2).
+- Envelope budgeting with per-envelope rollover, the income Floor, and the Unallocated Pool (§5.3).
+- CSV and OFX import on desktop web, with saved mappings, staged review, and duplicate flagging (§5.4).
+- Two-sided Settle-Up with proposal and acceptance, sealed Settlements with content hashes, Settlement
+  History, in-order sealing, carry-forward, and back-dated handling (§5.5).
+- The affordability check (§5.6).
+- Full CSV export, device recovery, and deletion (§5.7).
+- iOS and Android native apps; desktop web limited to Import and Settle-Up.
+### 13.2 Out of Scope for MVP
+- **Bank linking** — permanent non-goal, not a deferral (§12).
+- **Receipt OCR** — the product owner has flagged it as a possible later addition. `[NOTE FOR PM:
+  this is the one deferred item that was raised unprompted and may be emotionally load-bearing.
+  Revisit if timeline permits.]`
+- **Automatic categorisation** — deferred; the manual trade is deliberate for v1 (§12).
+- **Multi-currency Households** — deferred (NFR-9), and questionable given the freelancer persona.
+- **More than two personal devices per Partner** — v1 allows one additional device (FR-52).
+- **Tablet-specific layouts, watch app, public API** — deferred (§6).
+- **A third ledger type or more than two Partners** — permanent non-goal (§12).
+- **Dispute workflow** — permanent non-goal (§12).
+- **Recurring or scheduled transactions** — `[ASSUMPTION: not discussed. Rent and utilities are the
+  most predictable shared costs a Household has, and re-entering them monthly is friction in exactly
+  the place the product promises relief. Flagged as a probable gap — see Open Questions.]`
+## 14. Success Metrics
+Each metric names what it validates. The counter-metrics exist because three of the primaries can be
+moved by making the product worse.
+**Primary**
+- **SM-1 — Paying Households.** 1,000 Households with an active subscription at 12 months from
+  launch. Validates the product proposition as a whole.
+- **SM-2 — Six-month retention.** Above 60% of Households still subscribed six months after their
+  first payment. Validates §5.3, §5.5, §5.7 — the loop that makes the product a habit rather than a
+  purchase.
+- **SM-3 — Second-Partner activation.** `[ASSUMPTION — drafted as a candidate, not supplied.]`
+  Two gates, because pairing is not participation:
+  - **SM-3a — Paired:** at least 75% of paying Households have a second Partner paired within 7 days
+    of the first payment. Validates FR-14, FR-15, FR-16, FR-17.
+  - **SM-3b — Engaged:** at least 60% of paired second Partners accept a Settlement (FR-37) *and*
+    record at least one Entry of their own (FR-1) within their first two Periods. Validates the
+    product's central claim that the household accountant has been retired rather than re-housed.
+**Secondary**
+- **SM-4 — Settlement completion.** Above 80% of opened Periods reach a sealed Settlement within 30
+  days. Validates §5.5 end to end; a low figure means the two-sided design is stalling (FR-44).
+- **SM-5 — Import adoption.** Share of Households that complete at least one import in their first
+  Period. Validates §5.4 as the on-ramp away from the spreadsheet.
+**Counter-metrics (do not optimize)**
+- **SM-C1 — Notifications per Partner per week.** Must not rise. The obvious lever for SM-3b is to
+  nag the second Partner, which produces exactly the dynamic the product exists to end. Counterbalances
+  SM-3b and SM-4.
+- **SM-C2 — Settlement review time.** The share of acceptances made within seconds of opening the
+  proposal. A rising figure means Partners are rubber-stamping, and SM-4 is being met by hollowing out
+  the two-sidedness that justifies it. Counterbalances SM-4.
+- **SM-C3 — Time to record an Entry.** Must not rise above the NFR-2 budget as features land.
+  Counterbalances SM-1 and SM-5.
+- **SM-C4 — Share of retained Households that are dormant.** Subscriptions nobody uses are churn that
+  has not happened yet, not retention. Counterbalances SM-2.
+> `[NOTE FOR PM]` **These metrics may be unmeasurable by design.** §10.2 and NFR-5 forbid a readable
+> server-side copy of Household content. SM-1 and SM-2 are billing facts and are safe. SM-3a is
+> plausibly observable from pairing events. **SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and SM-C2 are all statements
+> about user behaviour inside encrypted data.** Measuring them requires either client-side aggregate
+> telemetry the user consents to, or giving them up. This is the sharpest unresolved tension in the
+> document — see Open Questions.
+## 15. Open Questions
+1. **How is success measured without betraying the privacy guarantee?** SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and
+   SM-C2 describe behaviour inside end-to-end encrypted data that the operator cannot read (§14,
+   §10.2, NFR-5). Opt-in client-side aggregate telemetry is the obvious candidate and is itself a
+   product decision with a trust cost. Unresolved. **Phase-blocker for architecture.**
+2. **Recurring and scheduled transactions.** Rent and utilities are a Household's most predictable
+   shared costs, and §13.2 currently defers them by omission rather than by decision. Confirm in or
+3. **Re-sharing a declined Transaction.** FR-11 returns a declined Transaction to its owner, who may
+   presumably mark it shared again (FR-10), which admits an unbounded loop. Cap it, or accept it as a
+   social problem the product should not police?
+4. **Single-device Personal Ledger loss.** FR-52 mitigates by allowing a second device, but a Partner
+   who declines one still has an unrecoverable Personal Ledger. Is periodic export prompting enough,
+   or does the product need to refuse to proceed until a second device or an export exists?
+5. **Multi-currency.** NFR-9 assumes one currency per Household. Freelancers are disproportionately
+   paid across borders. Confirm the exclusion.
+6. **Price, trial length, and annual plan.** Undecided (§11).
+7. **Minimum OS versions.** Unset, and constrained by available secure-storage and cryptographic
+   primitives (§6).
+8. **Does Settle-Up need a per-category Split Rule audit in Settlement History?** FR-41 retains the
+   rules applied; whether a Partner can see *when a rule changed* relative to a sealed Settlement is
+   unspecified.
+## 16. Assumptions Index
+Every `[ASSUMPTION]` in this document, for explicit confirmation.
+**Confirmed with the product owner during drafting** *(retained here for traceability)*
+- §5.4 — Import is desktop-web only in v1. **Confirmed.**
+- §5.4 — Imported rows default to the importer's Personal Ledger, reassignable per row. **Confirmed.**
+- §5.6 — The affordability check renders no verdict. **Confirmed.**
+- §5.7 — A Partner may hold one additional device as the mitigation for Personal Ledger loss.
+  **Confirmed.**
+**Open — awaiting confirmation**
+- §5.4 — CSV mappings are saved per source, named by the Partner, and auto-applied on header match.
+- §5.4 — Duplicates are flagged on matching amount within a small date window; nothing is auto-discarded.
+- §5.3 — The Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool visible to both Partners; each Personal Ledger has
+  its own, private to its owner.
+- §5.6 — The affordability check ignores the Unallocated Pool and any unsettled Settlement debt.
+- §6 — No minimum OS versions are specified; architecture to set them.
+- §7 — The entire Information Architecture is inferred, including the Today-first structure and the
+  treatment of Ledgers as peers.
+- §8 — The entire Aesthetic & Tone section is inferred from product decisions rather than specified.
+- NFR-3 — Launch to interactive within 2 seconds on mid-range hardware.
+- NFR-4 — Sync converges within 60 seconds when both devices are online.
+- NFR-7 — WCAG 2.1 AA on web; platform accessibility conventions on mobile.
+- NFR-9 — One currency per Household; multi-currency excluded from v1.
+- §10.2 — Analytics, if any, are limited to non-content signals. Collides with §14 — see Open Questions.
+- §10.3 — No on-call rotation, no support SLA, no component requiring a human within hours.
+- §11 — Exact price and the existence of an annual plan are undecided.
+- §11 — A free trial exists; its length and whether it requires pairing are undecided.
+- §13.2 — Recurring and scheduled transactions are out of scope by omission, not by decision.
+- §14 — SM-3 (second-Partner activation) and its two gates are drafted candidates, not supplied targets.

UJ = """
### 2.3 Key User Journeys

*Numbered UJ-1 through UJ-8. FRs reference them inline. Two protagonists run throughout:*

> **Sam**, 34, salaried operations manager. Has maintained the household spreadsheet for three years
> and is quietly sick of it. **Alex**, 31, freelance designer, earns between £1,800 and £5,000 a month
> and rarely knows which until it arrives. Alex has opened the spreadsheet twice, both times because
> Sam asked.

- **UJ-1. Alex splits a supermarket shop in the car park, one-handed, before starting the engine.**
  Alex has just paid £62 on their own card — some of it the household shop, some of it their own.
  Already authenticated by biometric. Alex opens Ledgerleaf, taps quick-add, enters 62.00 and the
  merchant; the app offers the Ledger Alex used last. Alex taps *split this purchase*, puts 40.00 into
  Ours as Groceries and leaves 22.00 in their own Personal Ledger. **Climax:** the whole thing is done
  in under fifteen seconds with no confirmation dialog, and an undo toast sits there for ten seconds
  in case Alex fat-fingered it. **Resolution:** one card payment, recorded once, sitting in two
  Ledgers. The 40.00 will surface at Settle-Up as *"Alex paid 40.00 for Ours"* — and nothing else
  about Alex's personal spending travels with it. *Realizes FR-1, FR-2, FR-3, FR-4.*

- **UJ-2. Alex checks whether a £78 jacket fits, while standing in the shop.**
  Alex is the partner who never opened the spreadsheet. They open Ledgerleaf, and the affordability
  check is right there on the first screen. Amount, category. **Climax:** *"£140 left in Clothing.
  £62 after this."* No verdict, no approval, no small green tick. **Resolution:** Alex decides, buys
  or doesn't, and nothing is recorded — Sam will never know the check happened. This single screen is
  the whole of Alex's relationship with the product, and that is a success condition.
  *Realizes FR-47, FR-48.*

- **UJ-3. Sam pairs Alex into the Household, in the kitchen, in about two minutes.**
  Sam installed Ledgerleaf a week ago and has already entered a month of transactions, so the app is
  not an empty shell to sell Alex on. Sam taps *invite partner*; a QR code appears. Alex installs the
  app and scans it off Sam's screen. Both phones show the same four-word verification code; both
  confirm. **Climax:** Alex is in — seeing Ours fully populated, their own Personal Ledger empty, and
  a prompt to enter their income for the split. **Resolution:** Sam's month of solo work is now shared
  — except Sam's Personal Ledger, which stays as private as it was on day one. Nothing became visible
  because Alex arrived. **Edge case:** if the codes don't match, nobody joins and the invite is burned.
  *Realizes FR-14, FR-15, FR-16, FR-17.*

- **UJ-4. Sam sets up November's envelopes on the 1st, in four taps.**
  Sam opens *This month*. October's envelopes are there with what was planned, rolled over, spent and
  left. Sam taps *copy last month*, adjusts Groceries upward because Christmas is coming, and is done.
  **Climax:** Alex's freelance income isn't in the plan at all — envelopes are funded against the
  Household's Floor, the lowest of the last six months. **Resolution:** when Alex's invoice lands
  mid-month at £4,100, the surplus goes to the Unallocated Pool, and the Household assigns it to
  envelopes *then*, with the money in hand. Nothing was promised against a month that hadn't happened.
  *Realizes FR-22, FR-24, FR-25, FR-26, FR-27, FR-28.*

- **UJ-5. Sam imports a bank statement at the kitchen table, on a laptop.**
  Sam downloads October's CSV from the bank, opens Ledgerleaf's web app, and scans the QR on screen
  with their phone to authorise the session. The saved mapping for this bank applies itself. **Climax:**
  48 rows staged for review, six flagged as likely duplicates of transactions Sam already entered by
  hand; Sam dismisses two and confirms four. **Resolution:** Sam commits. Everything lands in Sam's
  own Personal Ledger, private by default, and Sam marks the four household ones as shared from there.
  The browser session dies when Sam closes the tab. **Edge case:** no bank password was typed anywhere,
  because there is nowhere to type one. *Realizes FR-18, FR-29, FR-30, FR-31, FR-32, FR-33, FR-10.*

- **UJ-6. Sam and Alex close October on the 1st of November, from two different rooms.**
  Sam opens Settle-Up. October's shared spending is listed line by line: who paid, which Split Rule
  applied, which items were funded from someone's personal money — and at the bottom, *"Alex owes Sam
  137.00"*. The screen says plainly what is being disclosed and why. Sam taps **Propose**. Alex gets
  one notification, opens the same list, and reads it. **Climax:** Alex taps **Accept**, and the
  Settlement seals — immutable, hashed, filed in Settlement History. **Resolution:** Ledgerleaf does
  not move the money. Alex sends Sam £137 by bank transfer that evening and records it as a Transfer.
  The month took five minutes and ended in a payment rather than a conversation about whose turn it
  was. *Realizes FR-34, FR-35, FR-36, FR-37, FR-40, FR-41.*

- **UJ-7. Alex queries a line instead of accepting it.**
  Same screen as UJ-6, but Alex stops at a £40 lunch tagged to Ours. Alex taps the line and
  *ask about this*: **"wasn't this your work thing?"** Sam gets the note attached to that transaction.
  **Climax:** Sam agrees, moves it out of Ours while the Period is still open, and the proposal
  withdraws and re-forms around the corrected number by itself — Alex's earlier reading never becomes
  an acceptance of a figure that has since moved. **Resolution:** Alex accepts £97 instead. There was
  no dispute workflow, no arbitration, no escalation — a question, an edit, and a number both people
  looked at. *Realizes FR-38, FR-39, FR-9.*

- **UJ-8. Alex leaves, alone, immediately, and takes their data with them.**
  The relationship has ended. Alex opens Settings and dissolves the Household. **Climax:** it takes
  effect at once. Sam's access to shared data stops going forward; sync between the devices ends;
  Alex needs nobody's agreement and gives no reason. **Resolution:** Sam is told only that the
  Household was dissolved. Both export Ours, their own Personal Ledger, and every sealed Settlement
  as CSV. Alex's Personal Ledger was never visible to Sam and still isn't. Ledgerleaf divides nothing
  and adjudicates nothing. **Edge case:** no screen, record, or notification anywhere in the product
  reveals where Alex was when they did it. *Realizes FR-20, FR-21, FR-49.*

new_head = """## 0. Document Purpose

This PRD is written for the product owner, for downstream BMad workflows — UX, architecture, and
epic/story breakdown — and for anyone reviewing whether Ledgerleaf is worth building. It describes
**what** Ledgerleaf does and for whom; it does not describe how it is built.

**How to read it.** §3 Glossary fixes the vocabulary: every domain noun is defined once and used
verbatim everywhere else, so a downstream reader never has to guess whether two words mean the same
thing. §4 Privacy Model is cross-cutting and load-bearing — it defines what each Partner can see of
the other, and the Features in §5 reference it rather than restating it. §5 groups capabilities into
seven Features with Functional Requirements nested beneath, numbered globally FR-1 through FR-52 so
downstream artifacts have stable references even if the Features are reorganised. §2.3 Key User
Journeys, UJ-1 through UJ-8, are the narrative spine the FRs serve.

Inferences the product owner has not confirmed are tagged `[ASSUMPTION]` inline and collected in §16.

**Companion document.** `addendum.md` holds depth that belongs to architecture rather than to this
PRD — the sync and key-exchange mechanism, browser session key transport, the Settlement hash
construction, and the import pipeline's internals. Where this PRD states a promise, the addendum is
where the means of keeping it are worked out.

**No UX or architecture document exists yet.** This PRD is the first artifact in the chain.
"""
