902	- Carry-forward is offered on a Period that has an outstanding or unproposed Settle-Up.
903	- Carry-forward requires both Partners to accept, like any Settlement.
904	- The resulting Settlement covers every Period merged into it and names them.

909

933

935

937	
938	**Consequences (testable):**
939	- The check is reachable in one tap from the app's default screen.
940	- It takes an amount and a category and requires nothing else.
941	- It reports the envelope's remaining balance and the balance that would remain after the amount.

946	
947	The check obeys the privacy boundary.
948

951	- A Personal Ledger envelope is checkable only by its owner.

953	- The check draws on envelope balances only, and not on the Unallocated Pool or any unsettled amount.

955	### 5.7 Data Ownership & Recovery
956	
957	*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*
958	
959	**Description.** Ledgerleaf asks for trust, so it is built to be easy to leave. Everything a Partner
960	can see, they can export as CSV, at any time, without asking anyone — including while the Household
961	is read-only on a lapsed subscription, and including after dissolution. A product that holds data
962	hostage has not earned the privacy claim in §1.
963	
964	The hard edge of end-to-end encryption is recovery. Keys live on devices; the operator holds nothing
965	readable and therefore can restore nothing. Losing a device must not mean losing a Personal Ledger,
966	and since Ledgerleaf cannot offer a server-side backstop, the answer is redundancy on the user's own
967	side: **a Partner may hold a second device** — a tablet, or a second phone — which carries a full
968	copy of everything that Partner can see. Two devices, and a lost phone is an inconvenience. One
969	device, and it is a loss nobody can undo.
970	
971	Ledgerleaf is therefore honest and insistent about the gap. A Partner running a single device is
972	told plainly what that means, and is reminded periodically to export. The Shared Ledger survives
973	regardless, because the other Partner's device holds it; it is the Personal Ledger — the private half,
974	the half nobody else has — that is at risk.
975

979

982	A Partner can export the full contents of what they can see.

987	- Export never includes any part of the other Partner's Personal Ledger.

993	
994	A Partner who loses a device can return to their Household.
995

997	- A replacement device re-pairs through the verification flow of FR-15.
998	- Re-pairing restores the Shared Ledger from the other Partner's device.
999	- The operator cannot restore any data, and the product states this plainly before it is relied on.
1000	- Where the Partner holds a second device, re-pairing restores their Personal Ledger in full from it.
1001	- Where the Partner held only the lost device, their Personal Ledger is not recoverable by any party,
1002	  including the operator, and the product states this before a Partner can come to depend on it.
1003	- A Partner running a single device is prompted periodically to export (FR-49).

1009	**Consequences (testable):**
1010	- Deletion removes the Household's data from the acting Partner's device.
1011	- Deletion is offered only after an export has been taken or explicitly declined.
1012	- Deletion does not reach the other Partner's device; each Partner deletes their own copy.

1026	## 6. Platform
1027	
1028	Phone-first, native, with a deliberately narrow desktop surface.
1029	
1030	- **iOS and Android native applications** are the product. Each Partner uses their own phone.
1031	- **A Partner may pair one additional personal device** — a tablet or second phone (FR-52).
1032	- **A desktop web application** exists only for Statement Import (§5.4) and Settle-Up (§5.5), the two
1033	  tasks that are genuinely worse on a phone. It is reached through a per-session browser

1	# Ledgerleaf — Addendum
2	
3	Depth the user supplied that belongs downstream (architecture, solution design, UX spec)
4	rather than in the PRD's main narrative. Captured as it arises; not a dumping ground for
5	audit or override information.
6	
7	## For Architecture / Solution Design
8	
9	### Storage and sync mechanism
10	- **Local-first storage.** The device holds the authoritative copy of household data; the
11	  app is expected to be fully usable with no network.
12	- **End-to-end encrypted sync between the two partners' devices.** Stated by the user as a
13	  product commitment. The PRD carries the *promise* (the operator cannot read household
14	  financial data); the *mechanism* — key exchange, pairing, conflict resolution, relay vs.
15	  peer-to-peer transport, key recovery on device loss — is an architecture decision and
16	  belongs here.
17	  - Open: device-loss / key-recovery story. Has real product surface (what the user is told,
18	    what they must do), so the user-visible half may be pulled back into the PRD once decided.
19	  - Open: concurrent-edit conflict semantics between two partners editing the same ledger.
20	
21	### Import pipeline
22	- **CSV/OFX import only — no bank credential aggregation, ever.** The *constraint* is a PRD-level
23	  product principle. The *implementation* — per-bank CSV column mapping, OFX parsing, duplicate
24	  detection across re-imported statement overlaps, category inference — is design work.
25	
26	### Pairing and session key transport
27	The PRD carries the user-visible flow (QR, one-time link, matching verification code, per-session
28	browser authorisation, revocation). The mechanism is architecture's:
29	- Device-to-device key exchange protocol and what, if anything, transits a relay.
30	- The verification code's construction and what attack it actually defeats.
31	- How a browser session receives key material "encrypted" from the phone, and where it lives for
32	  the session's lifetime (memory only? what survives a refresh?).
33	- Session expiry enforcement — client-side, server-assisted, or both — and how revocation reaches a
34	  live session.
35	- Sealed-Settlement content hash: what it covers, how it is computed, and what it is meant to prove
36	  to whom. The PRD promises it is displayed; it does not specify it.

## 8. Aesthetic & Tone
*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` — inferred from the product's stated purpose and from decisions already
made (no verdicts, no dispute workflow, no reason given on dissolution). Not specified directly.*

Ledgerleaf handles two things people are raw about: money, and their relationship. Every word it
says is said into that. The governing rule is that **the product reports and never judges** — it is
already how FR-47 works, and it should be how everything works.

- **Voice: plain, specific, unexcited.** Numbers and facts. "£140 left in Groceries." Not "You're
  doing great!" and not "Careful — you're close to your limit."
- **Never scold, never congratulate.** No streaks, no badges, no scores, no celebration animations,
  no red. A product that gamifies a couple's money becomes a third voice in the argument.
- **Never editorialise between Partners.** Ledgerleaf states what was spent and who paid. It does
  not characterise anyone's spending, flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault. At
  Settle-Up it presents arithmetic, not a case.
- **Say what is being disclosed, where it is being disclosed.** The §4 opening at Settle-Up is
  stated in plain language on that screen (FR-35). Privacy copy belongs at the moment of exposure,
  not in a policy nobody opens.
- **Silence is a feature.** Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44),
  one batched proposal change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10). Nothing else
  may notify.

**Anti-references:** budgeting apps that shame; aggregators that congratulate you on your own money;
anything with a mascot.

## 9. Cross-Cutting Non-Functional Requirements

**NFR-1 — Offline by default.** Every capability except sync, pairing, and browser authorisation
works with no network. The device holds the authoritative copy; connectivity is how two devices
agree, not how the app functions.

**NFR-2 — Entry speed.** Recording a single-Ledger Entry completes in under 15 seconds one-handed
(FR-1). This is a product-defining budget, not an aspiration: it is what replaces the spreadsheet.

**NFR-3 — Launch to usable.** `[ASSUMPTION: the app reaches the Today screen, interactive, within 2
seconds on mid-range hardware. The affordability check is a standing-in-a-shop interaction and a slow
launch destroys it.]`

**NFR-4 — Sync convergence.** `[ASSUMPTION: changes propagate to a Partner's other devices and to the
other Partner within 60 seconds when both are online, and converge without data loss after any period
offline. Conflict semantics are an architecture decision — see addendum.]`

**NFR-5 — No readable server-side copy.** No service operated by Ledgerleaf can read Household
financial content. This is a design constraint on every component, not a property of one.

**NFR-6 — History integrity.** Transfers and sealed Settlements are append-only (FR-6, FR-37). No
code path edits or deletes them, and export reproduces them faithfully.

**NFR-7 — Accessibility.** `[ASSUMPTION: WCAG 2.1 AA for the web surface; platform accessibility
conventions on mobile — dynamic type, screen-reader labelling on every control, and no colour-only
meaning. Primary actions sit within one-handed thumb reach.]`

**NFR-8 — Export completeness.** An export is a faithful, complete substitute for the app's own
record of everything the exporting Partner can see (FR-49). It is tested as such.

**NFR-9 — Currency and locale.** `[ASSUMPTION: a Household operates in a single currency, chosen at
creation. Multi-currency is not in v1. The persona includes freelancers, who are disproportionately
likely to be paid in another currency — confirm.]`

## 10. Constraints and Guardrails

### 10.1 Safety

The product is used by two people in a relationship, and relationships are not uniformly safe.

- **Unilateral exit, always.** Either Partner can dissolve the Household alone and immediately
  (FR-20). No consent, notice period, or cooling-off stands between a person and leaving.
- **No location data anywhere in the product.** Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
  transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input.
- **No reason, no attribution on dissolution.** The remaining Partner learns only that the Household
  ended (FR-20).
- **No activity surveillance.** Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked at,
  where they were, or what they checked. The affordability check records nothing (FR-47).
- **Disclosure is never retroactive.** Nothing a Partner did privately becomes visible later because
  of a change in Household state — not on joining (FR-16), not on dissolution (FR-21).

### 10.2 Privacy

- **No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or transmitted.** Permanent, not a v1 scope line.
- **No readable server-side copy of Household content** (NFR-5).
- **No sale, brokerage, or sharing of user data, in any form, ever.** No advertising.
- **No third-party analytics with access to financial content.** `[ASSUMPTION: product analytics, if
  any, are limited to non-content signals. See Open Questions — this collides with §14.]`
- **Privacy is stated where it is exercised**, not only in a policy document (§8).

### 10.3 Cost

Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive that.

- **Marginal server cost per Household must be near zero.** Content is opaque to the operator, so the
  service relays and stores ciphertext; it does not compute over user data.
- **No per-Household server-side computation.** Settle-Up, budgeting, and import all run on-device.
- **Operational load must suit a solo founder.** `[ASSUMPTION: no on-call rotation, no support SLA,
  and no component whose failure requires a human within hours.]`

## 11. Monetization

- **One subscription per Household**, billed through the platform app store to the Partner who created
  it (FR-12). The second Partner pays nothing and needs no payment method.
- **A few US dollars per month.** `[ASSUMPTION: exact price, and whether an annual plan exists, are
  undecided.]`
- **Lapse degrades, never locks out.** Shared data goes read-only after a 30-day grace period; each
  Partner keeps writing their own Personal Ledger, and export stays available in full (FR-13).
- **Export is never gated.** Not by subscription state, not by dissolution. A product whose pitch is
  trust cannot hold data for ransom.
- **No advertising, no data monetisation, no free tier subsidised by either** (§10.2).
- `[ASSUMPTION: a free trial exists before the first charge, but its length and whether it requires
  pairing are undecided.]`

## 12. Non-Goals (Explicit)

Ledgerleaf is not becoming these things, and v1 does not partially build toward them.

- **Not a bank aggregator.** No credential linking, ever — this is the product's identity, not a
  roadmap item.
- **Not a net-worth or investment tracker.** It budgets cash flow. No assets, no portfolios, no
  balances beyond the Ledgers themselves.
- **Not a payment rail.** Ledgerleaf states who owes whom and records what the Partners did about it.
  It never moves money and holds no payment credential (FR-40).
- **Not a dispute resolution system.** Disagreement is a conversation between two people who live
  together. The product carries the question (FR-39) and nothing more.
- **Not a separation or asset-division tool.** A Household can end (FR-20, FR-21); nothing divides
  balances, proposes a final reckoning, or adjudicates.
- **Not a group-expense app.** Exactly two Partners. Not roommates, not families, not three adults.
- **Not a bill-pay, tax, or allowance product.**
- **Not a zero-effort product.** Manual effort is the price of the privacy guarantee, charged openly.

## 13. MVP Scope

### 13.1 In Scope

- Three Ledgers per Household with Entries, splits, Payer attribution, and Transfers (§5.1).
- The §4 Privacy Model in full, including the deliberate Settle-Up opening.
- Household creation, subscription, invite, verified device pairing, second-device pairing, solo
  cold-start use, and unilateral dissolution (§5.2).
- Envelope budgeting with per-envelope rollover, the income Floor, and the Unallocated Pool (§5.3).
- CSV and OFX import on desktop web, with saved mappings, staged review, and duplicate flagging (§5.4).
- Two-sided Settle-Up with proposal and acceptance, sealed Settlements with content hashes, Settlement
  History, in-order sealing, carry-forward, and back-dated handling (§5.5).
- The affordability check (§5.6).
- Full CSV export, device recovery, and deletion (§5.7).
- iOS and Android native apps; desktop web limited to Import and Settle-Up.

### 13.2 Out of Scope for MVP

- **Bank linking** — permanent non-goal, not a deferral (§12).
- **Receipt OCR** — the product owner has flagged it as a possible later addition. `[NOTE FOR PM:
  this is the one deferred item that was raised unprompted and may be emotionally load-bearing.
  Revisit if timeline permits.]`
- **Automatic categorisation** — deferred; the manual trade is deliberate for v1 (§12).
- **Multi-currency Households** — deferred (NFR-9), and questionable given the freelancer persona.
- **More than two personal devices per Partner** — v1 allows one additional device (FR-52).
- **Tablet-specific layouts, watch app, public API** — deferred (§6).
- **A third ledger type or more than two Partners** — permanent non-goal (§12).
- **Dispute workflow** — permanent non-goal (§12).
- **Recurring or scheduled transactions** — `[ASSUMPTION: not discussed. Rent and utilities are the
  most predictable shared costs a Household has, and re-entering them monthly is friction in exactly
  the place the product promises relief. Flagged as a probable gap — see Open Questions.]`

## 14. Success Metrics

Each metric names what it validates. The counter-metrics exist because three of the primaries can be
moved by making the product worse.

**Primary**

- **SM-1 — Paying Households.** 1,000 Households with an active subscription at 12 months from
  launch. Validates the product proposition as a whole.
- **SM-2 — Six-month retention.** Above 60% of Households still subscribed six months after their
  first payment. Validates §5.3, §5.5, §5.7 — the loop that makes the product a habit rather than a
  purchase.
- **SM-3 — Second-Partner activation.** `[ASSUMPTION — drafted as a candidate, not supplied.]`
  Two gates, because pairing is not participation:
  - **SM-3a — Paired:** at least 75% of paying Households have a second Partner paired within 7 days
    of the first payment. Validates FR-14, FR-15, FR-16, FR-17.
  - **SM-3b — Engaged:** at least 60% of paired second Partners accept a Settlement (FR-37) *and*
    record at least one Entry of their own (FR-1) within their first two Periods. Validates the
    product's central claim that the household accountant has been retired rather than re-housed.

**Secondary**

- **SM-4 — Settlement completion.** Above 80% of opened Periods reach a sealed Settlement within 30
  days. Validates §5.5 end to end; a low figure means the two-sided design is stalling (FR-44).
- **SM-5 — Import adoption.** Share of Households that complete at least one import in their first
  Period. Validates §5.4 as the on-ramp away from the spreadsheet.

**Counter-metrics (do not optimize)**

- **SM-C1 — Notifications per Partner per week.** Must not rise. The obvious lever for SM-3b is to
  nag the second Partner, which produces exactly the dynamic the product exists to end. Counterbalances
  SM-3b and SM-4.
- **SM-C2 — Settlement review time.** The share of acceptances made within seconds of opening the
  proposal. A rising figure means Partners are rubber-stamping, and SM-4 is being met by hollowing out
  the two-sidedness that justifies it. Counterbalances SM-4.
- **SM-C3 — Time to record an Entry.** Must not rise above the NFR-2 budget as features land.
  Counterbalances SM-1 and SM-5.
- **SM-C4 — Share of retained Households that are dormant.** Subscriptions nobody uses are churn that
  has not happened yet, not retention. Counterbalances SM-2.

> `[NOTE FOR PM]` **These metrics may be unmeasurable by design.** §10.2 and NFR-5 forbid a readable
> server-side copy of Household content. SM-1 and SM-2 are billing facts and are safe. SM-3a is
> plausibly observable from pairing events. **SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and SM-C2 are all statements
> about user behaviour inside encrypted data.** Measuring them requires either client-side aggregate
> telemetry the user consents to, or giving them up. This is the sharpest unresolved tension in the
> document — see Open Questions.

## 15. Open Questions

1. **How is success measured without betraying the privacy guarantee?** SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and
   SM-C2 describe behaviour inside end-to-end encrypted data that the operator cannot read (§14,
   §10.2, NFR-5). Opt-in client-side aggregate telemetry is the obvious candidate and is itself a
   product decision with a trust cost. Unresolved. **Phase-blocker for architecture.**
2. **Recurring and scheduled transactions.** Rent and utilities are a Household's most predictable
   shared costs, and §13.2 currently defers them by omission rather than by decision. Confirm in or
   out (§13.2).
3. **Re-sharing a declined Transaction.** FR-11 returns a declined Transaction to its owner, who may
   presumably mark it shared again (FR-10), which admits an unbounded loop. Cap it, or accept it as a
   social problem the product should not police?
4. **Single-device Personal Ledger loss.** FR-52 mitigates by allowing a second device, but a Partner
   who declines one still has an unrecoverable Personal Ledger. Is periodic export prompting enough,
   or does the product need to refuse to proceed until a second device or an export exists?
5. **Multi-currency.** NFR-9 assumes one currency per Household. Freelancers are disproportionately
   paid across borders. Confirm the exclusion.
6. **Price, trial length, and annual plan.** Undecided (§11).
7. **Minimum OS versions.** Unset, and constrained by available secure-storage and cryptographic
   primitives (§6).
8. **Does Settle-Up need a per-category Split Rule audit in Settlement History?** FR-41 retains the
   rules applied; whether a Partner can see *when a rule changed* relative to a sealed Settlement is
   unspecified.

## 16. Assumptions Index

Every `[ASSUMPTION]` in this document, for explicit confirmation.

**Confirmed with the product owner during drafting** *(retained here for traceability)*

- §5.4 — Import is desktop-web only in v1. **Confirmed.**
- §5.4 — Imported rows default to the importer's Personal Ledger, reassignable per row. **Confirmed.**
- §5.6 — The affordability check renders no verdict. **Confirmed.**
- §5.7 — A Partner may hold one additional device as the mitigation for Personal Ledger loss.
  **Confirmed.**

**Open — awaiting confirmation**

- §5.4 — CSV mappings are saved per source, named by the Partner, and auto-applied on header match.
- §5.4 — Duplicates are flagged on matching amount within a small date window; nothing is auto-discarded.
- §5.3 — The Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool visible to both Partners; each Personal Ledger has
  its own, private to its owner.
- §5.6 — The affordability check ignores the Unallocated Pool and any unsettled Settlement debt.
- §6 — No minimum OS versions are specified; architecture to set them.
- §7 — The entire Information Architecture is inferred, including the Today-first structure and the
  treatment of Ledgers as peers.
- §8 — The entire Aesthetic & Tone section is inferred from product decisions rather than specified.
- NFR-3 — Launch to interactive within 2 seconds on mid-range hardware.
- NFR-4 — Sync converges within 60 seconds when both devices are online.
- NFR-7 — WCAG 2.1 AA on web; platform accessibility conventions on mobile.
- NFR-9 — One currency per Household; multi-currency excluded from v1.
- §10.2 — Analytics, if any, are limited to non-content signals. Collides with §14 — see Open Questions.
- §10.3 — No on-call rotation, no support SLA, no component requiring a human within hours.
- §11 — Exact price and the existence of an annual plan are undecided.
- §11 — A free trial exists; its length and whether it requires pairing are undecided.
- §13.2 — Recurring and scheduled transactions are out of scope by omission, not by decision.
- §14 — SM-3 (second-Partner activation) and its two gates are drafted candidates, not supplied targets.

cat > "/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-sherifmatta-Learnings-bmad-harness/1c9f5c21-36bb-427d-a54b-af04146a506b/scratchpad/subject-coaching/_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01/review-rubric.md" <<'XEOFX'
# PRD Quality Review — Ledgerleaf

## Overall verdict

This is a genuinely good PRD. It has a thesis it bets on ("three piles, not one pot, and the
operator can't read any of them"), two personas that actually drive the information architecture,
a cross-cutting Privacy Model that the FRs reference instead of restating, FR consequences that are
mostly testable, and a Success Metrics section with four counter-metrics that name the exact ways
the primaries could be gamed. The §14 `[NOTE FOR PM]` on metrics-versus-encryption is the kind of
self-indictment most PRDs never write down.

What is at risk is the arithmetic core. The PRD specifies, in crisp detail, every *interaction* with
an envelope and a Settlement, and never specifies what an envelope balance *is* (planned, or
transferred-in?) or what Settle-Up *sums* (does a Transfer into Ours count as something a Partner
paid?). There is also no FR anywhere that records income, though the Floor and Unallocated Pool both
depend on one. Story creation will hit these on day one. Separately, §7 and SM-3b define success for
the secondary Partner in contradictory terms, and the §4 privacy model has one unacknowledged leak
(the Floor) alongside the one it acknowledges scrupulously (the income ratio).

## Decision-readiness — strong

Decisions are stated as decisions, with the losing side named. "Ledgerleaf takes the opposite trade
— a little manual effort in exchange for fairness and privacy" (§1) is the product's thesis stated
as a cost. §5.5 does not hedge on dispute resolution — "There is no dispute mechanism in v1,
deliberately" — and §12 confirms it as a permanent non-goal rather than a deferral. §5.5 also makes
the harder call explicitly: "**The Settlement closes on both accepts, not on payment** — the
agreement and the money are separate acts, and conflating them would let an unpaid debt hold the
next month hostage." That is a decision with its reasoning and its rejected alternative in one
sentence.

The `[NOTE FOR PM]` placement is honest. The §14 note — "**These metrics may be unmeasurable by
design**" — sits at the sharpest tension in the document rather than at a safe checkpoint, and
Open Question 1 escalates it to "**Phase-blocker for architecture**" instead of leaving it as a
musing. Open Questions 2–8 are all genuinely open; none of them answer themselves in the next
sentence.

The one place the PRD is *not* honest with itself is §4's income claim, and the one decision it
leaves silently unmade is the settlement deadlock.

### Findings

- **high** The Floor leaks the other Partner's income, and §4 does not say so (§4, FR-26) — §4 goes
  out of its way to admit the one leak it knows about: "A Partner who knows their own income can
  solve the ratio for the other's figure, so Ledgerleaf does not claim otherwise." But FR-26 then
  publishes a second derived figure to both Partners — the Floor, "the lowest of the last six months
  of **combined** income" — and asserts "Individual income figures are never disclosed to the other
  Partner, per §4; only the Floor and any derived ratio are shared." A Partner who knows their own
  six-month history and sees the combined Floor subtracts one from the other and has the other
  Partner's income in the Floor month. Worse, FR-26 says the Floor "updates automatically as either
  changes", so each update is a fresh observation. Because §4 is the document's load-bearing promise
  and it explicitly disclaims a leak of exactly this shape, the silence here reads as an oversight
  rather than an accepted cost. *Fix:* either state the Floor leak in §4 in the same plain terms as
  the ratio leak and in FR-26's consequences, or change the Floor to a per-Partner figure that is
  never combined into a shared number.
- **high** A non-accepting Partner can deadlock the product indefinitely, and no FR names it
  (§5.5, FR-44/FR-45/FR-46) — FR-44 states "A proposal never auto-accepts and never expires"; FR-45
  states "A Period cannot be proposed while any earlier Period is unsealed"; FR-46's escape hatch,
  carry-forward, "requires both Partners to accept, like any Settlement." All three are individually
  reasonable and together they mean one Partner who simply stops tapping Accept freezes every future
  Settlement forever, with dissolution (FR-20) as the only exit. For a product whose §10.1 safety
  framing assumes relationships that go wrong, that is the realistic case, not the exotic one. The
  PRD does not acknowledge it as a decision anywhere — not in §5.5's prose, not in Open Questions.
  *Fix:* add a `[NOTE FOR PM]` and an Open Question naming the stall state, and decide whether
  there is a single-sided path (settle-without-acceptance marked as unaccepted in history, or a
  unilateral carry-forward) or whether permanent stall is the accepted answer.

## Substance over theater — strong

The Vision could not be swapped into another budgeting PRD. "Today one partner owns the spreadsheet,
maintains it, and resents it, while the other never opens it" is a specific diagnosis, and "Six
months in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant" is a specific claim about the end state that
SM-3b then tries to measure. Two personas, not six, and both are load-bearing: the whole of §7's
IA follows from their asymmetry ("A navigation built around ledgers would serve the first and lose
the second. So the default screen is not a ledger").

The NFRs are mostly real. NFR-2's 15 seconds, NFR-1's "every capability except sync, pairing, and
browser authorisation works with no network", and NFR-5's "No service operated by Ledgerleaf can
read Household financial content" are product-defining constraints with consequences elsewhere in
the document, not scalability boilerplate. §8's "Anti-references: budgeting apps that shame;
aggregators that congratulate you on your own money; anything with a mascot" does more work in one
line than most tone sections do in a page, and §8 correctly derives itself from decisions already
made (FR-47's no-verdict rule) rather than from taste.

§4 is the strongest section in the document and earns its "load-bearing" billing — it is referenced
by FR-3, FR-10, FR-11, FR-16, FR-17, FR-18, FR-22, FR-33, FR-34, FR-48 and FR-52 rather than
restated in any of them.

### Findings

- **medium** FR-8 is the one unmotivated requirement (§5.1, FR-8) — "Hide categories from a Personal
  Ledger view" is scoped entirely to the acting Partner's own view of their own Ledger, it is
  mentioned in no UJ, it is absent from §5.1's description, and nothing in §4 needs it. Its three
  consequences are all statements about what it does *not* do. Either it solves a real problem the
  PRD never states (shoulder-surfing? reducing a long category list?) or it is furniture in an
  otherwise lean feature set. *Fix:* state the job it does in §5.1's description, or cut it to §13.2.
- **low** NFR-7 is the one boilerplate NFR (§9) — "WCAG 2.1 AA for the web surface; platform
  accessibility conventions on mobile" is the generic answer. It is at least honestly tagged
  `[ASSUMPTION]` and the one specific clause ("Primary actions sit within one-handed thumb reach")
  is product-derived. *Fix:* if nothing more specific is known yet, leave it — but the one-handed
  clause deserves to be a testable consequence on FR-1 rather than an NFR aside.

## Strategic coherence — strong

The PRD has a thesis and the features serve it rather than accumulate around it. The order of §5 is
the order of the bet: the three-Ledger model (§5.1) makes the privacy claim possible, pairing (§5.2)
is identified as the point of failure the product lives or dies on ("The failure mode is known by
name: the partner who never opened the spreadsheet never opens this either"), and Settle-Up (§5.5)
is "The moment the product earns its keep." §13.1's scope is a coherent problem-solving MVP: it
includes "The §4 Privacy Model in full" as a scope line, which is the right shape — the privacy model
is not a feature you ship 70% of.

The Success Metrics are the best-constructed part of the document. SM-3 splits into 3a/3b
specifically because "pairing is not participation", and each of the four counter-metrics names the
primary it guards and the exact way that primary could be met by making the product worse — SM-C1
"The obvious lever for SM-3b is to nag the second Partner, which produces exactly the dynamic the
product exists to end"; SM-C2 "a rising figure means Partners are rubber-stamping, and SM-4 is being
met by hollowing out the two-sidedness that justifies it." No DAU/MAU anywhere.

Two things dent it: a direct contradiction between §7 and SM-3b about what success for the secondary
Partner even means, and an acquisition number with nothing behind it.

### Findings

- **high** §7 and SM-3b define the secondary Partner's success in opposite terms (§7 surface 1,
  §14 SM-3b) — §7 says of the Today screen: "The secondary Partner may never navigate past this
  screen, and that is a success condition, not a failure", echoing UJ-2's "This single screen is the
  whole of Alex's relationship with the product, and that is a success condition." SM-3b then sets
  the bar at "at least 60% of paired second Partners accept a Settlement (FR-37) *and* record at
  least one Entry of their own (FR-1) within their first two Periods" — both of which require
  navigating past that screen. One of these is wrong, and which one is wrong changes what §5.2 and
  §7 are optimising for. *Fix:* decide whether "retired the household accountant" means the
  secondary Partner participates or means they never have to, then rewrite either §7/UJ-2's success
  condition or SM-3b's gates to match. This is a thesis-level question, not a wording fix.
- **medium** SM-1's 1,000 Households is unanchored (§14) — "1,000 Households with an active
  subscription at 12 months from launch" is the metric that validates "the product proposition as a
  whole", and nothing in the PRD connects it to how those Households are reached. The thesis makes
  acquisition structurally hard — the product's pitch is *more* manual work in exchange for privacy,
  to a two-person household where both must install, and §10.3 rules out the paid-growth budget by
  implication. SM-5 ("the on-ramp away from the spreadsheet") is the closest the document comes to a
  demand thesis. *Fix:* one or two sentences anchoring SM-1 — the channel assumption and the
  conversion assumption behind the number — or demote it to a directional target and let SM-2/SM-3
  carry the validation weight.

## Done-ness clarity — adequate

Per-FR, the craft is high and well above what most PRDs offer. The consequences are overwhelmingly
testable and several are unusually disciplined about negative conditions: FR-1's "No confirmation
dialog is presented at any point in the flow", FR-6's "No edit or delete affordance is offered on a
committed Transfer", FR-47's "It records nothing; running a check creates no Entry and leaves no
trace for the other Partner", FR-20's "No notification, record, or export discloses where either
Partner was when they acted." FR-9's six consequences specify the full edit lattice (own-personal /
shared-open-Period / sealed) rather than hand-waving at "editable where appropriate". I found no
instances of "handles gracefully", "reasonable performance", or "user-friendly" anywhere in §5.

The gap is one level up. The FRs specify every interaction with the money model and never specify
the money model. Three concrete holes follow, and all three sit directly under the two FRs the whole
product rests on (FR-47 and FR-35).

### Findings

- **critical** What an envelope's balance *is* is never defined, and three FRs assume different
  answers (FR-5, FR-22, FR-23, FR-47) — FR-22 says an envelope displays "category, planned amount,
  rolled-over amount, spent, and remaining", which reads as `remaining = planned + rolled − spent`,
  a plan-based model. FR-5 then says "Transfers into a Shared Envelope are reflected in that
  Envelope's **available balance**" — a fourth quantity that appears nowhere in FR-22's list and
  implies a cash-based model where an envelope holds money actually moved into it. §5.1 reinforces
  the cash model ("Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit **Transfer** — to fund shared
  Envelopes at the start of a Period"), while FR-23 reinforces the plan model ("Total planned across
  Shared envelopes may exceed the Floor; the shortfall is shown rather than blocked"). FR-47, the
  secondary Partner's entire relationship with the product, "reports the envelope's remaining
  balance" without saying which of these it means — and the two give different numbers whenever a
  Partner under-funds a plan. An engineer cannot build FR-47 from this PRD. *Fix:* state the model
  once in §5.3's description — plan-based with Transfers as a separate reality check, or cash-based
  with planned amounts as targets — define `remaining` and `available balance` in §3 as one term or
  two, and make FR-5, FR-22, FR-23 and FR-47 use it verbatim.
- **critical** Settle-Up's inputs are unspecified where Transfers are concerned (§5.3, FR-35) —
  §5.3 states the rule as "Settle-Up compares what each Partner *paid* against their share of what
  was *spent*", and FR-35 says the statement "lists every Shared Ledger Transaction in the Period".
  A Transfer is, per §3, "an explicit Transaction pair moving money between two Ledgers", so a
  Partner funding Ours from their Personal Ledger creates a Shared Ledger Transaction — which FR-35
  would list, with no merchant and no Split Rule, and which §5.3's rule would count as something
  that Partner "paid". If Sam transfers £1,000 into Ours and Alex transfers £500, that imbalance is
  either the central thing Settle-Up must account for or something it must explicitly exclude, and
  the PRD says neither. This is the product's one load-bearing computation. *Fix:* add a consequence
  to FR-35 stating whether Transfers into the Shared Ledger are included, excluded, or netted, and
  extend §5.3's one-line rule to cover them — the existing rollover carve-out ("A rolled-over
  balance is excluded from Settle-Up and is attributed to neither Partner", FR-25) is the right
  model to follow.
- **high** No FR records income, though FR-26, FR-27 and FR-28 all depend on one (§5.3) — FR-27's
  first consequence is "Income recorded above the Floor accrues to the Unallocated Pool", and its
  third is "No envelope can be funded from income that has not been recorded." Nothing in the PRD
  says how income is recorded. FR-1 quick-add takes "amount and merchant"; §3 defines an Entry as
  "one real-world payment **or receipt**" but no FR distinguishes a receipt, flags an Entry as
  income, or routes above-Floor amounts to the Pool. FR-26 covers income *history* for deriving the
  Floor, which is a different act. UJ-4's climax — "when Alex's invoice lands mid-month at £4,100,
  the surplus goes to the Unallocated Pool" — has no FR behind it. *Fix:* add an FR for recording
  income (which Ledger receives it, how it is marked, how the above-Floor surplus is computed per
  Period and per Ledger), and add **Income** to §3.
- **medium** The Floor's derivation is stated two different ways (§3, §5.3, FR-26) — §3 and FR-26
  say "the lowest of the last six months of **combined** income"; §5.3's description says "the lowest
  of the last six months of income, **each Partner entering their own**". `min(A+B)` over six months
  and `min(A) + min(B)` are different numbers, and the second is the more conservative one a
  freelancer household would want. *Fix:* pick one and use the same phrase in all three places.
- **medium** Personal envelopes have no funding basis (§5.3, FR-23, FR-26) — the Floor is defined as
  a Household-level figure from combined income, but FR-23 lets each Partner create envelopes on
  their own Personal Ledger, and FR-27's `[ASSUMPTION]` gives each Personal Ledger its own
  Unallocated Pool. It is not stated what a Personal envelope funds against: the household Floor, the
  owner's own income, or nothing at all. Under §4 the household Floor cannot be decomposed per
  Partner without disclosing income. *Fix:* state in §5.3 whether Personal envelopes fund against the
  owner's own income floor (a per-Partner figure, never combined) and add it to FR-23's consequences.
- **low** FR-1's 15-second budget mixes human and system time (FR-1, NFR-2) — "A single-Ledger Entry
  completes in under 15 seconds for a one-handed user, measured from tapping quick-add to the entry
  being committed" is testable in principle but the number is dominated by typing speed, so the
  result depends entirely on an unstated test population and input. NFR-2 rightly calls it "a
  product-defining budget". *Fix:* name the test condition (a stated task, a defined cohort or a
  scripted input) so a regression against SM-C3 is detectable.

## Scope honesty — strong

§12 is a real Non-Goals section doing real work, and its most valuable move is distinguishing
permanent non-goals from deferrals — "**Bank linking** — permanent non-goal, not a deferral" versus
"**Automatic categorisation** — deferred". §13.2 repeats the distinction per line. "**Not a
zero-effort product.** Manual effort is the price of the privacy guarantee, charged openly" is a
non-goal that costs the product something and is stated anyway.

§16 is better than most Assumptions Indexes because it separates "Confirmed with the product owner
during drafting" from "Open — awaiting confirmation", so a reader knows which inferences carry
weight. The §13.2 note on receipt OCR — "`[NOTE FOR PM: this is the one deferred item that was raised
unprompted and may be emotionally load-bearing]`" — is a genuinely useful piece of provenance that a
less honest PRD would have dropped. Recurring transactions are flagged as deferred *by omission*
rather than quietly left out, which is the right call for the one gap most likely to bite.

Open-items density is appropriate: 17 open assumptions, 8 Open Questions, 3 `[NOTE FOR PM]` callouts
for a PRD that declares itself "the first artifact in the chain" with no UX or architecture document
yet. These are not blockers at this stage; they would be if this were a green light.

### Findings

- **high** The MVP's size is never treated as a scope decision (§13.1, §10.3) — §13.1 puts all seven
  Features, 52 FRs, two native platforms and a web surface in scope, and nothing anywhere proposes a
  thin slice, a build order, or a candidate for deferral if the thing runs long. This sits directly
  against §10.3's own framing — "Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive
  that" — which applies the solo-founder constraint to running costs but never to build scope. Among
  the seven, §5.4 (import, 5 FRs, desktop web only, per-bank mappings, duplicate detection) and
  §5.2's browser-session surface (FR-18, FR-19, plus the addendum's unresolved key-transport work)
  are the obvious candidates: both are the spreadsheet-keeper's convenience, and neither is needed
  for UJ-1, UJ-2, UJ-4 or UJ-6. *Fix:* add a §13.3 naming the sequencing — what the first shippable
  slice is, and which in-scope Features are the first to go if the timeline moves. De-scoping under
  pressure later is worse than naming the order now.

## Downstream usability — adequate

This matters more than usual here: §0 states "**No UX or architecture document exists yet.** This PRD
is the first artifact in the chain", so UX, architecture and story creation all source from this
document alone. On the mechanical side it holds up well — FR-1 through FR-52 are contiguous with no
gaps or duplicates, every `FR-n` reference in the document resolves to a defined FR, UJ-1 through
UJ-8 are complete, each UJ names Sam or Alex inline and carries its own context, and the §16 index
round-trips cleanly against the inline `[ASSUMPTION]` tags. §4 is referenced by section number from
eleven FRs rather than restated, which is exactly the pattern that lets a UX workflow pull one
Feature out and still know the privacy rule.

The problems are vocabulary, not structure. §3 sets an unusually strict rule on itself — "Downstream
readers and workflows must use these terms exactly; no synonyms elsewhere in this PRD" — and the PRD
then breaks it in the two places a downstream reader is most likely to parse literally.

### Findings

- **high** "Ours" and "Mine" are undefined synonyms for Shared Ledger and Personal Ledger, including
  inside a testable consequence (§3, FR-13, §5.3, §7) — neither appears in §3, and both are used as
  if they were defined terms: FR-13's consequence reads "no new shared Entries, **Transfers into
  Ours**, proposals, or Settlements"; §5.3 says "A Shared envelope that rolls over keeps its balance
  **in Ours**"; §7's navigation lists "**Ledgers** — Ours and Mine". In UJ prose this is harmless
  colour, but inside an FR consequence and inside the IA it is the term an engineer or UX workflow
  will extract. *Fix:* either add **Ours** and **Mine** to §3 as the product's user-facing labels for
  Shared Ledger and the acting Partner's own Personal Ledger, and say which register each belongs to,
  or replace them with the glossary terms everywhere outside §2.3.
- **medium** Transfers break the Entry/Transaction model stated in §3 (§3, FR-5) — §3 says
  "**Transaction** — ... Belongs to exactly one Entry" and "An Entry has a Payer and produces one or
  more Transactions", but §3 also defines a Transfer as "an explicit Transaction pair" and FR-5
  collects only "amount, from-Ledger, and to-Ledger; a note is optional. No other field is
  collected" — so a Transfer's Transactions belong to no Entry and have no Payer. Anyone building the
  data model from §3 will hit this immediately, and it compounds the Settle-Up gap above (a
  Transaction with no Payer appearing in an FR-35 statement that lists a Payer per line). *Fix:*
  either give Transfers a parent Entry with a Payer, or amend §3 so a Transaction belongs to at most
  one Entry and state that Transfer Transactions have no Payer — then make FR-35 say what the
  statement shows for them.
- **low** FR-23 is realized by no UJ (§2.3, FR-23) — UJ-4 lists "FR-22, FR-24, FR-25, FR-26, FR-27,
  FR-28" and skips FR-23, the FR that creates an envelope in the first place, presumably because UJ-4
  is the copy-last-month path. Creating a Household's first envelopes is a first-run moment with no
  narrative anywhere. *Fix:* add FR-23 to UJ-4's realizes list, or note in §5.3 that first-Period
  envelope creation is a UX-owned flow.

## Shape fit — strong

The shape matches the product. This is a two-sided consumer application with meaningful UX, so UJs
are load-bearing rather than ceremony, and §2.3 treats them that way: eight journeys, each with a
named protagonist, a physical setting ("in the car park", "at the kitchen table, on a laptop", "from
two different rooms"), an explicit **Climax** and **Resolution**, and an inline FR mapping. The
protagonist pair is doing real work — Sam and Alex are the two personas from §2 instantiated, and
UJ-2 and UJ-5 would be different products if they were the same person. None of the eight is a
floating UJ written to fill a template; UJ-8 in particular (dissolution) earns its place by driving
FR-20, FR-21 and the whole of §10.1.

The chain-top position is handled correctly. The addendum is a genuinely good split: it holds the
sync and key-exchange mechanism, browser session key transport, the Settlement hash construction and
the import pipeline's internals, with the division stated as a principle — "The PRD carries the
*promise* (the operator cannot read household financial data); the *mechanism* ... belongs here." The
addendum is also honest about which of its open items have product surface ("device-loss /
key-recovery story. Has real product surface ... so the user-visible half may be pulled back into the
PRD once decided"), and FR-50 and FR-52 show that pull-back has already happened for the half that
matters to the user.

Nothing is over-formalized. There is no stakeholder matrix, no RACI, no phased rollout, and §9's
NFRs are nine lines rather than a conformance table — right for a solo-built commercial product. The
one place the shape under-serves the stakes is build sequencing, covered under Scope honesty.

## Mechanical notes

- **ID continuity: clean.** FR-1 … FR-52 are contiguous, uniquely defined, with no duplicates and no
  gaps. Every `FR-n` cross-reference in the document resolves to a defined FR. UJ-1 … UJ-8 likewise.
  SM-1 … SM-5 and SM-C1 … SM-C4 are consistent, and every SM names what it validates.
- **Assumptions Index round-trip: clean.** Every inline `[ASSUMPTION]` appears in §16, and every §16
  entry traces back to an inline tag or a §5 feature preamble. The confirmed/open split is accurate.
- **Broken cross-reference: §5.1 "Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2"** (line 264). UJ-2 is the affordability check
  and declares itself as realizing FR-47 and FR-48, which live in §5.6 — which also, correctly, says
  "Realizes UJ-2". §5.1's FRs (FR-1 … FR-11) have nothing to do with UJ-2. Drop UJ-2 from §5.1.
- **Glossary drift: Envelope.** §3 defines **Envelope** capitalized; §5.3 uses lowercase "envelope"
  almost throughout ("the envelope list", "Shared envelopes", "a Personal Ledger envelope"), as do
  FR-22 … FR-28 and FR-47/FR-48. Harmless to a human, but §3 asserts verbatim usage. Normalize, or
  soften §3's rule to cover case.
- **Glossary gaps.** "Ours" / "Mine" (see Downstream usability), and **Income**, which is used as a
  modelled quantity in §3's own Floor and Unallocated Pool definitions, in FR-26, FR-27 and FR-28,
  without being defined.
- **Terminology: "the operator".** Used in §1, §5.7, FR-50 and §10.3 to mean the party running the
  service. It is doing load-bearing work in the privacy promise and is not in §3.
- **Required sections.** All present for the agreed stakes and product type. Enterprise ceremony
  sections (stakeholders/approvals, business case, rollout plan, operational SLAs, formal compliance)
  are excluded by agreement and are not counted against the PRD here.

The PRD is a faithful carrier of *mechanics*. All three corrections the run made mid-flight
(lapsed subscription, income-ratio honesty, second device) landed correctly — see §2. The damage is
concentrated in three places: the product owner's own words, several stale markers that now
contradict decisions the owner later made, and a tier of untagged inferences that read as settled
decisions but have no memlog origin.

## 1. Lost decisions

Entries whose substance appears in neither document.

### L-1 — The vision pitch, in the owner's own words (memlog line 27)

> `(decision) Vision pitch (user's words): 'Your money, your partner's money, and the money you
> share — finally three separate piles, with the month-end argument done for you in one tap, and no
> bank password ever leaving your phone.'`

Logged as a *decision*, and explicitly marked **(user's words)** — the owner was fixing a form of
words, not just a concept.

**What the PRD says instead:** §1 paraphrases the concept across three paragraphs ("three genuinely
separate piles", "never asks for a bank credential and never will"). The sentence itself appears
nowhere. There is no pitch line, no positioning statement, no quotable one-liner anywhere in the
document, and §8 Aesthetic & Tone — the section that should hold voice — is tagged entirely inferred
and does not reference the pitch at all.

Two specific losses inside it:

- **"the month-end argument done for you in one tap."** The PRD's Settle-Up is deliberately *not*
  one tap: it is a two-sided Propose → review → Accept flow (FR-36, FR-37) that UJ-6 budgets at five
  minutes across two people in two rooms. That may well be the better design, but the owner's stated
  promise and the designed mechanic diverge, and **nothing in the PRD flags the divergence.** It is
  lost rather than resolved.
- **"no bank password ever leaving your phone."** The PRD renders this as a negative capability
  ("never asks for a bank credential", §10.2 "No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or
  transmitted"). Accurate, but the owner's framing was the *felt* one — your password stays on your
  phone — which is a different and warmer claim than a policy prohibition. The FR structure converted
  a reassurance into a constraint.

**Verdict: lost.** Add the sentence verbatim to §1 as the stated pitch, and either reconcile "one tap"
with FR-36/FR-37 or record that the owner's phrasing was superseded by the two-sided design.

### L-2 — The rigor calibration (memlog line 9)

> `(decision) Stakes: serious commercial side project (paying subscribers); rigor above internal
> tooling, below enterprise launch`

**What the PRD says:** silent. §0 Document Purpose states who the PRD is for and how to read it, but
records no calibration of depth. §11 and §10.3 carry "solo founder" economics; nothing carries the
*stakes* judgement. This is the entry that justifies every "we are not doing enterprise ceremony"
call downstream (memlog line 24), and a downstream UX or architecture reader has no record of the
bar they are being held to. Low blast radius, but it is a decision and it is gone.

### L-3 — "Keys never leave devices" as a stated product promise (memlog line 26)

> `(decision) v1 also includes a lightweight desktop web app scoped to CSV import and month-end
> settle-up only — same E2E-encrypted data, keys never leave devices`

The scope half is reflected (§6). The promise half is not stated anywhere in the PRD in those terms.
§6 says the web app "holds no standing access"; FR-18 says the phone "grants that browser session its
keys, delivered encrypted" — which is a mechanism, not a promise, and is in fact a *weaker* claim
than the owner made. Memlog line 63 (browser authorisation) refines the mechanism but does not
retract the promise. NFR-5 covers the server ("No readable server-side copy") but not the device
boundary. The addendum lists the question but the PRD never makes the commitment.

**Verdict: degraded to silence.** The owner asserted a user-facing guarantee; the PRD carries only
the plumbing.

### L-4 — "SEVERE" as a risk rating (memlog line 85)

> `(assumption) A partner losing their only device recovers the Shared Ledger by re-pairing, but
> their own Personal Ledger is unrecoverable without a second device or an export — SEVERE, unresolved`

The *facts* survive (FR-50, §5.7, Open Question 4). The owner's severity rating does not. The PRD has
**no risk section at all**, so there is no place where this sits next to anything else as the worst
thing in the document. OQ-4 is item four of eight in a list where item six is "price and trial length",
giving a data-loss-with-no-recovery risk the same visual weight as a pricing to-do. Compare OQ-1,
which the drafter did mark "**Phase-blocker for architecture**" — the owner's own SEVERE flag got no
equivalent.

**Verdict: the fact is kept, the weight is lost.**

### L-5 — The Finalize / reviewer gate the owner authorised (memlog line 92)

> `(decision) User authorised: draft all remaining sections in one pass, then run Finalize including
> the reviewer gate with all reviewers in parallel, applying what they raise; real decisions deferred
> to the end`

This is two authorisations. The first (draft in one pass) was executed — memlog line 93 records the
full draft. **The second — run Finalize including the reviewer gate with all reviewers in parallel,

drafting findings. The PRD's status is still `draft` and the stale markers catalogued in §2 below are
exactly what a reviewer gate would have caught.

**Verdict: an instruction from the product owner that appears never to have been carried out, and
is not recorded as skipped.** This is the single highest-value item in this reconciliation, because
it is the step that would have found most of the rest.

### C-4 — FR-26 claims an income-privacy guarantee the Floor mechanism does not support

FR-26: "Individual income figures are never disclosed to the other Partner, per §4; only the **Floor**
and any derived ratio are shared."

Memlog line 38 established the governing principle: *reword the promise honestly rather than engineer
around it* — applied to the ratio leak. The same leak exists in the Floor and is **not** disclosed.
Per memlog line 73 and the §3 Glossary, the Floor defaults to "the lowest of the last six months of
combined income" and is visible to both Partners. A Partner who knows their own six-month history and
sees the shared combined Floor can solve for the other's figure in the governing month — the exact
inference §4 ¶3 goes out of its way to admit for the ratio.

This is not a lost decision; it is the PRD applying the owner's honesty principle in one place and
silently not applying it in another. **Flag for the owner: either extend the §4 disclosure language to
the Floor, or record a decision that the Floor leak is acceptable.**

### C-5 — FR-42 narrows the back-dating rule and leaves the owner's actual case unspecified

Memlog line 53: `Back-dated transactions: a 28-Oct receipt entered 3 Nov lands in November, flagged
'dated October', and settles in November. Settled months are never reopened.`

FR-42 scopes itself to "A Transaction dated **within a sealed Period** but entered after it sealed".
But the owner's worked example is a 28-Oct receipt entered 3 November — and per FR-35, October's
Settle-Up only becomes *available* on 1 November and seals only on both accepts (FR-37). On 3
November October is very likely **open**, not sealed. The owner's own example therefore falls outside
FR-42's stated trigger, and the PRD does not say what happens to it.

The owner stated a flat rule (entry date determines Period, full stop). The PRD restated it as a
conditional rule and lost the common case. **Material gap in a mechanic the owner specified by
example.**

### C-6 — Title still marked unconfirmed

PRD line 9: `*Working title — confirm.*` The memlog names the product Ledgerleaf from line 6 onward
and never records it as provisional. Trivial, but it is a question the PRD is asking that the memlog
already answered.

## 3. Qualitative content silently dropped

This is where a memlog-to-FR distillation characteristically loses the most, so it is worth being
precise about what *survived*, to make clear that the losses below are not inevitable.

**Preserved well — the drafter did carry texture through in these places:**

| Memlog | Where it survived |
|---|---|
| line 43 "append-only history keeps the record honest" | §5.1: "nobody can quietly rewrite what happened. That property is load-bearing for the product's promise" |
| line 82 "a product that retires the household accountant should not install a new one" | §5.6, almost verbatim; echoed in §8 "the product reports and never judges" |
| line 38 "reword the promise honestly rather than engineer around it" | §4 ¶3 — the full reasoning, not just the rule |
| line 70 SAFETY framing | §10.1 "This is a safety requirement before it is a convenience one"; §5.2 "a person who needs to leave must be able to, now, and without asking" |
| line 23 "so neither partner can re-litigate" | §1 "settled by looking it up rather than by memory" |
| line 28 target end-state | §1 ¶3, as a dated six-months-in picture |
| line 73 "Nothing is promised to an envelope until the money exists" | §5.3 "A freelancer's good month is not a promise, and Ledgerleaf will not spend it until it has arrived" |

That is a high hit rate. The losses are specific.

### Q-1 — The owner's voice is nowhere in the document (highest-value gap)

The single memlog entry explicitly marked **"(user's words)"** (line 27) is the one piece of prose the
owner authored, and it is the one piece that did not make it in. Everything in §1 is the drafter's
prose about the owner's ideas. See L-1.

The consequence is structural, not cosmetic: §8 Aesthetic & Tone — the section that governs every
string the product will ever show a user — is tagged `[ASSUMPTION] — inferred from the product's
stated purpose and from decisions already made ... **Not specified directly.**` That is true only
because the one directly-specified piece of voice in the record was not used. The owner *did* supply a
sample of how Ledgerleaf should sound, and §8 was written as though they had not.

### Q-2 — "One tap" became a five-minute two-sided workflow with no note of the trade

The owner's stated feel for the product's central moment was *done for you in one tap*. The PRD's
Settle-Up is a considered, two-sided, propose-and-accept protocol whose §5.5 rationale is strong
("a number one person computed alone is exactly the spreadsheet problem Ledgerleaf exists to
retire"). The reasoning is excellent and probably right.

But the owner asked for effortlessness and received deliberation, and **no line in the PRD
acknowledges that the design chose against the owner's stated feel.** UJ-6's "five minutes" and §1's
"settle-up takes five minutes" are presented as the goal rather than as a revision of one. The
*mechanic* was reasoned about; the *felt promise* it displaced was not.

This is the archetypal FR-flattening failure: the requirement structure has somewhere to put
"Proposing notifies the other Partner" and nowhere to put "this is supposed to feel like nothing."

### Q-3 — "Portability as part of trust posture" survived; "privacy as a trade the user accepts" partly did not

Memlog line 19 (`portability as part of trust posture`) is well carried by §5.7 and §11 ("A product
whose pitch is trust cannot hold data for ransom").

Memlog line 29 — `Core trade the product asks the user to accept: some manual effort in exchange for
privacy and fairness` — survives as §12's "Not a zero-effort product. Manual effort is the price of
the privacy guarantee, **charged openly**" and §2.2's "that trade is the product". Good. But the
third term, **fairness**, dropped out of both restatements: both render the trade as effort-for-privacy.
Fairness is half of what the owner said the user is buying, and it is the half the entire Settle-Up
and Split Rule apparatus exists to deliver. §1 keeps it ("in exchange for fairness and privacy"); §12
and §2.2 do not.

### Q-4 — The reason the desktop web app is narrow was replaced with a different reason

Memlog line 26 scopes the web app to import and settle-up and gives no reason beyond scope. §6 and
§5.4 supply one: "the two tasks that are genuinely worse on a phone" / "reconciling a month of rows is
miserable on a phone". That rationale is plausible and well written — but it is the **drafter's**
rationale, presented in the same register as the owner's decisions and untagged. The owner's actual
stated reason (if any) is not in the record, so this is invention filling a vacuum rather than
distortion. Noted as texture *added*, not lost — but it should be tagged as inferred.

### Q-5 — The "SEVERE" tone of the device-loss problem

See L-4. §5.7's prose is actually good on this ("Two devices, and a lost phone is an inconvenience.
One device, and it is a loss nobody can undo"), which makes the flattening in §15 more conspicuous:
the owner's alarm lives in a feature description and not in the list of things that are unresolved.

as something the product owner settled.

Dissolution and export are discussed at length (lines 68–70); data deletion never is. FR-51 is wholly invented and untagged. |
