# Ledgerleaf PRD — Privacy & Safety Coherence Review

**Date:** 2026-10-01
**Scope:** `prd.md` (all sections, with §4, §10, and every FR in §5 read closely) and `addendum.md`.
**Lens:** Does the product keep the privacy promise it makes, and is the safety surface in §10.1
adequate for the threat model it names?

---

## Verdict

**The privacy claim in §4 is not kept by the FRs in §5.** §4 makes two absolute statements — that a
Partner sees *nothing* of the other's Personal Ledger, with "no aggregate that hints at the detail,"
and that a disclosure reveals nothing else "inferable" — and then §5 defines at least four standing
channels that violate both, plus a dozen narrower ones. Three of the four are not edge cases: they
are the Floor, the Unallocated Pool, and the category set, which is to say they are the budgeting
model, the irregular-income model, and the taxonomy every Transaction must use. Every Household hits
all three on day one.

The safety section (§10.1) is a good list of four things, written by someone who has thought about
leaving. It is also written almost entirely about *dissolution*, which is the last five seconds of
the problem. It has nothing to say about the months before it: the device that an abusive partner
can plant, the notification channel they can hold open, the settlement chain they can freeze, the
subscription they can cancel, the export they can compel, or the category the leaving partner cannot
create without announcing it.

Fourth, and structurally: §4 is described in §0 as "cross-cutting and load-bearing," and almost none
of its mechanism exists. The Glossary marks the Personal Ledger's "Visibility boundary TBD" while §4
states it as settled. The addendum, which §0 says is "where the means of keeping it are worked out,"
contains four bullets and six items marked "Open," none of which is *how Personal Ledger data is kept
off the other Partner's device*. The promise is currently unbacked.

This is fixable, and most of it is fixable in the PRD rather than in architecture — but not by
patching individual FRs. §4 needs to be rewritten from "nothing is inferable" to an explicit,
exhaustive enumeration of every channel that crosses the boundary, with the ones that cannot be
closed named and priced. The document's own honesty about the income-proportional Split Rule
("Ledgerleaf does not claim otherwise") is exactly the right instinct, applied in exactly one place
out of ten.

**Counts:** 7 critical, 11 high, 9 medium, 4 low (31 findings).

---

## 1. Leak paths

### PS-01 — CRITICAL — The Floor is a live income oracle, under *every* Split Rule
*§4 ¶3; FR-26; §5.3 Description; UJ-4*

§4 says individual income is never shared, that only a derived ratio is, and — explicitly — that
"the even and custom-per-category Split Rules remain available and **reveal nothing**."

FR-26 then defines the Floor as "the lowest of the last six months of **combined** income," derived
from both Partners' figures, **shared**, and automatically updated "as either changes."

A Partner who knows their own income — which every Partner does — can:

1. Subtract their own figure from the Floor to obtain the other's income in the binding month.
2. Watch the Floor move when the other edits their income history, and read the delta exactly.
3. **Probe it.** FR-26 gates changing the *derivation method* behind mutual acceptance but places no
   gate at all on editing one's own income figures. A Partner can edit their own income up and down
   and watch whether the Floor follows, determining for each of the six months whose income is the
   binding minimum, and by how much.

Over six months of observation this yields the other Partner's income **time series**, not a single
figure. None of this involves the income-proportional Split Rule, so the one disclosure statement the
product does make (FR-34) never fires. A Household on an even split believes, on §4's own authority,
that nothing is revealed.

This is the single clearest contradiction in the document: §4 ¶3 asserts a property that FR-26 ¶1
removes.

**Needed:** either the Floor is derived locally per-Partner and only a non-invertible household
figure is shared (hard — any shared scalar derived from two private scalars is invertible by either
holder), or the Floor becomes a manually agreed number both Partners enter and accept, or §4 drops
the claim and FR-26 gains a disclosure statement equivalent to FR-34's. The third option is the only
one that is honest and cheap; it also means the product has no privacy-preserving Split Rule at all,
which is a product decision the owner has not been asked to make.

### PS-02 — CRITICAL — The shared Unallocated Pool discloses each Partner's above-Floor income, continuously
*FR-27, FR-28; §5.3 Description; UJ-4*

FR-27: "Income recorded above the Floor accrues to the Unallocated Pool rather than to any envelope."
FR-27's `[ASSUMPTION]`: "the Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool **visible to both Partners**."
UJ-4 makes it concrete: "when Alex's invoice lands mid-month at £4,100, the surplus goes to the
Unallocated Pool, and the Household assigns it to envelopes *then*."

Income is private under §4. Above-Floor income is income. If the surplus lands in a Pool both
Partners can see, then **Sam reads Alex's monthly income, to the penny, every month**, by watching
the Pool rise. Alex's variable income is the entire reason the Floor/Pool machinery exists, and the
secondary persona is a freelancer — so the Partner whose income this leaks is the Partner the product
is built around.

FR-28 compounds it: "An unassigned Pool balance carries into the next Period rather than lapsing," so
the figure is cumulative and historical, and "Shared Pool assignment is available to either Partner,"
so one Partner can also *spend* the other's surplus income.

Two further defects in how this is recorded:

- The decision is parked as an unconfirmed `[ASSUMPTION]` in §16's open list. A load-bearing privacy
  decision — arguably the most consequential one in §5.3 — is sitting in a "confirm this" queue
  alongside CSV mapping names and WCAG levels.
- §4 does not mention the Unallocated Pool at all, so §4's "exactly two cases" enumeration is already
  false before §5.3 is read.

**Needed:** above-Floor income accrues to the *earner's own* Personal Pool by default. Moving surplus
into the Shared Pool becomes an explicit, owner-initiated act — which makes it a §4 disclosure of a
known amount, consistent with the rest of the model.

### PS-03 — CRITICAL — The Household category set makes creating a category a disclosure
*FR-7, FR-8; §4 ¶1; §10.1*

FR-7: "the **single category set shared by all three** of the Household's Ledgers," and "Changes to
the category set apply to the Household and are **visible to both Partners**."

So every Personal Ledger Transaction must be categorised from a vocabulary both Partners can see, and
**adding to that vocabulary is a disclosure**. §4 ¶1 says a Partner opening the other's Personal
Ledger sees "no Transactions, no categories" and that "there is no aggregate that hints at the
detail." The category set is precisely an aggregate that hints at the detail, and it is pushed to the
other Partner the moment it changes.

The privacy consequence is bad. The **safety** consequence is severe. A person preparing to leave
needs to track money that must not be announced: a solicitor's fees, a deposit, a therapist, a
locksmith, travel. Under FR-7 they cannot create a category for any of it without the other Partner
seeing the category appear. Their alternatives are to mislabel it — degrading the only record they
may later need — or to keep it outside the product, which defeats the product.

FR-8 ("Hide categories from a Personal Ledger view") looks like the mitigation and is not: it is
"scoped to the hiding Partner's own view of their own Personal Ledger," and explicitly "remains
available in the Shared Ledger and **in the other Partner's views**." It hides the category from the
person who wants it hidden, from nobody else. See also PS-28.

**Needed:** Personal Ledgers get a private category namespace — the Household set plus owner-only
additions, with owner-only additions never synced. If a privately-categorised Transaction is later
disclosed (FR-10/FR-3), the category is stripped or remapped (which PS-08 requires anyway).

### PS-04 — CRITICAL — An Entry can be allocated, and a Transfer made, into the other Partner's Personal Ledger
*FR-2, FR-5; Glossary "Transfer"*

FR-2, consequence 4: "An Entry may allocate across **any combination of the Household's three
Ledgers**." The Household's three Ledgers are Ours, mine, and **theirs**.

FR-5: "A Partner can move money between **two Ledgers of their Household**." Its consequences list
required fields and atomicity and place no restriction whatsoever on which Ledgers.

As written, Sam can:

- Allocate part of an Entry into Alex's Personal Ledger — writing a Transaction into the ledger §4
  says Sam cannot see, and thereby knowing a Transaction that exists in it;
- Transfer *out of* Alex's Personal Ledger, which is both an unconsented debit and a **balance
  oracle** (a transfer that succeeds proves the balance was at least X; a transfer that is refused
  proves it was less). Repeated, this binary-searches the balance §4 says is never revealed. §4's
  "no balance total" is defeated without ever displaying a balance.

I believe this is drafting oversight rather than intent — §5.1's prose says "each Ledger sees only
its own share" — but it is written as a positive capability in a testable consequence, and a
downstream story writer will implement what FR-2 says.

**Needed:** FR-2 and FR-5 each gain an explicit consequence: a Partner may allocate to, and transfer
between, only the Shared Ledger and their *own* Personal Ledger. The other Partner's Personal Ledger
is not a selectable destination or source anywhere in the product.

### PS-05 — CRITICAL — Second-device pairing and browser sessions are an unguarded surveillance vector
*FR-52, FR-18, FR-19; §10.1 "No activity surveillance"*

FR-52: "A Partner's second device carries a **full copy of everything that Partner can see,
including their Personal Ledger**," pairing "does not involve the other Partner," and "A Partner's
second device is invisible to the other Partner."

FR-18: scanning a QR from the phone "grants that browser session its keys," the session "expires
after 12 hours **idle**," and it "exposes only what the authorising Partner can see" — which is
everything, Personal Ledger included.

In a coercive relationship, physical access to an unlocked phone for sixty seconds is the baseline
assumption, not the worst case. Under these FRs that access yields:

- A permanently paired device, under the abuser's control, receiving a live mirror of the victim's
  Personal Ledger forever;
- or a browser session whose 12-hour *idle* timer resets on every poll, making it indefinite in
  practice.

The FRs supply no counter-measures:

- **No notification** on second-device pairing. FR-52 has five consequences and none of them says the
  Partner is told, persistently, that a second device exists. ("Invisible to the other Partner" is
  about the wrong person.)
- **No listing requirement.** FR-19 requires *browser sessions* to be listed with start times; there
  is no equivalent FR for devices. §7 mentions "devices and browser sessions" in Settings, but §7 is
  flagged as entirely inferred and carries no testable consequence.
- **No notification** on browser-session authorisation either — FR-18 lists five consequences, none
  is "the Partner is notified."
- **FR-52: "Either of a Partner's devices can unpair the other."** The planted device can evict the
  victim's real phone.
- No re-authentication, no periodic "you have 2 devices" reminder, no geographic or
  first-use-elsewhere signal (and §10.1 forbids the location signal that would otherwise catch it).

§10.1's "No activity surveillance — nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked
at, or what they checked" is true of the designed features and completely false in the presence of a
planted device, which exposes all of it plus the contents.

**Needed:** FR-52 and FR-18 each gain: a notification to all of that Partner's existing devices on
pairing/authorisation; a persistent, non-dismissable device list with last-seen times; a required
re-confirmation from an *already-trusted* device; and removal of "either device can unpair the other"
in favour of a designated primary. Consider a cooling period before a new device receives Personal
Ledger history.

### PS-06 — CRITICAL — Dissolution broadcasts the moment of exit, and deletion is gated behind an export
*FR-20, FR-51, FR-21; §10.1; UJ-8*

§10.1 and UJ-8 get the *location* question right and miss the *time* question entirely.

FR-20: "Dissolution takes effect immediately," and "The remaining Partner is informed that the
Household was dissolved." §8 permits this as a notification. So the remaining Partner receives a push
notification, in real time, at the moment the other acts. In the scenario §10.1 is written for, the
two people are frequently in the same building. "She did it four minutes ago" is the single most
dangerous fact the product holds, and the product sends it unprompted.

There is no:

- **Quiet or deferred exit.** No option to stop syncing now and surface the dissolution notice later,
  at a time the leaving Partner chooses, or on the other Partner's next app open rather than by push.
- **Local-only severance.** Nothing lets a Partner stop their device from sharing *before* the formal
  dissolution that announces itself.
- **Duress affordance.** No decoy passcode, no quick-hide, no way to make the app not look like what
  it is.

And FR-51 actively obstructs: "**Deletion is offered only after an export has been taken or
explicitly declined.**" A person deleting under time pressure or duress is routed through an export
dialogue first. Worse, if they accept it, a plaintext CSV of their entire Personal Ledger lands in
the phone's Files/Downloads — a readable artefact in a place the other Partner can reach, created by
the act of trying to be safe. The guardrail written to prevent accidental data loss is a hazard in
the one scenario §10.1 exists for.

**Needed:** an explicit *safe exit* path in §10.1 and in §5.2's FRs: severance takes effect
immediately and silently on the acting device; the notice to the other Partner is delivered without
push, on their next app open, or on a delay the leaving Partner sets; deletion is always available in
one action with no export prompt; export produces an encrypted archive by default (see PS-13).

### PS-07 — CRITICAL — §4 is load-bearing and has no mechanism; the addendum does not contain one either
*§0; §4; Glossary; addendum in full; NFR-4, NFR-5*

§0 says §4 "is cross-cutting and load-bearing" and that the addendum is "where the means of keeping
it are worked out." The addendum is 37 lines. It contains four topic headings and six items marked
"Open." **None of them is the partitioning of Personal Ledger data in sync.**

The specific gaps:

- **Sync partitioning is unaddressed.** NFR-4 promises convergence between devices; the addendum's
  sync bullet lists transport, conflict resolution, and key recovery as open — but never states that
  Personal Ledger records must not transit to, or rest on, the other Partner's device in any form.
  §4's "no aggregate that hints at the detail" is a constraint on the *sync protocol* above all else,
  and it is unwritten. If a partner's device holds the other's ciphertext, record counts, object
  sizes, and write timestamps are all visible locally — an aggregate that hints at the detail,
  arriving by the clock.
- **Metadata is out of scope by omission.** NFR-5 forbids a readable server-side copy of *content*.
  Nothing anywhere constrains what the relay observes: pairing events, per-device sync frequency,
  ciphertext volume, online times. §10.1's "nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app" is a
  promise about the *other Partner*; the operator's view of the same signal is never scoped, and
  §10.3 ("the service relays and stores ciphertext") confirms a relay exists.
- **The Glossary contradicts §4.** `Personal Ledger — a Partner's own money. One per Partner.
  *(Visibility boundary TBD.)*` The document's own definition of the central term marks the central
  property unresolved, while §4 states it as settled and §13.1 puts "the §4 Privacy Model in full" in
  MVP scope. Downstream readers are instructed by §0 to treat the Glossary as authoritative.
- **No negative requirements.** There is no FR and no NFR that says "no surface, query, aggregate,
  count, timestamp, or error message reveals the existence, number, size, or recency of the other
  Partner's Personal Ledger records." §4 says it in prose. Prose is not testable, and §5's FRs are
  the only things that become stories.

**Needed:** an NFR-level non-inference requirement with testable consequences; an explicit addendum
section on ledger partitioning and metadata minimisation; and the Glossary's "TBD" either resolved or
§4 demoted to draft until it is.

### PS-08 — HIGH — The Settle-Up statement discloses category and notes, which §4 and FR-3 say it does not
*§4 ¶2; FR-3; FR-35; FR-39; FR-41*

§4: the disclosure carries "merchant, amount, and date," and "its **categories** ... [are not]
revealed."
FR-3: the funding-side allocation "becom[es] visible to the other Partner at Settle-Up per §4,
carrying merchant, amount, and date **only**."
FR-35: "The statement lists every Shared Ledger Transaction in the Period with date, merchant,
amount, **category**, Payer, and the Split Rule applied. Funded-from-personal Transactions are
visually marked as such."

FR-35 is a strict superset of what §4 and FR-3 authorise. Either the funded-from-personal lines are
exempted from the category column (and FR-35 must say so), or §4 and FR-3 are wrong. Category is not
a trivial addition: category plus merchant plus the §4-mandated "funded from personal" marker is a
much sharper picture of private spending than merchant alone.

FR-39 adds a second unauthorised field: notes. The Glossary defines a Transaction as carrying "amount,
category, **and note**." Notes written by the owner for their own use are not in §4's enumeration, and
FR-39's "Notes are visible to both Partners on the Transaction and are **retained in Settlement
History**" (plus FR-41's export and FR-49's CSV) makes the disclosure permanent and portable.

§4 also never scopes *retention*: it describes a disclosure as an event, and the FRs make it an
immutable, exported, un-deletable record held by the other Partner for the life of the Household and
beyond (FR-21, FR-49).

### PS-09 — HIGH — The disclosure is continuous, not confined to Settle-Up
*§5.1 Description; FR-22; FR-47; §4 ¶4*

§5.1 says a funding-side disclosure "surfaces at Settle-Up rather than in the other Partner's
day-to-day view," and §4 frames Settle-Up as the single, bounded, announced moment of opening.

FR-22 requires every Shared envelope to display "spent" to both Partners, continuously, for the open
Period. Shared spending includes spending the other Partner funded from personal money. FR-47's
affordability check reads the same remaining balance, one tap from the default screen.

So: Alex pays for a shared cost from personal money at 14:10; Sam's Groceries envelope shows the
reduced remaining balance as soon as sync lands (NFR-4: 60 seconds). Sam does not see merchant or
date yet, but Sam sees **that** Alex spent and **how much**, in near real time, every single time.
Polling the affordability check — which by design "records nothing and leaves no trace" (FR-47) —
turns this into continuous, undetectable monitoring of the other Partner's shared-cost spending
timing and amounts.

This matters in three ways: it contradicts §5.1's explicit statement; it means the "opening is never
silent" guarantee in §4 does not hold, because the disclosure statement is on the Settle-Up screen
and this channel never passes through it; and the untraceability of FR-47, written as a privacy
feature for the checker, doubles as a surveillance feature against the spender.

### PS-10 — HIGH — "No location data anywhere in the product" is not keepable, and merchant strings are the reason
*§10.1 ¶2; FR-3; FR-35; FR-29; UJ-8*

§10.1: "No location data anywhere in the product. Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input."

Merchant is a required field of every Entry (FR-1), is carried on every disclosure (FR-3), is
displayed on the Settle-Up statement (FR-35), is exported (FR-49), and — for imported rows (FR-29) —
is the raw bank description string, which routinely encodes a town, a branch, an ATM, or a transit
operator. Merchant plus date is a place and a time.

This is not pedantry about the word "location." The concrete case §10.1 exists for: a Partner
planning to leave pays for a shared cost from personal money while in another city, at a hotel, or at
a clinic. FR-3 discloses that merchant and that date to the other Partner. The claim that "nothing
else about the Personal Ledger is revealed or inferable" is wrong in the way that matters most.

UJ-8's edge case — "no screen, record, or notification anywhere in the product reveals where Alex was
when they did it" — is correct and narrow, and §10.1 generalises it into a claim the product cannot
support.

**Needed:** restate §10.1 as "no location is collected from the device, derived from any sensor, or
attached to any record" and acknowledge separately that merchant text supplied by the user or the
bank may describe a place, that it is disclosed under §4, and that the user should know this at the
point of sharing.

### PS-11 — HIGH — FR-10/FR-11 are an unrate-limited, attacker-controlled channel into the other Partner's phone
*FR-10, FR-11, FR-39; §8; Open Question 3*

FR-10: "The other Partner is **notified** when a Transaction is marked shared." No rate limit, no cap.
FR-11: "The owner is **notified** that the Transaction was declined." No rate limit.
FR-39: "The note is attached to that Transaction and **the other Partner is notified**." Free text.
Open Question 3 concedes the loop: "FR-11 returns a declined Transaction to its owner, who may
presumably mark it shared again (FR-10), which admits an **unbounded loop**. Cap it, or accept it as
a social problem the product should not police?"

Compare FR-38, which *is* rate-limited ("batched to at most one per Partner per day") and FR-44
(exactly two reminders, ever). The authors applied rate limits where the sender is the system and
omitted them in precisely the three places where the sender is a person.

What this gives one Partner over the other: an uncapped push notification channel, with
attacker-chosen content in the merchant and note fields, that the recipient cannot block, mute, or
rate-limit — because the product has no block, no mute, and no per-Partner notification controls
anywhere. The only exit is dissolution (PS-06), which is a disproportionate remedy and announces
itself.

The PRD frames this as a budgeting edge case. It is a harassment channel, and Open Question 3's
framing ("a social problem the product should not police") is the wrong lens: the product chose to
build the channel.

**Needed:** cap re-shares of a declined Transaction at one; rate-limit and batch all
Partner-originated notifications on the FR-38 pattern; add a mute that does not require dissolution.

### PS-12 — HIGH — One Partner can freeze every future Settlement indefinitely
*FR-44, FR-45, FR-46; §12*

FR-44: "A proposal **never auto-accepts and never expires**." Two reminders, then nothing.
FR-45: "A Period **cannot** be proposed while any earlier Period is unsealed."
FR-46: carry-forward "requires **both Partners to accept**."

A Partner who simply does not accept blocks the settlement of October, and therefore of November, and
of every month thereafter, permanently. Carry-forward is not an escape because it needs their
consent too. §12 has removed dispute resolution by design. The only unilateral action left is
dissolution.

So the product's answer to "my partner won't settle" is "end the relationship," and the leverage
runs: *accept my number or we never settle again*. For a Partner who is owed money and whose only
record of the obligation is an unsealed statement, that is a meaningful financial hold.

FR-13 compounds it: nothing about an unsealed chain is time-bounded, but a lapsed subscription makes
the Shared Ledger read-only after 30 days, which (per FR-13) blocks "proposals, or Settlements"
outright.

**Needed:** a unilateral path that preserves the record without requiring consent — e.g. after N
days a Partner may seal a Period *as unagreed*, recorded as such in history and excluded from the
running balance, so later Periods can proceed. This is not a dispute workflow; it is a timeout.

### PS-13 — HIGH — The coerced-device threat model is absent, and export is its sharpest edge
*FR-49, FR-51, FR-21; §5.2 Description; §10.1*

The entire §4 boundary reduces to one assumption, stated once in §5.2: "each Partner holds their own
device credentials, and neither can unlock the other's phone into the app." In the relationship §10.1
is written about, compelled unlocking is the normal case, not the exception.

Given one unlocked session, FR-49 hands over everything: "Export covers the Shared Ledger, the
exporting Partner's **own Personal Ledger**, all envelopes they can see, the category set, and all
sealed Settlements," "available at any time, without the other Partner's involvement or knowledge,"
as plaintext CSV. There is no re-authentication before export, no second factor, no encryption of
the output, no notice to the Partner's other device that an export was taken, and no record of it.

The same unlocked session also yields PS-05's planted device and PS-06's forced deletion.

§10.1 does not acknowledge that the privacy model is device-possession-only. It should, because the
honest framing changes what the product owes the user: at minimum a biometric/passcode re-prompt in
front of export, Personal Ledger view, and device pairing; an encrypted-by-default export archive;
and plain copy telling the user that the boundary protects them from their partner's *account*, not
from their partner's *hands*.

### PS-14 — HIGH — §8 permits three notification types; the FRs define seven
*§8 ¶6; FR-10, FR-11, FR-20, FR-36, FR-38, FR-39, FR-44; SM-C1*

§8: "Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44), one batched proposal
change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10). **Nothing else may notify.**"

The FRs define notifications in: FR-10 (shared), FR-11 (declined), FR-20 (dissolved), FR-36
(proposed), FR-38 (re-proposed), FR-39 (ask-about), FR-44 (reminders). Seven sources, four of them
Partner-triggered, three of them not in §8's list.

This is not just an inconsistency to tidy. Notification timing and volume is the primary
non-content side channel in the product — each one tells the recipient that the other Partner was
awake, holding their phone, and using the app at time T, which is exactly what §10.1 says nothing
exposes. It is also the thing SM-C1 ("notifications per Partner per week — must not rise") is
supposed to hold down, and the counter-metric is calibrated against a list that is less than half
the real surface.

Separately: **notification content is specified nowhere in the document.** If FR-10's notice carries
merchant and amount, it is rendered on a lock screen, visible to anyone near the phone — a
third-party disclosure of a §4 disclosure, and in the PS-05/PS-13 threat model, a disclosure to the
abuser of a partner who has not yet left.

### PS-15 — HIGH — The income-proportional ratio leaks a time series, and rule changes are invisible
*§4 ¶3; FR-26, FR-34; Open Question 8*

§4 is commendably honest that an income-proportional Split Rule reveals *relative income* once. It
understates two things:

1. **It reveals it repeatedly.** FR-26: the derivation "updates automatically as either changes."
   Each update yields a new ratio and therefore a new solve. A Partner observing ratios across twelve
   Periods reconstructs the other's income month by month — including the months they had a bad
   quarter, which is a materially different disclosure from "you earn roughly 1.4× what I do."
2. **The disclosure statement fires once.** FR-34 presents the §4 statement "before it can be
   applied." Nothing re-states it when the ratio subsequently moves, which is when the actual
   information is transmitted.

Open Question 8 then undermines the justification for the whole Settle-Up opening: "whether a Partner
can see *when a rule changed* relative to a sealed Settlement is unspecified." §4's entire argument
for opening the boundary is that "without this, the computation is unverifiable." A statement whose
Split Rule may have been changed, by the other Partner, at an unknown time, with no visible audit, is
not verifiable. The opening is being paid for with a guarantee the product does not currently deliver.

### PS-16 — HIGH — The Settlement hash proves nothing specified, and conflict semantics can produce divergent seals
*FR-37, FR-41, FR-49; NFR-4, NFR-6; addendum "Pairing and session key transport"; §1*

§1 rests the product's second core promise on this: "a disagreement about what was agreed is settled
by looking it up." FR-37 seals "with a hash of its contents," FR-41 "displays its content hash,"
FR-49 exports it.

The addendum is explicit that none of it is defined: "Sealed-Settlement content hash: what it covers,
how it is computed, and what it is meant to prove to whom. **The PRD promises it is displayed; it
does not specify it.**"

Two concrete problems the PRD must resolve, not architecture:

- **Against what does a Partner verify?** Both devices compute the hash from their own local copy. If
  the copies differ, the hashes differ and the product has detected a problem it has no FR to
  resolve. If a device is modified, it can display any hash it likes. A hash with no counter-signature
  and no independent reference is a number on a screen.
- **Divergent seals.** The addendum lists "concurrent-edit conflict semantics between two partners
  editing the same ledger" as **Open**, while NFR-4 allows 60 seconds of divergence and FR-38
  withdraws a proposal on any material change. Two Partners can accept within the same convergence
  window against different underlying sets, producing two "sealed" Settlements with different
  contents and different hashes, both immutable under NFR-6. The product then has two
  un-editable, contradictory records of the same month — the exact failure §1 says it prevents.

### PS-17 — HIGH — Single-payer subscription is an unaddressed coercion lever
*FR-12, FR-13, FR-20; §11; §10.1*

FR-12: "A Household carries exactly **one** subscription, billed to the **creating** Partner."
§11: "The second Partner pays nothing and needs no payment method."
FR-13: after a 30-day grace period, lapse makes the Shared Ledger read-only for both — "no new shared
Entries, Transfers into Ours, **proposals, or Settlements**."

The creating Partner can therefore, at any time and by doing nothing, remove the other Partner's
ability to record shared spending or to settle what is owed. There is no FR to transfer the
subscription, no FR to let the second Partner start one, and §5.2's dissolution FRs say nothing about
what happens to billing or to the non-paying Partner's app afterwards.

FR-13's third consequence shows the authors saw the shape of this — "One Partner's lapsed billing
never freezes the other Partner's private data" — and stopped at the Personal Ledger. The shared
half, including the settlement record of money owed, is freezable at will by one party. §10.1
considers physical and informational safety and not economic leverage, which in practice is the most
common form.

### PS-18 — HIGH — Five success metrics require measuring behaviour inside end-to-end encrypted data
*§14 NOTE FOR PM; §15 Q1; §10.2; NFR-5*

Flagged by the authors, and correctly: "SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and SM-C2 are all statements about
user behaviour inside encrypted data." I record it here because it is a privacy-coherence finding,
not only a measurement one, and because the escape hatch named in §15 is itself a leak.

"Opt-in client-side aggregate telemetry" means a device computing facts about the Household —
settlements completed, notifications received, entries recorded, seconds spent reviewing a proposal —
and transmitting them to the operator. Those are aggregates about household financial behaviour. They
are not content, so they do not technically breach NFR-5, and they comfortably breach the spirit of
§10.2 and §1's "no readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to mine."

SM-C2 is the sharpest: "the share of acceptances made within **seconds of opening** the proposal"
requires the operator to receive per-Partner interaction timing, which is precisely the "activity
surveillance" §10.1 forbids between Partners. The product would be collecting about its users what it
promises their partners cannot see.

**Needed:** decide now, in the PRD, which metrics are abandoned. Treat §10.1's surveillance ban as
binding on the operator, not only on the other Partner.

## 2. The deliberate opening — does §5.5 open exactly what §4 authorises?

**No. It opens wider in four dimensions, and narrower in one that matters.**

§4 authorises: *every shared-category Transaction with who paid, plus any funded-from-personal
Transactions carrying merchant, amount and date* — announced in plain words, at the moment of
disclosure.

| Dimension | §4 authorises | §5.5 (and others) deliver | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fields | merchant, amount, date | + category, + Split Rule (FR-35), + notes (FR-39) | PS-08 |
| Timing | at Settle-Up, announced | continuously, via Shared envelope "spent" (FR-22) and the affordability check (FR-47) | PS-09 |
| Retention | silent on it | permanent, immutable, exported, held by the ex-Partner after dissolution (FR-41, FR-49, FR-21) | PS-08 |
| Verifiability | the justification for opening at all | Split-Rule change history unspecified (OQ-8); hash semantics undefined (addendum) | PS-15, PS-16 |
| Announcement | "the opening is never silent" | FR-35 puts the statement on the Settle-Up screen only — the FR-22/FR-47 channel and the FR-10 notification never pass it | PS-09 |

And the narrower side, which is a *defect against the product's own goal*: FR-35's statement cannot
be verified by the accepting Partner against anything independent, so the two-sidedness §5.5 is built
on reduces to "the other person's device showed them the same screen." SM-C2 already anticipates the
consequence — rubber-stamping.

One thing §5.5 gets right and should be preserved verbatim: FR-38's auto-withdraw ("No acceptance
ever carries over from a withdrawn proposal to its replacement") is a genuinely good piece of design
and closes the obvious bait-and-switch.

---

## 3. Safety surface — what §10.1 misses

§10.1 contains four commitments. All four are correct. Collectively they cover **the act of leaving**
and nothing else. The gaps, by category:

**Notification content and timing** — PS-06 (dissolution is pushed in real time), PS-14 (content
unspecified anywhere; seven notification sources against §8's three; lock-screen disclosure), PS-11
(uncapped Partner-triggered notifications with free text).

**Export contents** — PS-13 (plaintext CSV of the whole Personal Ledger behind a single unlock, no
re-auth, no notice, no encryption), PS-06 (export prompted in front of deletion, creating a
discoverable file at the worst moment), PS-08 (the ex-Partner's export permanently retains every
funding-side disclosure and every note, with no revocation).

**What the remaining Partner can reconstruct** — PS-01 (income from the Floor), PS-02 (income from
the Pool), PS-03 (intent from new categories — the "solicitor" problem), PS-09 (spending timing from
envelope balances), PS-19 (allocation deltas from edit marks). §10.1's "Disclosure is never
retroactive" is kept; the problem is that disclosure is *prospective and continuous*.

**Timing signals** — PS-06 (exit time), PS-09 (spend time), PS-14 (app-use time inferable from every
notification), and the unaddressed sync-liveness signal in PS-07 (a peer-to-peer or
relay-mediated sync makes one device's online/offline state observable to the other; nothing forbids
a "last synced" indicator, and products of this shape almost always grow one).

**Coercive use of ordinary product features** — PS-05 (planted device/session), PS-11 (harassment
channel), PS-12 (settlement freeze), PS-17 (subscription freeze), PS-21 (recovery hostage), PS-23
("waiting on Alex" as a standing public reproach).

**Missing outright, with no finding elsewhere to attach them to:**

- **No duress or quiet mode.** No decoy passcode, no app-hiding, no non-obvious icon, no panic wipe.
  Standard in products that take this threat model seriously.
- **No safety guidance in the product.** §10.1 is a set of engineering constraints with no
  user-facing counterpart: nothing tells a Partner what their partner *can* see, or what leaving
  will and will not reveal. The person who needs this information most is the one least able to ask.
- **No "leaving" state between normal and dissolved.** The product offers full participation or
  full severance, with the severance announced. The months of preparation in between — which is when
  people are actually at risk — are unserved by design.
- **Dissolution's reach is undefined** (PS-24): it is silent on outstanding proposals, on the other
  Partner's browser sessions and second devices, and on what happens if the other Partner is offline
  when "immediately" happens.

One thing to keep: **FR-20's "no reason, no attribution"** and **FR-47's "records nothing"** are both
correct instincts, and UJ-8's edge case is exactly the right kind of requirement. The problem is that
they are the only four of their kind in a document that needed twenty.

## 4. Promise vs. mechanism

Promises stated in the PRD whose mechanism is undefined, deferred, or contradicted:

| Promise | Where | Mechanism | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| "no aggregate that hints at the detail" | §4 ¶1 | none; no FR or NFR states it as testable; sync partitioning absent from the addendum | PS-07 |
| "nothing else ... is revealed or **inferable**" | §4 ¶2 | contradicted by FR-26, FR-27, FR-7, FR-22 | PS-01–03, PS-09 |
| even/custom Split Rules "reveal nothing" | §4 ¶3 | false; the Floor leaks under all rules | PS-01 |
| "the opening is never silent" | §4 ¶4 | FR-35 announces one of at least three channels | PS-09 |
| "not a route around §4" (browser) | FR-18 | addendum: key transport, lifetime, and what survives refresh all Open | PS-05, PS-07 |
| sealed Settlement content hash | FR-37, FR-41, §1 | addendum: "promises it is displayed; does not specify it" | PS-16 |
| append-only history, no divergence | NFR-6, NFR-4 | addendum: conflict semantics Open | PS-16 |
| "No readable server-side copy" | NFR-5, §10.3 | content only; metadata unscoped despite an admitted relay | PS-07 |
| "No location data anywhere" | §10.1 | merchant strings are stored, disclosed, and exported | PS-10 |
| "No activity surveillance" | §10.1 | contradicted by seven notification sources, envelope deltas, and planted devices | PS-05, PS-09, PS-14 |
| Visibility boundary | Glossary | marked **TBD** while §13.1 scopes it into MVP | PS-07 |
| Success measurement | §14, §15 Q1 | authors' own phase-blocker; the proposed fix is itself a leak | PS-18 |

The pattern: the addendum was given the *hard* half of §4 and received it as a list of open
questions. §0 tells downstream readers the addendum is "where the means of keeping [the promise] are
worked out." Right now it is where the means are *named*. Architecture cannot resolve PS-01 through
PS-04 — those are product decisions about what the Floor, the Pool, the category set, and Entry
allocation *are*, and they have to be made here.

## Remaining findings

### PS-19 — MEDIUM — Edit-marking on a split Entry leaks the personal allocation delta
*FR-9; FR-2*

FR-9: "Editing the Shared Ledger allocation of an Entry marks it as edited to the other Partner and
**displays the previous amount alongside the current one**."

On a split Entry (FR-2 — one card payment across Ours and the owner's Personal Ledger), the Entry
total is fixed by the real-world payment. If the shared allocation moves from 40.00 to 30.00, the
other Partner learns that 10.00 moved into the Personal Ledger — a change to a private balance,
derived from a disclosed field. Over repeated edits this is a slow read of the private side of every
split Entry. FR-9's own "The edit history of a Personal Ledger Entry is visible to its owner only"
shows the intent; the split case defeats it.

### PS-20 — MEDIUM — Duplicate detection's match scope is undefined
*FR-32; §5.4 `[ASSUMPTION]`*

"A staged row matching an existing Transaction on amount and within a small date window is flagged.
A flagged row is shown **alongside the Transaction it may duplicate**." Against which Transactions is
the match run, and what is shown when it matches? If the search set is ever allowed to include the
other Partner's records, the importer gains an oracle: stage a row for an amount and a date, see
whether it flags. The PRD never scopes it, and the behaviour is parked in an unconfirmed
`[ASSUMPTION]`. Add a consequence: matching is scoped to the importing Partner's own Personal Ledger
and the Shared Ledger, and a flag never surfaces a record the Partner could not otherwise see.

### PS-21 — MEDIUM — Device recovery depends on the other Partner's cooperation
*FR-50, FR-15, FR-21*

FR-50: "A replacement device re-pairs through the verification flow of **FR-15**," which requires
both devices to display and both Partners to confirm a matching code. So a Partner who loses their
phone can only return to the Household if the other Partner agrees to perform the pairing. A Partner
who refuses denies the other access to the Shared Ledger and to Settlement History — the record of
money owed. After dissolution it is impossible by construction, which means FR-21's "each Partner
keeps a usable copy" depends on an export having been taken *before* the device was lost. Worth an
explicit consequence and a prompt.

### PS-22 — MEDIUM — "Restoring its privacy" is not a thing a decline can do
*FR-11*

"Declining returns the Transaction to the owner's Personal Ledger in full, **restoring its privacy**
under §4." The declining Partner has already read its merchant, amount, and date — that is what they
declined. A disclosure is not reversible, and describing it as reversible will mislead a user into
sharing something they would not otherwise share, on the understanding that it can be pulled back.
Restate as: the Transaction returns to the Personal Ledger and is excluded from Settle-Up; what was
already shown cannot be unseen.

### PS-23 — MEDIUM — "Waiting on [Partner]" is a standing reproach, against §8's own rule
*FR-44; §8*

FR-44: "The Period remains open and is **labelled as waiting on the named Partner, to both
Partners**." §8: "Never editorialise between Partners ... It does not characterise anyone's spending,
flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault." A persistent badge naming one person as the
reason the month is not closed is a fault attribution rendered continuously on the other Partner's
home screen. Prefer a neutral state ("October is open") visible to both, with the actionable prompt
shown only to the Partner who can act.

### PS-24 — MEDIUM — Dissolution's reach over in-flight state and other surfaces is undefined
*FR-20, FR-18, FR-52, FR-36*

FR-20 stops sync and tells the other Partner. It is silent on: an outstanding proposal (does it
vanish, or sit forever?); the other Partner's authorised browser sessions, which hold keys and may
survive; the acting Partner's own second device (FR-52); and what "immediately" means when the other
device is offline — the dissolution is one-sided until it reconnects, during which that device
continues to present live shared data and to accept writes that will never sync. Each needs a
consequence.

### PS-25 — MEDIUM — "No attribution" on dissolution is vacuous in a two-Partner system
*FR-20; §10.1*

FR-20 promises the remaining Partner is "given no reason, **no attribution**, and no further
detail." A Household has exactly two Partners (FR-12). If you did not dissolve it, the other person
did. Stating non-attribution as a protection suggests a degree of concealment the product cannot
provide and may lead a user to assume ambiguity that does not exist. Say instead that no reason,
timing detail, or context is given — and then make the *timing* claim true (PS-06).

### PS-26 — MEDIUM — The Glossary marks the central privacy boundary "TBD"
*Glossary "Personal Ledger"; §0; §4; §13.1*

`Personal Ledger — a Partner's own money. One per Partner. *(Visibility boundary TBD.)*` §0 instructs
downstream readers and workflows to treat the Glossary as the authoritative vocabulary. §4 states the
boundary as settled and §13.1 scopes "the §4 Privacy Model in full" into MVP. A story writer reading
the Glossary will conclude the boundary is an open design question. Resolve the parenthetical.

### PS-27 — MEDIUM — Notification content is specified nowhere
*FR-10, FR-11, FR-20, FR-36, FR-39, FR-44; §8*

Seven notifications exist and not one FR says what any of them contains. Lock-screen rendering means
their content is disclosed to whoever is near the phone — a category of disclosure §4 does not
model at all, and which in the §10.1 threat model lands in front of exactly the wrong person. Every
notification FR needs a consequence constraining its payload; the safe default is that no
notification carries a merchant, an amount, a note, or a category — only "something needs your
attention in Ledgerleaf."

### PS-28 — LOW — FR-8 reads as a privacy control and is not one
*FR-8; FR-7*

"Hide categories **from a Personal Ledger view**" sits in a document whose central subject is
privacy, directly after FR-7's category management, and does nothing for privacy: it is scoped to the
hiding Partner's own view of their own ledger, and the category "remains available ... in the other
Partner's views." A user looking for a way to conceal something will find this control and believe
they have used it. Rename it to describe what it does (declutter), and state in the FR that it has no
effect on what the other Partner sees. This becomes moot if PS-03 is fixed.

### PS-29 — LOW — The affordability check's behaviour is undefined when a category has both a Personal and a Shared envelope
*FR-47, FR-48, FR-23*

FR-23 allows "at most one envelope per category **per Ledger**," so Groceries can exist in both Ours
and a Personal Ledger. FR-47 takes "an amount and a category" and nothing else. Which envelope
answers? If the check sums or silently prefers one, the ten-second answer is wrong; if it discloses
both, FR-48's "A check against a Shared envelope reveals no Personal Ledger state" needs restating
for the owner's own case. Specify the resolution and whether the Partner chooses.

### PS-30 — LOW — FR-37 contradicts FR-36 and UJ-6 on what seals a Settlement
*FR-36, FR-37; UJ-6*

FR-37's title and first consequence describe the non-initiating Partner accepting and sealing; its
second consequence says "A Settlement seals only when **both** Partners have accepted." UJ-6 shows
Sam proposing and Alex's single accept sealing it. Either proposing constitutes acceptance (say so)
or a third step exists (define it).

### PS-31 — LOW — The solo period lets the founder classify a month of shared costs with no decline path
*FR-16, FR-11, FR-17*

FR-16 lets the founding Partner record a full Period before the second joins, and that work "syncs to
the second Partner on joining." FR-11's decline is available only "while the Period is open," so a
joining Partner may inherit shared classifications from Periods they could never have declined, which
then flow into the first Settlement. Not a privacy leak, but it undercuts §5.5's "a number one person
computed alone is exactly the spreadsheet problem Ledgerleaf exists to retire" at the one moment the
second Partner is most likely to disengage (SM-3b).

---

## Recommended order of resolution

1. **PS-04** — one-sentence scope fix to FR-2 and FR-5. Cheapest critical in the document.
2. **PS-02** — change the Pool default to the earner's own Personal Pool. Product decision, small.
3. **PS-03** — private category namespace for Personal Ledgers. Product decision, moderate.
4. **PS-01** — decide whether the Floor can exist at all in its current form, or whether §4 drops
   the "reveal nothing" claim. This is the one that may change the product.
5. **PS-05, PS-06, PS-13** — the safety set. Device notifications and listing; silent/deferred exit;
   export re-auth and encryption; ungated deletion.
6. **PS-07** — rewrite §4 as an exhaustive enumeration of crossing channels, add a non-inference NFR
   with testable consequences, resolve the Glossary TBD, and expand the addendum's sync section to
   cover ledger partitioning and metadata.
7. Everything else.

A note on §16: four `[ASSUMPTION]`s in the open list are load-bearing privacy decisions (the
Unallocated Pool's visibility, the duplicate-match rule, the affordability check's inputs, the import
default). They should be lifted out of the general confirmation queue and decided first, because
three Features are unbuildable until they are.
REVIEWEOF

# Adversarial Review — Ledgerleaf PRD

Reviewer stance: adversarial. The question is not "is this well written" (it is) but
"can an architect, a UX designer, and a story-writer build from this without
inventing the product themselves, and does the business survive contact with
reality?" The answer to both is no.

Document under review: `prd.md` (1,329 lines, 52 FRs, 9 NFRs, 8 UJs) and `addendum.md`.

**Verdict: NOT READY TO BUILD FROM.** This PRD is unusually articulate and that is
the problem — the prose is confident enough to hide that the product's three
load-bearing mechanics (how Settle-Up computes, how money gets into the Shared
Ledger, how income enters the system) are not specified anywhere, and that §4,
the section the document itself calls "cross-cutting and load-bearing," makes a
privacy promise that §5.3 breaks in two separate places. The surface is finished;
the spine is missing. 7 critical, 14 high, 21 medium, 8 low.

---

## CRITICAL

### C-1. Settle-Up cannot be computed from what this document specifies
**Location:** §5.3 (rollover paragraph), §3 (Payer), FR-3, FR-5, FR-35, FR-40.

§5.3 states the settlement rule: *"Settle-Up compares what each Partner **paid**
against their share of what was **spent**, and balances do not enter into it."*
§5.1 states the funding rule: *"Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit
**Transfer** — to fund shared Envelopes at the start of a Period."*

Put these together. Sam Transfers £800 from their Personal Ledger into the Shared
Ledger. Alex Transfers £200. Ours spends £1,000 on groceries, paid out of Ours.
Split Rule: even.

- Each Partner's share of what was spent: £500.
- What each Partner "paid": **nothing.** No Partner's own money funded any of
  those Entries; the Shared Ledger did. §3 defines Payer as *"the Partner whose
  own money funded an Entry"* — for a joint-account purchase there is no Payer.
- Transfers are explicitly excluded: "balances do not enter into it."

Settle-Up therefore reports £0 owing, and Sam is £300 out of pocket with no
remedy anywhere in the product. The envelope-funding model (§5.3) and the
settlement model (§5.5) are two mutually incompatible accounting systems bolted
together, and the PRD never notices because every example (UJ-1, UJ-6) uses the
other case — a Partner paying a shared cost from personal money.

It gets worse. FR-3 says *"Payer defaults to the Partner recording the Entry."*
So for a purchase made from the joint account, the app will mark whoever typed it
in as Payer, and Settle-Up (FR-35, which lists "Payer" on every line) will credit
them with having paid for it. **The default behaviour produces a materially false
settlement**, in the one feature the document calls "the moment the product earns
its keep."

There is no FR anywhere describing "an Entry paid from the Shared Ledger's own
money." The case is not handled, not excluded, and not acknowledged.

**Impact:** the central feature's arithmetic is undefined. Architecture cannot
build it; stories cannot be written against it; QA cannot test it. Everything in
§5.5 is downstream of a hole.

### C-2. Three load-bearing capabilities have no FR at all

**(a) Reading a Ledger.** §5.1 is titled "Ledgers & Transactions" and contains
FR-1 through FR-11. Every one of them is a write or a management operation:
quick-add, split, payer, undo, transfer, reverse, categories, hide, edit, share,
decline. **No FR specifies viewing a Ledger's transactions.** No FR specifies a
Ledger balance, despite §3 defining a Ledger as "a named pile of money" and §4
promising that a Partner "sees... no balance total" of the other's Personal Ledger
— a promise about a quantity nothing in the document defines or computes. §7 lists
a "Ledgers" navigation destination with no FR behind it. The only specified read
path through a Ledger's contents is CSV export (FR-49).

**(b) Recording income.** FR-26 requires each Partner to enter "their own income
history." FR-27 governs "income recorded above the Floor." FR-28 moves it from the
Pool. UJ-4 has "Alex's invoice lands mid-month at £4,100." **No FR specifies
recording income.** FR-1 quick-add collects "amount and merchant" with no
direction, no sign, no income flag. §3 defines Entry as "one real-world payment
**or receipt**" and then nothing ever creates a receipt. Nor is the relationship
between the income *history* a Partner types into FR-26 and income *Entries*
recorded in a Ledger defined — are they the same data? Does recording a salary
Entry update the Floor? Can they contradict each other? Unanswerable.

**(c) Sync.** The product's defining technical claim — E2EE sync between the two
partners' devices — has **zero functional requirements**. NFR-4 asserts
convergence as an `[ASSUMPTION]` and defers conflict semantics to the addendum,
which lists them as "Open." §13.1 "In Scope" does not list sync as a line item.
Nothing specifies what a Partner sees when the other is offline, what sync status
looks like, what a failed sync does, or how long a Partner can diverge. FR-36
("Proposing notifies the other Partner"), FR-37 ("sees the same statement... line
for line"), FR-20 ("Sync... stops") all assume a delivery mechanism no requirement
owns.

**Impact:** a downstream team will invent all three, each differently.

### C-3. NFR-1 (offline) makes four FR invariants unenforceable
**Location:** NFR-1 vs FR-2, FR-23, FR-28, FR-45, FR-14.

NFR-1: *"Every capability except sync, pairing, and browser authorisation works
with no network."* Two writers, both authoritative locally, both offline. Now:

- **FR-23:** "A Ledger holds at most one envelope per category per Period."
  Both Partners create a Groceries envelope on the Shared Ledger offline. On
  merge, the invariant is already violated. No resolution rule exists.
- **FR-28:** "Assignment cannot exceed the Pool's balance." Pool holds £500; each
  Partner assigns £400 offline. On merge, the Pool is £300 overdrawn. No rule.
- **FR-45:** "A Period cannot be proposed while any earlier Period is unsealed."
  Both Partners propose different Periods offline. No ordering authority exists —
  there is deliberately no server that can compute one (§10.3).
- **FR-14:** "A Household already holding two Partners cannot issue an invite."
  Enforced by what, against a device that has not synced?

These are stated as testable consequences. They are not testable, because they are
not achievable. The PRD's own addendum flags "concurrent-edit conflict semantics"
as Open while the PRD builds normative requirements on top of the answer.

**Impact:** architecture will have to either break NFR-1 or rewrite these FRs.
Either is a PRD-level decision being made by an engineer at 2am.

### C-4. §4 promises income privacy that FR-26 and FR-27 break
**Location:** §4 (third paragraph) vs FR-26, FR-27, FR-28, UJ-4.

§4 states, as a positive claim the product is proud of: *"Each Partner enters
their own income. It is stored encrypted and the figure itself is never
transmitted to the other Partner... choosing an income-proportional Split Rule
states plainly that it reveals relative income, and the **even and
custom-per-category Split Rules remain available and reveal nothing**."*

That last clause is false, twice over, regardless of Split Rule:

**(a) The Floor is an invertible function of both incomes.** FR-26: "the Floor
defaults to the lowest of the last six months of **combined** income... The Floor
is derived from both Partners' incomes and **updates automatically as either
changes**... only the Floor and any derived ratio are shared." A Partner who knows
their own six months of income and sees the combined Floor solves for the other's
figure by subtraction. Worse, because the Floor updates live, every change to the
other Partner's income history is observable as a delta. §4's claim that only an
income-proportional Split Rule reveals income is wrong, and the product makes no
disclosure here — the whole point of §4's honesty about the proportional split was
that Ledgerleaf "does not claim otherwise." Here it does claim otherwise.

**(b) The Unallocated Pool discloses above-Floor income.** FR-27 carries
`[ASSUMPTION: the Shared Ledger has one Unallocated Pool visible to both
Partners]`. UJ-4: *"when Alex's invoice lands mid-month at £4,100, the surplus
goes to the Unallocated Pool, and **the Household** assigns it to envelopes."*
"The Household" assigning means the Shared Pool, visible to Sam. Sam therefore
sees the exact magnitude of Alex's good month. The feature the PRD designed
specifically for the freelancer persona is the feature that exposes the
freelancer's income to their partner. If instead the surplus goes to Alex's
Personal Pool (private, FR-28), then UJ-4's narrative is wrong and the
envelope-funding story for irregular income does not work at all.

reading it means. §16 lists this as an open assumption about *pool topology*; it
is actually an unresolved question about whether the product's headline privacy
promise holds.

false privacy statement.

### C-5. §14's metrics are unmeasurable, and the PRD's own triage of which ones are safe is wrong
**Location:** §14 (NOTE FOR PM), §15 OQ-1, §10.2, NFR-5, FR-15, §10.3.

To its credit the PRD flags that SM-3b, SM-4, SM-5, SM-C1 and SM-C2 describe
behaviour inside encrypted data. It then says: *"SM-1 and SM-2 are billing facts
and are safe. SM-3a is plausibly observable from pairing events."* Both
reassurances are wrong.

- **SM-3a is not observable.** FR-15: "Key material is exchanged **between the two
  devices**; no server holds a readable copy." §10.3: "No per-Household
  server-side computation." A QR scanned off a screen in a kitchen, with a
  device-to-device exchange, produces no server event. If the server *does* learn
  that a pairing occurred and for which Household, that is a per-Household record
  the operator holds, which is exactly what §10.2 and §10.3 forbid.
- **SM-C3 and SM-C4 are also unmeasurable** and the NOTE does not list them.
  SM-C3 ("time to record an Entry") is a client-side interaction timing. SM-C4
  ("share of retained Households that are dormant") requires knowing whether an
  encrypted Household is being used — the purest possible example of the thing
  NFR-5 forbids.
- **SM-2 is not a clean billing fact either.** It measures *Households*; billing
  measures *subscriptions*. See M-19.

So the honest tally is: of eleven metrics, **two** (SM-1 and SM-2, with
caveats) are measurable without building a telemetry channel the product's
positioning cannot survive. The PRD labels this "the sharpest unresolved tension
in the document" and a "Phase-blocker for architecture" — and then proceeds to
treat every other section as ready. It is not a tension; it is a product strategy
decision that must be made before anything is built, because a consented
client-side aggregate telemetry pipeline is a feature with FRs, UI, and a trust
cost, and it exists nowhere in §5, §13.1, or the addendum.

## HIGH

### H-1. "Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit Transfer" — except in FR-10 and FR-11
**Location:** §5.1 vs FR-10, FR-11; §3 (Transfer).

§5.1 states it as an invariant with a stated purpose: *"Money moves between
Ledgers only by explicit **Transfer**... so the history stays append-only and
nobody can quietly rewrite what happened. **That property is load-bearing** for
the product's promise."*

FR-10 moves a Transaction from a Personal Ledger to the Shared Ledger with no
Transfer. FR-11 moves it back, also with no Transfer. §3 defines Transfer as
"an explicit Transaction pair moving money between two Ledgers of the same
Household" — which is precisely what FR-10 does and refuses to call one. So there
are two unrelated mechanisms for inter-Ledger movement with different audit
properties, and the document asserts there is one.

Compounding it: §5.1's "append-only, nobody can quietly rewrite" is false in
general. FR-9 permits in-place editing of a Personal Ledger Entry "at any time
before it is drawn into a Settlement," with an edit history *"visible to its owner
only."* That is, by construction, quiet rewriting. NFR-6 scopes append-only
correctly (Transfers and sealed Settlements); §5.1's prose overclaims it to the
whole history, and §1 leans on the overclaim.

### H-2. FR-38 contradicts itself in adjacent bullets
**Location:** FR-38, FR-36, FR-37, UJ-7.

FR-38's consequences:
- *"A withdrawn proposal is **re-proposed automatically** against the updated statement."*
- *"**No acceptance ever carries over** from a withdrawn proposal to its replacement."*

If no acceptance carries over, the replacement proposal has zero acceptances —
including the initiator's. But it was "re-proposed automatically," i.e. the system
proposed on the initiator's behalf, against a statement the initiator has not
seen, with a different number. That *is* carrying the initiator's consent over;
the PRD just relocates it from "acceptance" to "proposal" and declares the problem
solved. UJ-7 makes the asymmetry explicit and praises it: *"Alex's earlier reading
never becomes an acceptance of a figure that has since moved"* — while Sam, who
made the edit, has their proposal of the new figure manufactured by the app. The
two-sidedness §5.5 calls the whole justification for the feature is one-sided
here.

Related, and unresolved: **does Propose constitute the initiator's accept?** FR-37
is titled "Accept a Settlement" and says the non-initiating Partner "can accept
the proposed statement, **sealing it**," then immediately says *"A Settlement
seals only when **both** Partners have accepted."* §5.5 says "On both accepts the
Settlement is sealed." No FR defines the initiator's accept. UJ-6 shows Alex's
single tap sealing it. Either FR-36 implies acceptance (say so) or there is a
third step nobody has specified.

### H-3. There is no way to pair a replacement or second device
**Location:** FR-50, FR-52 vs FR-14, FR-15.

FR-50: *"A replacement device re-pairs through the verification flow of FR-15."*
FR-52: *"Pairing a second device uses the verification flow of FR-15 and **does
not involve the other Partner**."*

FR-15 is the Household-join flow. It *requires* the other Partner: *"Both devices
display a short verification code... Pairing completes only when **both Partners**
confirm the codes match."* And reaching FR-15 requires an invite, which FR-14
forbids: *"A Household already holding two Partners cannot issue an invite."*

So the cited mechanism cannot do what FR-50 and FR-52 cite it for, and FR-52
explicitly contradicts the mechanism it cites. Meanwhile FR-50 says *"Re-pairing
restores the Shared Ledger from the other Partner's device"* — which does involve
the other Partner, contradicting FR-52 again.

There is a deeper hole underneath: **identity is the device, and there is no
recovery credential.** When Sam's only phone is destroyed, nothing in this
document authenticates the new phone as Sam to Alex's device. Whatever flow fills
this gap is, by construction, the product's primary account-takeover surface —
convince Alex to approve a pairing and you get the entire Shared Ledger and
Settlement History. For an E2EE product this is the single most security-sensitive
flow and it is specified as a cross-reference to a requirement that says the
opposite.

§8: *"Notifications are rare by construction: two settle-up reminders (FR-44), one
batched proposal change per day (FR-38), a shared-transaction notice (FR-10).

### H-5. Notifications have no specification and collide with §10.1 and §10.3
**Location:** FR-10, FR-11, FR-20, FR-36, FR-38, FR-39, FR-44 vs §10.1, §10.3, NFR-1, NFR-5.

Seven FRs send notifications. No FR specifies the notification mechanism, and the
product's constraints make it genuinely hard:

- FR-44 sends reminders at 7 and 14 days to a Partner who may not have opened the
  app. A local scheduled notification can do that only on the stalling Partner's
  own device, which must therefore already know a proposal exists — i.e. have
  synced. If they have not synced in 14 days, no reminder fires.
- FR-38's "batched to at most one per Partner per day" implies an intermediary
  that counts, i.e. per-Household server-side state and logic — forbidden by
  §10.3 ("No per-Household server-side computation").
- Push notification delivery leaks timing metadata to the operator and the
  platform: when a settlement was proposed, when a transaction was shared, when a
  Household was dissolved. §10.1 states flatly: *"No activity surveillance.
  Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app."* FR-10's share-notice and FR-20's
  dissolution notice *are* activity timestamps delivered to the other Partner, and
  the push infrastructure delivers them to the operator too.
- NFR-1 claims everything but sync/pairing/browser-auth works offline. Notification
  delivery does not.

### H-6. A Partner can permanently disable Settle-Up by doing nothing, and §10.1 does not see it
**Location:** FR-44, FR-45, FR-46, §10.1.

FR-44: *"A proposal never auto-accepts and never expires. The Period remains
open."* FR-45: *"A Period cannot be proposed while any earlier Period is
unsealed."* FR-46 (the only escape): *"Carry-forward requires **both Partners to
accept**."*

So one Partner who simply never taps Accept freezes settlement for the Household
permanently, and both remedies require that Partner's cooperation. The only exit
is Dissolution — ending the relationship's financial record-keeping entirely —
which the product reserves for a safety scenario.

§10.1 is written explicitly because "relationships are not uniformly safe," and it
catalogues exit, location, attribution, and surveillance. It does not consider
**coercive control via product state**, of which this document contains at least
three instances:

- **Settlement stonewall** (above): refuse to accept, and the other Partner can
  never close a month, forever.
- **Billing hostage** (FR-13 + §11): the subscription belongs to the creating
  Partner; "the second Partner pays nothing and needs no payment method." Let it
  lapse and after 30 days the Shared Ledger is read-only for both, with **no FR
  allowing the second Partner to take over the subscription**. One Partner holds a
  unilateral off-switch on the shared record.
- **Decline loop** (FR-10 + FR-11, flagged as OQ-3 but only as a "social
  problem"): share, decline, re-share indefinitely, each cycle withdrawing and
  re-forming the proposal under FR-38.

A product that makes safety claims this explicit (§10.1, UJ-8) and then ships
three unilateral levers over the other person's financial records has done the
hard part and missed the obvious part.

### H-7. The affordability answer's arithmetic is undefined
**Location:** FR-5, FR-22, FR-23, FR-47, FR-48, §3 (Envelope).

§3: an Envelope is "a per-category **budget allocation** for a Period" — a plan.
FR-22 displays "planned, rolled-over, spent, and remaining." FR-23 lets planned
exceed the Floor, showing "the shortfall." FR-5, however, introduces a different
thing entirely: *"Transfers into a Shared Envelope are reflected in that
Envelope's **available balance**."* "Available balance" appears nowhere else in
the document and is not in §3.

So an envelope has a *planned* amount (what you intend), possibly a *funded*
amount (what Transfers actually put there), and a *remaining* figure. FR-47
answers "can we afford it" from *"the envelope's remaining balance."* Remaining
against what — plan, or money? These diverge the moment FR-23's permitted
over-planning happens, which the PRD expects ("the shortfall is shown rather than
blocked"). The ten-second answer that is the secondary persona's entire
relationship with the product can be off by the whole shortfall, and the document
does not say which number it means.

FR-48 compounds it: *"The check draws on envelope balances only, and not on the
Unallocated Pool or **any unsettled amount**."* So Alex, who owes Sam £137 from
an unsealed October, is told Clothing has £140 left. The answer is systematically
optimistic in exactly the circumstance where it matters.

### H-8. UJ-7's central action has no FR
**Location:** UJ-7 vs FR-9, FR-10, FR-11.

UJ-7's climax: *"Sam agrees, **moves it out of Ours** while the Period is still

- FR-11 (decline) returns a Transaction to its owner, but is *"available to the

So the journey the PRD uses to justify having no dispute workflow — "a question,

### H-9. Subscription entitlement across two app stores, with no server-side account
**Location:** FR-12, FR-13, §11, §10.3, NFR-5, §5.2.

FR-12: "A Household carries exactly one subscription, billed to the creating
Partner through the platform app store." §11: "The second Partner pays nothing and
needs no payment method."

Sam subscribes on iOS. Alex is on Android. Alex's device must know whether the
Household's subscription is active, in order to enforce FR-13's read-only
degradation. A StoreKit receipt is validated against Apple by an account Google
knows nothing about. Making this work requires a server that maps a receipt to a
Household identifier and answers entitlement queries for both devices — which is
per-Household server-side state and computation (§10.3 forbids it), tied to a
stable Household identity that **no FR anywhere in this document defines**. There
is no account, no user identity, no Household ID in §3 or §5.

Secondary: FR-13's "30-day grace period" is the PRD's invention; the stores run
their own billing retry and grace windows, which the app does not control.

### H-10. NFR-8 (export completeness) vs FR-49 (what export contains)
**Location:** NFR-8, FR-49, §1, FR-2, §11.

NFR-8: *"An export is a **faithful, complete substitute** for the app's own record
of everything the exporting Partner can see. It is tested as such."* §1: "Everything
exports to CSV at any time."

FR-49 enumerates: Shared Ledger, own Personal Ledger, visible envelopes, the
category set, sealed Settlements. **Not exported:** Transfers, Payer attribution,
Entry→Transaction structure, notes, edit history (FR-9), Split Rules, the Floor,
income history, the Unallocated Pool and its assignments, adjustments (FR-43),
carry-forward markers (FR-46), proposal state. An enumerated list and a
completeness guarantee cannot both be normative; one of them has to go.

Structurally worse: FR-2 requires that *"The Entry is counted once in reporting
and export; allocations never double-count the payment."* A single flat CSV cannot
represent one Entry producing N Transactions across Ledgers without either
duplicating the Entry row or losing the linkage. The format is specified ("CSV")
and the invariant is specified; the reconciliation between them is not.

### H-11. No FR specifies authentication or app lock
**Location:** FR-15, UJ-1, §5.2 vs all of §4, §10.1.

UJ-1 opens with "Already authenticated by biometric." §5.2's prose says "The
joining Partner sets their own passcode or biometric — each Partner holds their
own device credentials, and neither can unlock the other's phone into the app."
FR-15 mentions it in one consequence, as a side effect of pairing.

**No FR owns app lock.** Nothing specifies: whether the app locks at all, lock
timeout, behaviour after failed attempts, what happens when the device passcode
changes or biometrics are re-enrolled, whether the web session (FR-18) locks,
or whether a second device (FR-52) has its own credential. For a product whose
entire §4 rests on "the other Partner cannot see my Personal Ledger" while living
on a phone the other Partner can physically pick up, this is the first line of
defence and it is a sentence of prose.

### H-12. Nothing deletes the server-side copy, and no data-protection obligations are specified
**Location:** FR-51, §10.2, §10.3, NFR-5.

§10.3 says the service "relays and stores ciphertext." FR-51 "Delete a Household
and its data" consists of three consequences, all local: *"Deletion removes the
Household's data from **the acting Partner's device**... Deletion does not reach
the other Partner's device."*

So the operator's ciphertext store is never deleted, has no retention policy, and
no FR governs it. "We can't read it" is not an answer to erasure obligations —
ciphertext tied to an identifiable Household is still personal data, and the
operator is still the controller. Nothing in this PRD covers data subject access,
erasure, breach notification, a retention window, or a privacy policy. For a
product whose *entire differentiation* is privacy, shipped in the UK/EU (prices in
£, the personas are British), run by a solo founder, this is not a detail.

Also: FR-51's *"Deletion is offered only after an export has been taken or
explicitly declined"* puts a gate in front of the delete button for a user who may
be deleting under duress — directly against §10.1's logic.

### H-13. The business case does not close
**Location:** §11, §13.1, §14 (SM-1, SM-2), §10.3, §13.2.

- **Revenue at target is not a business.** SM-1: 1,000 paying Households at 12
  months. §11: "a few US dollars per month." At $5/month that is $60k gross ARR,
  ~$45–51k after the store cut — the *entire* company, after a year, at the moment
  the target is hit. That has to pay for a solo founder's year of building and the
  next year of operating.
- **The scope does not fit the funder.** §13.1 commits to: two native apps, a
  desktop web app, E2EE device-to-device sync with conflict resolution, a QR key
  exchange with verification codes, browser session key transport, OFX and CSV
  parsing with per-bank mapping and duplicate detection, envelope budgeting with
  rollover and a derived income Floor, a two-sided settlement protocol with content
  hashing, in-order sealing, carry-forward and adjustments, multi-device pairing,
  and full export. 52 FRs. This is multiple engineer-years of work including a
  hand-rolled cryptographic sync protocol, for one person, before the first dollar.
- **The funnel maths are brutal.** 1,000 *at* 12 months with 60% six-month
  retention implies roughly 1,600–2,000 gross subscribers acquired in year one:
  ~5 new paying households every day from launch, sustained.
- **No acquisition channel is named anywhere in the document.** No §14 metric
  measures install→trial→paid. There is no free tier (forbidden by §11), no
  referral mechanic, no content/SEO surface, no public API or integration, and the
  one viral edge — the second Partner — pays nothing and is defined as the
  reluctant one. At ~$30 net LTV, paid acquisition in personal finance (CAC
  commonly $30–100+) is arithmetically impossible.
- **The retention target is unevidenced and fights the design.** >60% at six months
  is far above typical consumer subscription benchmarks, and this is a
  *manual-entry* budgeting app — historically the highest-churn category there is.
  §13.2 then defers **recurring and scheduled transactions** "by omission rather
  than by decision" (its own words, OQ-2). Rent, utilities and subscriptions are a
  household's most predictable shared costs; requiring them to be re-typed every
  month, by the person who already resents being the accountant, is the single
  largest churn driver available, and it is deferred by accident.
- **The product's acquisition path runs through a declared non-user.** §2.2:
  "Solo budgeters. The entire model is two-party; a single user has nothing to
  settle." §5.2/FR-16 then make solo use a first-class, fully-featured capability
  and the designed entry point. SM-3a concedes up to 25% of paying Households never
  pair. So up to a quarter of the revenue comes from a segment the PRD says the
  product is wrong for — and those are exactly the subscriptions SM-2 will lose.
- **Support is unmodelled and unsurvivable.** §10.3 assumes "no support SLA, no
  component whose failure requires a human within hours." But FR-50 guarantees
  *permanent, unrecoverable data loss* for single-device Partners, and pairing is a
  hand-rolled crypto flow. "I lost everything and you say you can't help" tickets
  arrive on a paid product with public app-store reviews. No support story exists
  anywhere in the document.

### H-14. Dissolution leaves an orphaned, undefined product state
**Location:** FR-20, FR-21, FR-12, §2.2.

After dissolution: the subscription keeps billing the creating Partner (FR-12 ties
it to them; nothing cancels it). Both Partners hold a frozen app that cannot
settle (needs two Partners), cannot pair (FR-14 logic undefined post-dissolution),
and serves a user §2.2 declares a non-user. No FR says whether a Household can be
re-formed, whether either Partner can create a new Household, what the dissolved
app does on next launch, or whether the dissolving Partner's data survives on the
*other* device (it does — Sam keeps a full copy of the Shared Ledger including
every funding-side disclosure Alex ever made, which is correct but unstated).
UJ-8's "Resolution" ends at export and the product's lifecycle ends with it.

### M-1. §4 does not say whether the disclosed "amount" is the Entry's or the allocation's

### M-2. FR-35 discloses more than §4 permits
§4 fixes the funding-side disclosure at "merchant, amount, and date." FR-35

### M-3. "Settle-Up is the one place the boundary opens" — it is not
§4 calls Settle-Up "the one place." FR-10 notifies the other Partner the moment a

copy.

§4: *"A Transaction in a Personal Ledger **becomes visible to the other Partner**"*
in two cases. But in case 1 (FR-10) the Transaction is *moved out* of the Personal
Ledger into the Shared Ledger, and in case 2 (FR-3) it is a Shared Ledger
allocation from the start. Nothing in a Personal Ledger is ever disclosed in
place. The load-bearing section describes a mechanism the FRs do not implement,
which matters because the two differ at the edges (e.g. what FR-11's decline

§5.1 "Realizes UJ-1, **UJ-2**." UJ-2 is the affordability check, realized by FR-47

### M-6. The Feature→UJ map and the UJ→FR map contradict each other
UJ-5 cites FR-10 and UJ-7 cites FR-9, both of which live in §5.1 — whose
"Realizes" line names neither UJ-5 nor UJ-7. The two mapping directions were
