1	---
2	title: Ledgerleaf
3	status: draft
4	created: 2026-10-01
5	updated: 2026-10-01
6	---
7	
8	# PRD: Ledgerleaf
9	*Working title — confirm.*
10	
11	## 0. Document Purpose
12	
13	This PRD is written for the product owner, for downstream BMad workflows — UX, architecture, and
14	epic/story breakdown — and for anyone reviewing whether Ledgerleaf is worth building. It describes
15	**what** Ledgerleaf does and for whom; it does not describe how it is built.
16	
17	**How to read it.** §3 Glossary fixes the vocabulary: every domain noun is defined once and used
18	verbatim everywhere else, so a downstream reader never has to guess whether two words mean the same
19	thing. §4 Privacy Model is cross-cutting and load-bearing — it defines what each Partner can see of
20	the other, and the Features in §5 reference it rather than restating it. §5 groups capabilities into
21	seven Features with Functional Requirements nested beneath, numbered globally FR-1 through FR-56 so
22	downstream artifacts have stable references even if the Features are reorganised. §2.3 Key User
23	Journeys, UJ-1 through UJ-8, are the narrative spine the FRs serve.
24	
25	Inferences the product owner has not confirmed are tagged `[ASSUMPTION]` inline and collected in §16.
26	Items needing a decision are tagged `[NOTE FOR PM]` inline and, where unresolved, listed in §15.
27	
28	**Companion document.** `addendum.md` holds depth that belongs to architecture rather than to this
29	PRD — the sync and key-exchange mechanism, browser session key transport, the Settlement hash
30	construction, and the import pipeline's internals. Where this PRD states a promise, the addendum is
31	where the means of keeping it are worked out.
32	
33	**No UX or architecture document exists yet.** This PRD is the first artifact in the chain.
34	
35	## 1. Vision
36	
37	> *"Your money, your partner's money, and the money you share — finally three separate piles, with
38	> the month-end argument done for you in one tap, and no bank password ever leaving your phone."*
39	> — the product owner's pitch, and the sentence the rest of this document is accountable to.
40	
41	Ledgerleaf is a budgeting app for two-person households that treats **mine**, **yours**, and
42	**ours** as three genuinely separate piles of money rather than one merged pot with labels on
43	it. Each partner keeps a personal ledger; the household keeps a shared one; money moves
44	between them by explicit transfer. At the end of each month Ledgerleaf computes who owes whom
45	on shared spending — under whatever split the couple agreed to, whether that is even, scaled
46	to income, or set per category — so the month closes with a single transfer instead of an
47	argument. Every closed month is kept as a record, so a disagreement about what was agreed is
48	settled by looking it up rather than by memory.
49	
50	It is privacy-first by construction, not by policy. Ledgerleaf never asks for a bank
51	credential and never will. Transactions are entered by hand or imported from CSV/OFX files the
52	user already has. Data lives on the partners' own devices and syncs between them end-to-end
53	encrypted, so there is no readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to
54	mine or sell. Everything exports to CSV at any time, because a product that asks for trust
55	should be easy to leave.
56	
57	The point is to retire the household accountant. Today one partner owns the spreadsheet,
58	maintains it, and resents it, while the other never opens it; bank-linked apps solve the effort
59	problem by exposing every transaction to both partners and monetising the data behind their
60	backs. Ledgerleaf takes the opposite trade — a little manual effort in exchange for fairness
61	and privacy. Six months in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant: the partner who never
62	opened the spreadsheet checks "can we afford this" before a big purchase on their own, settle-up
63	takes five minutes, and neither person feels surveilled by the other.
64	
65	## 2. Target User
66	
67	Two-adult households, roughly 25-45, both partners employed, with at least one irregular income
68	source — freelance, tips, or commission. They already share some expenses and deliberately keep
69	others separate.
70	
71	**Primary — the spreadsheet keeper.** Owns and maintains the shared budget today. Competent with
72	it, and resents being the household's accountant. Does the imports, the categorising, and the
73	month-end reconciliation, and carries the social cost of raising it.
74	
75	**Secondary — the partner who doesn't open it.** Not disengaged about money, just not willing to
76	operate someone else's spreadsheet. Wants a ten-second answer to "can we afford this" and to not
77	be surprised at month end.
78	
79	### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done
80	
81	- Keep personal and shared money genuinely separate without running two systems.
82	- Know in seconds whether a purchase fits, without opening a spreadsheet or doing arithmetic.
83	- Close out shared spending at month end without reconstructing who paid for what.
84	- Stop being the household accountant — or stop feeling managed by one.
85	- Spend personal money without feeling watched by a partner.
86	- Settle a disagreement about a past month by pointing at a record, not by recalling it.
87	- Budget against income that is not the same number every month.
88	- Use a money app without handing over bank credentials or becoming the product.
89	
90	### 2.2 Non-Users (v1)
91	
92	- **Solo budgeters.** The entire model is two-party; a single user has nothing to settle.
93	- **Households of more than two adults.** Roommate groups, multi-generational households.
94	- **People who want everything categorised automatically.** Ledgerleaf trades effort for privacy;
95	  that trade is the product, and it is the wrong trade for them.
96	- **Net-worth and investment trackers.** Ledgerleaf budgets cash flow; it does not track assets.
97	
98	### 2.3 Key User Journeys
99	
100	*Numbered UJ-1 through UJ-8. FRs reference them inline. Two protagonists run throughout:*
101	
102	> **Sam**, 34, salaried operations manager. Has maintained the household spreadsheet for three years
103	> and is quietly sick of it. **Alex**, 31, freelance designer, earns between £1,800 and £5,000 a month
104	> and rarely knows which until it arrives. Alex has opened the spreadsheet twice, both times because
105	> Sam asked.
106	
107	- **UJ-1. Alex splits a supermarket shop in the car park, one-handed, before starting the engine.**
108	  Alex has just paid £62 on their own card — some of it the household shop, some of it their own.
109	  Already authenticated by biometric. Alex opens Ledgerleaf, taps quick-add, enters 62.00 and the
110	  merchant; the app offers the Ledger Alex used last. Alex taps *split this purchase*, puts 40.00 into
111	  Ours as Groceries and leaves 22.00 in their own Personal Ledger. **Climax:** the whole thing is done
112	  in under fifteen seconds with no confirmation dialog, and an undo toast sits there for ten seconds
113	  in case Alex fat-fingered it. **Resolution:** one card payment, recorded once, sitting in two
114	  Ledgers. The 40.00 will surface at Settle-Up as *"Alex paid 40.00 for Ours"* — and nothing else
115	  about Alex's personal spending travels with it. *Realizes FR-1, FR-2, FR-3, FR-4.*
116	
117	- **UJ-2. Alex checks whether a £78 jacket fits, while standing in the shop.**
118	  Alex is the partner who never opened the spreadsheet. They open Ledgerleaf, and the affordability
119	  check is right there on the first screen. Amount, category. **Climax:** *"£140 left in Clothing.
120	  £62 after this."* No verdict, no approval, no small green tick. **Resolution:** Alex decides, buys
121	  or doesn't, and nothing is recorded — Sam will never know the check happened. This single screen is
122	  the whole of Alex's relationship with the product, and that is a success condition.
123	  *Realizes FR-51, FR-52.*
124	
125	- **UJ-3. Sam pairs Alex into the Household, in the kitchen, in about two minutes.**
126	  Sam installed Ledgerleaf a week ago and has already entered a month of transactions, so the app is
127	  not an empty shell to sell Alex on. Sam taps *invite partner*; a QR code appears. Alex installs the
128	  app and scans it off Sam's screen. Both phones show the same four-word verification code; both
129	  confirm. **Climax:** Alex is in — seeing Ours fully populated, their own Personal Ledger empty, and
130	  a prompt to enter their income for the split. **Resolution:** Sam's month of solo work is now shared
131	  — except Sam's Personal Ledger, which stays as private as it was on day one. Nothing became visible
132	  because Alex arrived. **Edge case:** if the codes don't match, nobody joins and the invite is burned.
133	  *Realizes FR-16, FR-17, FR-18, FR-19.*
134	
135	- **UJ-4. Sam sets up November's envelopes on the 1st, in four taps.**
136	  Sam opens *This month*. October's envelopes are there with what was planned, rolled over, spent and
137	  left. Sam taps *copy last month*, adjusts Groceries upward because Christmas is coming, and is done.
138	  **Climax:** Alex's freelance income isn't in the plan at all — envelopes are funded against the
139	  Household's Floor, the lowest of the last six months. **Resolution:** when Alex's invoice lands
140	  mid-month at £4,100, the surplus goes to the Unallocated Pool, and the Household assigns it to
141	  envelopes *then*, with the money in hand. Nothing was promised against a month that hadn't happened.
142	  *Realizes FR-25, FR-27, FR-28, FR-29, FR-30, FR-31.*
143	
144	- **UJ-5. Sam imports a bank statement at the kitchen table, on a laptop.**
145	  Sam downloads October's CSV from the bank, opens Ledgerleaf's web app, and scans the QR on screen
146	  with their phone to authorise the session. The saved mapping for this bank applies itself. **Climax:**
147	  48 rows staged for review, six flagged as likely duplicates of transactions Sam already entered by
148	  hand; Sam dismisses two and confirms four. **Resolution:** Sam commits. Everything lands in Sam's
149	  own Personal Ledger, private by default, and Sam marks the four household ones as shared from there.
150	  The browser session dies when Sam closes the tab. **Edge case:** no bank password was typed anywhere,
151	  because there is nowhere to type one. *Realizes FR-20, FR-32, FR-33, FR-34, FR-35, FR-36, FR-12.*
152	
153	- **UJ-6. Sam and Alex close October on the 1st of November, from two different rooms.**
154	  Sam opens Settle-Up. October's shared spending is listed line by line: who paid, which Split Rule
155	  applied, which items were funded from someone's personal money — and at the bottom, *"Alex owes Sam
156	  137.00"*. The screen says plainly what is being disclosed and why. Sam taps **Propose**. Alex gets
157	  one notification, opens the same list, and reads it. **Climax:** Alex taps **Accept**, and the
158	  Settlement seals — immutable, hashed, filed in Settlement History. **Resolution:** Ledgerleaf does
159	  not move the money. Alex sends Sam £137 by bank transfer that evening and records it as a Transfer.
160	  The month took five minutes and ended in a payment rather than a conversation about whose turn it
161	  was. *Realizes FR-37, FR-39, FR-40, FR-41, FR-44, FR-45.*
162	
163	- **UJ-7. Alex queries a line instead of accepting it.**
164	  Same screen as UJ-6, but Alex stops at a £40 lunch tagged to Ours. Alex taps the line and
165	  *ask about this*: **"wasn't this your work thing?"** Sam gets the note attached to that transaction.
166	  **Climax:** Sam agrees, moves it out of Ours while the Period is still open, and the proposal
167	  withdraws and re-forms around the corrected number by itself — Alex's earlier reading never becomes
168	  an acceptance of a figure that has since moved. **Resolution:** Alex accepts £97 instead. There was
169	  no dispute workflow, no arbitration, no escalation — a question, an edit, and a number both people
170	  looked at. *Realizes FR-42, FR-43, FR-11.*
171	
172	- **UJ-8. Alex leaves, alone, immediately, and takes their data with them.**
173	  The relationship has ended. Alex opens Settings and dissolves the Household. **Climax:** it takes
174	  effect at once. Sam's access to shared data stops going forward; sync between the devices ends;
175	  Alex needs nobody's agreement and gives no reason. **Resolution:** Sam is told only that the
176	  Household was dissolved. Both export Ours, their own Personal Ledger, and every sealed Settlement
177	  as CSV. Alex's Personal Ledger was never visible to Sam and still isn't. Ledgerleaf divides nothing
178	  and adjudicates nothing. **Edge case:** no screen, record, or notification anywhere in the product
179	  reveals where Alex was when they did it. *Realizes FR-23, FR-24, FR-53.*
180	
181	## 3. Glossary
182	*Seeded from the user's own vocabulary — to confirm and extend as Features are worked.
183	Downstream readers and workflows must use these terms exactly; no synonyms elsewhere in this PRD.*
184	
185	- **Household** — the unit of account: exactly two Partners in v1. Owns three Ledgers.
186	- **Partner** — one of the two adults in a Household. Each has their own device(s).
187	- **Ledger** — a named pile of money holding Transactions. Exactly three per Household:
188	  two Personal Ledgers (one per Partner) and one Shared Ledger.
189	- **Personal Ledger** — a Partner's own money. One per Partner. Private to its owner per §4.
190	- **Shared Ledger** — the Household's joint money. One per Household, visible to both Partners.
191	  Named **Ours** in the interface; this document uses *Shared Ledger* except when quoting a screen.
192	  A Partner's own Personal Ledger is named **Mine** in the interface.
193	- **Entry** — one real-world payment or receipt, recorded once. An Entry has a date, a Payer, and
194	  produces one or more Transactions whose amounts sum to the Entry amount.
195	- **Payer** — the Partner whose own money funded an Entry.
196	- **Transaction** — a single dated money movement in one Ledger, with amount, category, and note.
197	  Belongs to exactly one Entry.
198	- **Transfer** — a dated movement of money between two Ledgers of the same Household, recorded as
199	  its own kind of Entry. A Transfer has no Payer and no category: it moves money that is already
200	  inside the Household rather than recording money entering or leaving it. It produces one debit
201	  Transaction and one credit Transaction.
202	- **Income** — a dated receipt of money into a Ledger, recorded as an Entry. Each Partner records
203	  their own; see §4 for what is and is not disclosed.
204	- **Envelope** — a per-category budget allocation for a Period, with a balance that can roll over.
205	- **Rollover** — carrying an Envelope's unspent balance into the next Period.
206	- **Period** — a calendar month. The unit over which Envelopes are funded and Settle-Up runs.
207	- **Current Period** — the calendar month in progress. Exactly one at any time; new Entries are
208	  recorded here.
209	- **Open Period** — any Period that has not yet been sealed by a Settlement. Because Periods seal
210	  oldest-first (FR-49), more than one Period may be open at once, and the Current Period is always
211	  one of them.
212	- **Split Rule** — how a shared-category cost is divided between Partners: even, income-proportional,
213	  or a custom per-category ratio.
214	- **Settle-Up** — the end-of-Period computation of the net amount one Partner owes the other,
215	  derived from Shared Ledger spending and the applicable Split Rules.
216	- **Settlement** — the closed, immutable record of one Period's Settle-Up, retained as history.
217	- **Floor** — the conservative figure a Household funds Shared Envelopes against. Each Partner sets
218	  their own **Contribution Floor**: the amount they commit to the Shared Ledger each Period. The
219	  Household Floor is their sum. Contribution Floors are commitments, not incomes — see §4.
220	- **Unallocated Pool** — money held in a Ledger but not yet assigned to any Envelope. One per
221	  Ledger. A Personal Ledger's Pool is private to its owner; the Shared Ledger's Pool is visible to
222	  both Partners.
223	- **Dissolution** — the unilateral, immediate ending of a Household by either Partner.
224	
225	## 4. Privacy Model
226	*Cross-cutting. Defines what each Partner can see of the other's money. Every FR that touches
227	visibility references this section rather than restating it.*
228	
229	**Default — Personal Ledgers are private at the transaction level.** A Partner opening the
230	other's Personal Ledger sees nothing: no Transactions, no categories, and no balance total. The
231	absence is complete; there is no aggregate that hints at the detail.
232	
233	**Disclosure is per-Transaction and owner-initiated.** A Transaction in a Personal Ledger becomes
234	visible to the other Partner in exactly two cases:
235	
236	1. The owner explicitly tags it as shared.
237	2. It is the funding side of a shared expense — the owner paid a Shared Ledger cost from personal
238	   money.
239	
240	In both cases exactly one Transaction is disclosed, carrying its date, merchant, amount, and the
241	category under which it will be split — the category is disclosed because Settle-Up cannot apply a
242	per-category Split Rule without it. Nothing else about the Personal Ledger — its balance, its other
243	Transactions, its other categories, its Envelopes, or its Unallocated Pool — is disclosed.
244	
245	**Income figures are never shared, but an income-proportional split reveals relative income —
246	and the product says so.** Each Partner enters their own income. It is stored encrypted and the
247	figure itself is never transmitted to the other Partner. An income-proportional Split Rule derives
248	a ratio, and only that ratio and the resulting percentages (e.g. "58/42") are shared. A Partner who
249	knows their own income can solve the ratio for the other's figure, so Ledgerleaf does not claim
250	otherwise: choosing an income-proportional Split Rule states plainly that it reveals relative
251	income, and the even and custom-per-category Split Rules remain available and derive nothing from
252	income at all.
253	
254	**What the Shared Ledger necessarily reveals.** Two Partners funding a joint pot can always reason
255	about each other's contributions, and Ledgerleaf does not pretend otherwise. A Partner can see the
256	other's **Contribution Floor** — the amount they commit to Ours each Period — because that number
257	*is* the shared agreement. A Contribution Floor is deliberately **not** an income: it is what
258	someone commits, not what they earn, and a Partner earning £5,000 may commit £900. Income itself is
259	never shared, never aggregated into a shared figure, and never inferable from one. Money a Partner
260	receives above their Contribution Floor stays in their Personal Ledger's Unallocated Pool, which is
261	private, and reaches Ours only when they choose to move it.
262	
263	**Settle-Up is the one place the boundary opens, deliberately.** Settle-Up shows its work: every
264	Shared Ledger Transaction with who paid, plus any funded-from-personal Transactions as described
265	above. Without this, the computation is unverifiable and the product's central promise fails. The
266	Settle-Up surface states in plain words what is being disclosed and why, at the moment of
267	disclosure — the opening is never silent.
268	
269	A funding-side disclosure is made **when the Entry is recorded, not held back until Settle-Up**.
270	A Shared Ledger Transaction affects the Shared Envelope it is categorised under, and both Partners
271	can see that Envelope's spent figure, so the disclosure is already made the moment the money lands
272	in Ours. Ledgerleaf shows it plainly at that point rather than letting a Partner believe it is
273	private until month end.
274	
275	**No Partner can write into the other's Personal Ledger.** Not by Entry allocation, not by Transfer,
276	not by import. A Ledger a Partner cannot read is also one they cannot change, and a settling payment
277	between Partners is recorded by each on their own side (FR-44).

279	## 5. Features
280	
281	### 5.1 Ledgers & Transactions
282	
283	
284	
285	**Description.** The spine of the product: three Ledgers per Household, and the act of putting
286	money into them. Recording a purchase is the single most repeated thing anyone does in
287	Ledgerleaf, so it is built for the hallway and the supermarket car park — one hand, under
288	fifteen seconds, no confirmation dialog standing between the user and being done.
289	
290	The awkward case is the common one: one card payment covering both household and personal
291	spending. Ledgerleaf models this as a single **Entry** — one real-world payment, with one
292	**Payer** — that produces one or more **Transactions** across Ledgers. The payment is recorded
293	once and never double-counted, while each Ledger sees only its own share. When the Payer funded a
294	Shared Ledger cost from personal money, that is the funding-side disclosure described in §4, and
295	it surfaces at Settle-Up rather than in the other Partner's day-to-day view.
296	
297	Money moves between Ledgers only by explicit **Transfer** — to fund shared Envelopes at the start
298	of a Period, or to reimburse. Transfers are never edited. A mistaken Transfer is corrected by a new,
299	opposite Transfer, so the history stays append-only and nobody can quietly rewrite what happened.
300	That property is load-bearing for the product's promise (§1): a Settlement nobody can retroactively
301	alter is the thing that ends the argument.
302	
303	Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2.

472	### 5.2 Household Setup, Pairing & Dissolution
473	
474	
475	
476	**Description.** Ledgerleaf is worth nothing as a single-player app, so pairing is not onboarding
477	plumbing — it is the feature on which the product's stated success metric rests. The failure mode is
478	known by name: the partner who never opened the spreadsheet never opens this either.
479	
480	One Partner creates the Household and subscribes; billing is one subscription per Household through
481	the app store. They can then use Ledgerleaf fully alone — entering and importing a whole Period of
482	Transactions — so the product is useful before it is two-sided and nobody has to sell their partner
483	on an empty app. That solo work syncs across when the second Partner joins, and the first Partner's
484	Personal Ledger stays private from the first day, exactly as §4 describes; nothing becomes visible in
485	retrospect because a second person arrived.
486	
487	Pairing is deliberately physical. An invite produces a QR code and a one-time link valid for 24 hours;
488	the key exchange runs device-to-device, and both phones must display the same short verification code
489	before anyone joins. A pairing that cannot be verified does not complete. The joining Partner sets
490	their own passcode or biometric — each Partner holds their own device credentials, and neither can
491	unlock the other's phone into the app.
492	
493	The desktop web app is reached the same way. The browser shows a QR code, the Partner scans it from
494	the phone, and the phone hands that browser session its keys. The session is per-browser and
495	short-lived — it expires after 12 hours idle or when the tab closes — and the phone can revoke it at
496	any moment. Each Partner authorises their own browser, and a browser session sees only what that
497	Partner can see; the web surface is not a back door around §4.
498	
499	A Household can also end. Ledgerleaf builds no features for dividing assets or unwinding a
500	relationship — that is an explicit non-goal (§7) — but it does let a Household be dissolved by
501	**either Partner alone, immediately, without the other's cooperation**. This is a safety
502	requirement before it is a convenience one: a person who needs to leave must be able to, now, and
503	without asking. The remaining Partner is told that the Household was dissolved and nothing else —
504	no reason, no negotiation, no appeal. Both walk away with their data.
505	
506	Realizes UJ-3, UJ-8.

638	### 5.3 Envelope Budgeting
639	
640	
641	
642	**Description.** Envelopes are how a Household decides what money is *for* before it is spent, and
643	they are what makes §5.6 answerable in ten seconds. On the 1st, a Partner opens **This month** and
644	sees the envelope list: category, planned amount, rolled-over amount, spent, and left. Setting up a
645	month is mostly not a decision — **copy last month** is one tap and is the path most months take.
646	
647	Envelopes exist on the Shared Ledger and on each Partner's own Personal Ledger. Personal envelopes
648	are private to their owner under §4 in exactly the way personal Transactions are: the other Partner
649	sees no personal envelope, its planned amount, or its balance.
650	
651	Irregular income is handled by refusing to pretend. Each Partner sets a **Contribution Floor** — the
652	amount they commit to Ours each Period, proposed by the app as the lowest of their own last six
653	months of income but chosen by them — and Shared Envelopes are funded against the sum of the two.
654	A Contribution Floor is a commitment, not an income, which is what makes it shareable: it says what
655	someone will put in, not what they earn (§4).
656	
657	Money arriving above a Partner's Contribution Floor is not budgeted in advance. It lands in that
658	Partner's own **Unallocated Pool**, which is private, and reaches Ours only if and when they move it
659	there. A freelancer's good month is not a promise, and Ledgerleaf will neither spend it before it
660	arrives nor announce it to the other Partner when it does.
661	
662	**What an Envelope's numbers mean.** An Envelope's *planned* amount is an intention. Its *available*
663	balance is cash: the money actually moved into the Ledger and assigned to that Envelope, plus any
664	rolled-over balance, minus what has been spent against it. Planned and available are shown side by
665	side and are not the same number — an Envelope planned at £400 that has only been funded with £250
666	has £250 available, and the affordability check (FR-51) answers from available, never from planned.
667	Under-funding is shown, never hidden, and never blocked.
668	
669	Rollover is chosen per envelope: carry the unspent balance forward, or reset to zero. A Shared
670	envelope that rolls over keeps its balance in Ours, owned by the Household, and is never attributed
671	to either Partner at Settle-Up — Settle-Up compares what each Partner *paid* against their share of
672	what was *spent*, and balances do not enter into it.
673	
674	Realizes UJ-4.
675

763	### 5.4 Statement Import
764	
765	
766	*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*
767	
768	**Description.** Ledgerleaf will never ask for a bank credential, so the bridge between a bank and a
769	Ledger is a file the Partner already has the right to download. Import accepts CSV and OFX. It is a
770	desk activity — reconciling a month of rows is miserable on a phone — so it lives on the desktop web
771	surface, and not on the phone in v1.
772	
773	Import is staged, never silent. A file is parsed into a review list, and nothing reaches a Ledger
774	until the Partner commits it. Rows land by default in the importing Partner's own Personal Ledger —
775	a bank statement is one person's account, and §4 says that is private — and the Partner then marks
776	individual rows as shared via FR-12, which is precisely the retroactive catch-up path that FR-12
777	exists for. Rows can be reassigned to any Ledger the Partner can write to, per row, during review.
778	
779	Banks disagree about everything, so CSV column mapping is per source and remembered. OFX carries its
780	own structure and needs no mapping. `[ASSUMPTION: saved mappings are named by the Partner and reused
781	on subsequent imports from the same bank.]`
782	
783	Duplicates are the failure that destroys trust in an import, and overlapping statement downloads make
784	them routine. Ledgerleaf flags likely duplicates rather than deciding alone. `[ASSUMPTION: a row is
785	flagged as a likely duplicate when an existing Transaction shares its amount and falls within a few
786	days of its date; the Partner confirms or dismisses each flag, and nothing is auto-discarded.]`
787	
788	Realizes UJ-5.
789	
790	**Functional Requirements:**
791	
792	#### FR-32: Import a CSV or OFX file
793	
794	A Partner can load a statement file into a staged review list.
795	
796	**Consequences (testable):**
797	- CSV and OFX are accepted; no other format is.
798	- No bank credential is requested, stored, or transmitted at any point.
799	- Import is available on the desktop web surface to an authorised browser session (FR-20).
800	- A file that cannot be parsed is rejected with the reason, and nothing is staged.
801	
802	#### FR-33: Map CSV columns to fields
803	
804	A Partner can tell Ledgerleaf which columns of a CSV mean what.
805	
806	**Consequences (testable):**
807	- Date, amount, and description can each be mapped to a column.
808	- A mapping can be saved under a name and reapplied to later imports.
809	- A saved mapping is applied automatically when a file's header matches it.
810	- OFX files require no mapping.
811	
812	#### FR-34: Review staged rows before committing
813	
814	Nothing enters a Ledger until the Partner commits it.
815	
816	**Consequences (testable):**
817	- Staged rows are listed with date, amount, description, and destination Ledger and category.
818	- Each row's destination Ledger and category can be changed before commit.
819	- Rows can be excluded individually.
820	- Abandoning a review discards the staged rows and changes no Ledger.
821	- Committing creates one Entry per committed row, with the importing Partner as Payer.
822	
823	#### FR-35: Flag likely duplicates
824	
825	Re-importing an overlapping statement does not silently double-count.
826	
827	**Consequences (testable):**
828	- A staged row matching an existing Transaction on amount and within a small date window is flagged.
829	- A flagged row is shown alongside the Transaction it may duplicate.
830	- No flagged row is discarded automatically; the Partner confirms or dismisses each.
831	- Dismissing a flag commits the row normally.
832	
833	#### FR-36: Default imported rows to the importer's Personal Ledger
834	
835	Imported rows are private until their owner says otherwise.
836	
837	**Consequences (testable):**
838	- Committed rows default to the importing Partner's own Personal Ledger.
839	- Imported Personal Ledger Transactions are invisible to the other Partner per §4.
840	- A row can be reassigned to the Shared Ledger during review, or marked shared afterwards via FR-12.
841	
842	### 5.5 Settle-Up & Settlement History
843	
844	
845	
846	**Description.** The moment the product earns its keep. From the 1st of a Period onward, either
847	Partner can open the close for the Period just ended. Ledgerleaf presents a single statement: every
848	Shared Ledger Transaction, who paid it, the Split Rule applied, the funded-from-personal ones marked
849	as such, and one number at the bottom — *"Alex owes Sam 137.00"*. This is the surface where the
850	privacy boundary deliberately opens, and per §4 it says so in plain words, where the user is looking.
851	
852	Settle-Up is two-sided by design, because a number one person computed alone is exactly the
853	spreadsheet problem Ledgerleaf exists to retire. This is a deliberate departure from the §1 pitch's
854	"one tap": the close costs each Partner a tap rather than costing the Household one, and that second
855	tap is the whole guarantee. It should still take five minutes, not an evening. The initiator **Proposes**; the other Partner is
856	notified, reviews the same statement, and **Accepts**. Acceptance is always of the exact list on
857	screen — if anything underneath changes, the proposal is withdrawn and re-proposed automatically,
858	so nobody ever accepts a number that has since moved. On both accepts the Settlement is **sealed**:
859	immutable, retained in Settlement History with a hash of its contents.
860	
861	Ledgerleaf does not move money, and does not want to. It says who owes whom and then gets out of
862	the way; the Partners pay each other however they already do. When that happens, the app offers to
863	record it as a Transfer. **The Settlement closes on both accepts, not on payment** — the agreement
864	and the money are separate acts, and conflating them would let an unpaid debt hold the next month
865	hostage.
866	
867	There is no dispute mechanism in v1, deliberately. Disagreement is a conversation between two people
868	who live together, not a workflow. Tapping any line offers **ask about this**, which attaches a note
869	to that Transaction for the other Partner; whoever entered it then edits it while the Period is
870	still open, and the proposal re-forms around the corrected figure. The product carries the question;
871	the couple settles it.
872	
873	Settled Periods are never reopened. A Transaction dated inside a sealed Period but entered after it
874	closed lands in the current Period, flagged with its true date, and settles there.
875	
876	Realizes UJ-6, UJ-7.
877	
878	**Functional Requirements:**
879	
880	#### FR-37: Configure Split Rules
881	
882	A Household can set how shared costs divide between Partners, as a default and per category.
883	
884	**Consequences (testable):**
885	- A Household default Split Rule is one of: even, income-proportional, or a custom ratio.
886	- Any category can carry a Split Rule overriding the Household default.
887	- Selecting income-proportional presents the §4 disclosure statement that it reveals relative income
888	  before it can be applied.
889	- Each Partner enters their own income; neither figure is transmitted to the other Partner.
890	- A change to a Split Rule applies to the open Period onward and never alters a sealed Settlement.
891	
892	#### FR-38: Compute the Settle-Up position for a Period
893	
894	Ledgerleaf derives, from a Period's Shared Ledger activity, a single amount one Partner owes the other.
895	
896	> `[ASSUMPTION — the computation below is drafted, not supplied. It is the arithmetic at the centre
897	> of the product and must be confirmed before anything is built on it. See Open Questions.]`
898	
899	The computation, for a Period:
900	
901	1. **Shared spending** is every Shared Ledger Transaction in the Period, whatever funded it.
902	2. **Each Partner's share of spending** is the sum, over categories, of that category's spending
903	   multiplied by the Partner's proportion under the Split Rule applying to that category (FR-37).
904	3. **Each Partner's contributions** are the sums they put into Ours during the Period: Transfers they
905	   made into the Shared Ledger (FR-5), plus Shared Ledger Transactions for which they are the Payer
906	   — the funding-side disclosures of §4.
907	4. **The Shared Ledger's residue** is total contributions minus total spending — money contributed
908	   but not yet spent, which remains the Household's and is attributed to neither Partner. Each
909	   Partner's share of the residue is their proportion under the Household default Split Rule.
910	5. **Each Partner's target** is their share of spending plus their share of the residue. **The
911	   settlement** is the difference between a Partner's target and their contributions. The two
912	   differences are equal and opposite, so one number names who owes whom.
913	
914	**Consequences (testable):**
915	- The two Partners' computed positions are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign; they sum to zero.
916	- Spending paid from the Shared Ledger's own balance is attributed to no Partner as a contribution,
917	  because the money was contributed when it was Transferred in.
918	- Rolled-over and unspent Shared Envelope balances sit in the residue and are owed to neither Partner.
919	- Amounts are computed to the currency's smallest unit; any rounding remainder is assigned to the
920	  Partner with the larger share, deterministically, so both devices compute an identical figure and
921	  an identical hash (FR-41).
922	- A Period with no Shared Ledger activity produces a settlement of zero rather than no Settlement.
923	
924	#### FR-39: Open the Settle-Up statement for a closed Period
925	
926	Either Partner can open Settle-Up for a Period from its first day onward.
927	
928	**Consequences (testable):**
929	- Settle-Up for a Period is available from the first day of the following Period.
930	- The statement lists every Shared Ledger Transaction in the Period with date, merchant, amount,
931	  category, Payer, and the Split Rule applied.
932	- Funded-from-personal Transactions are visually marked as such.
933	- The statement resolves to a single net figure naming the owing Partner and the amount.
934	- The statement states, in plain language and on the statement itself, what is being disclosed and why.
935	
936	#### FR-40: Propose a Settlement
937	
938	A Partner can propose the statement to the other Partner for acceptance.
939	
940	**Consequences (testable):**
941	- Proposing notifies the other Partner.
942	- A proposal is bound to the exact contents of the statement at the moment it was proposed.
943	- Either Partner may be the initiator; the role is not fixed to one Partner.
944	
945	#### FR-41: Accept a Settlement
946	
947	The non-initiating Partner can accept the proposed statement, sealing it.
948	
949	**Consequences (testable):**
950	- The accepting Partner sees the same statement the initiator proposed, line for line.
951	- A Settlement seals only when both Partners have accepted.
952	- On sealing, the Settlement becomes immutable and is written to Settlement History with a hash of
953	  its contents.
954	- Every Transaction drawn into a sealed Settlement becomes frozen per FR-11.
955	
956	#### FR-42: Auto-withdraw a proposal on change
957	
958	A proposal is withdrawn and re-formed whenever the data beneath it changes.
959	
960	**Consequences (testable):**
961	- A material change to a shared line — its amount, Payer, Split Rule, or category — withdraws an
962	  outstanding proposal. Immaterial changes, such as editing a note, do not.
963	- A withdrawn proposal is re-proposed automatically against the updated statement.
964	- No acceptance ever carries over from a withdrawn proposal to its replacement.
965	- Re-proposal notifications are batched to at most one per Partner per day.
966	
967	#### FR-43: Ask about a line
968	
969	A Partner can attach a question to any Transaction on the statement.
970	
971	**Consequences (testable):**
972	- Ask-about is available from any line of the Settle-Up statement.
973	- The note is attached to that Transaction and the other Partner is notified.
974	- Asking does not block, reject, or alter the proposal.
975	- Notes are visible to both Partners on the Transaction and are retained in Settlement History.
976	
977	#### FR-44: Record the settling Transfer
978	
979	After a Settlement is sealed, a Partner can record the real-world payment as a Transfer.
980	
981	**Consequences (testable):**
982	- Ledgerleaf initiates no payment and holds no payment credential.
983	- A sealed Settlement offers each Partner the entry that belongs on their own side, pre-filled with
984	  the settled amount: the paying Partner records money leaving their Personal Ledger, the receiving
985	  Partner records it arriving. Neither writes into the other's Ledger (§4).
986	- Recording is optional for each Partner independently and may be done at any time after sealing.
987	- A Settlement's sealed state is unaffected by whether its Transfer was recorded.
988	
989	#### FR-45: Review Settlement History
990	
991	Either Partner can read any sealed Settlement from any past Period.
992	
993	**Consequences (testable):**
994	- Every sealed Settlement is retained for the life of the Household.
995	- A historical Settlement renders the statement as it was sealed, including Payers, Split Rules
996	  applied, and any attached notes.
997	- A historical Settlement displays its content hash.
998	- No affordance edits, deletes, or reopens a sealed Settlement.
999	- Settlement History is included in CSV export (§5.7).
1000	
1001	#### FR-46: Place a back-dated Transaction
1002	
1003	A Transaction dated before the Current Period is recorded in the Current Period and settles there.
1004	
1005	**Consequences (testable):**
1006	- A Transaction entered with a date earlier than the Current Period is recorded in the Current
1007	  Period, whether or not the Period its date falls in has sealed.
1008	- The Transaction retains and displays its true date, flagged as dated outside the Period it settles in.
1009	- No sealed Period is reopened, recomputed, or amended.
1010	- An earlier Period that is open but not current is not retrospectively altered either; Periods are
1011	  closed in sequence and Transactions settle where they are entered.
1012	
1013	#### FR-47: Correct a sealed Entry by adjustment
1014	
1015	A Partner can correct an error inside a sealed Settlement by recording an offsetting adjustment in
1016	the open Period.
1017	
1018	**Consequences (testable):**
1019	- An adjustment is a Shared Ledger Transaction referencing the Settlement and Transaction it corrects.
1020	- An adjustment settles in the Period it was recorded in, not the one it corrects.
1021	- The original sealed Settlement is unchanged, and both figures remain visible in history.
1022	
1023	#### FR-48: Remind on a stalled proposal
1024	
1025	An outstanding proposal prompts the Partner it is waiting on, without ever resolving itself.
1026	
1027	**Consequences (testable):**
1028	- One reminder is sent to the non-accepting Partner 7 days after the proposal, and a second at 14 days.
1029	- No further reminders are sent after the second.
1030	- A proposal never auto-accepts and never expires.
1031	- The Period remains open and is labelled as waiting on the named Partner, to both Partners.
1032	
1033	#### FR-49: Seal Periods in order
1034	
1035	Settlements seal oldest first; a later Period cannot be proposed while an earlier one is unsealed.
1036	
1037	**Consequences (testable):**
1038	- A Period cannot be proposed while any earlier Period is unsealed.
1039	- A Period with an unsealed predecessor remains fully usable: Entries, imports, Transfers, and
1040	  Envelope activity all continue normally.

1	# Ledgerleaf — Addendum
2	
3	Depth the user supplied that belongs downstream (architecture, solution design, UX spec)
4	rather than in the PRD's main narrative. Captured as it arises; not a dumping ground for
5	audit or override information.
6	
7	## For Architecture / Solution Design
8	
9	### Storage and sync mechanism
10	- **Local-first storage.** The device holds the authoritative copy of household data; the
11	  app is expected to be fully usable with no network.
12	- **End-to-end encrypted sync between the two partners' devices.** Stated by the user as a
13	  product commitment. The PRD carries the *promise* (the operator cannot read household
14	  financial data); the *mechanism* — key exchange, pairing, conflict resolution, relay vs.
15	  peer-to-peer transport, key recovery on device loss — is an architecture decision and
16	  belongs here.
17	  - Open: device-loss / key-recovery story. Has real product surface (what the user is told,
18	    what they must do), so the user-visible half may be pulled back into the PRD once decided.
19	  - Open: concurrent-edit conflict semantics between two partners editing the same ledger.
20	
21	### Import pipeline
22	- **CSV/OFX import only — no bank credential aggregation, ever.** The *constraint* is a PRD-level
23	  product principle. The *implementation* — per-bank CSV column mapping, OFX parsing, duplicate
24	  detection across re-imported statement overlaps, category inference — is design work.
25	
26	### Pairing and session key transport
27	The PRD carries the user-visible flow (QR, one-time link, matching verification code, per-session
28	browser authorisation, revocation). The mechanism is architecture's:
29	- Device-to-device key exchange protocol and what, if anything, transits a relay.
30	- The verification code's construction and what attack it actually defeats.
31	- How a browser session receives key material "encrypted" from the phone, and where it lives for
32	  the session's lifetime (memory only? what survives a refresh?).
33	- Session expiry enforcement — client-side, server-assisted, or both — and how revocation reaches a
34	  live session.
35	- Sealed-Settlement content hash: what it covers, how it is computed, and what it is meant to prove
36	  to whom. The PRD promises it is displayed; it does not specify it.
37	
38	### Settle-Up determinism
39	FR-45 requires both devices to compute an identical settlement figure and an identical content hash.
40	That makes the arithmetic a consensus problem, not just a calculation:
41	- Fixed-point money representation and a single rounding rule applied in a defined order.
42	- What exactly the content hash covers — the input transactions, the split rules as applied, the
43	  output figure, or all three — and what it proves to whom.
44	- How two devices that have not fully synced avoid proposing different statements.
45	
46	### Sync partitioning and metadata
47	§4 requires that a Partner's Personal Ledger reaches only their own devices while the Shared Ledger
48	reaches both. That is a partitioning requirement on the sync layer, not an application-level filter:
49	- Separate key scopes per Ledger, so the other Partner's device cannot decrypt personal data it may
50	  relay.
51	- Metadata leakage — message sizes, timing, and counts can reveal personal-ledger activity even when
52	  contents cannot be read. §4 claims nothing about a Personal Ledger is inferable; the sync design
53	  has to make that true.
54	- Conflict semantics for concurrent edits to the Shared Ledger by both Partners.
55	
56	### Telemetry (unresolved, blocks §14)
57	Nine of eleven success metrics describe behaviour inside encrypted data. If opt-in client-side
58	aggregate telemetry is adopted, its design is a privacy-critical component: what is aggregated, on
59	device or off, with what anonymity guarantee, and how a user sees and revokes it.

1231	## 8. Aesthetic & Tone
1232	*Partly inferred. The product owner supplied the voice directly in the §1 pitch — concrete, plain,
1233	slightly dry, no exclamation marks — and the rules below extend it using decisions already made
1234	(no verdicts, no dispute workflow, no reason given on dissolution). The visual direction is
1235	`[ASSUMPTION]`; the voice is not.*
1236	
1237	Ledgerleaf handles two things people are raw about: money, and their relationship. Every word it
1238	says is said into that. The governing rule is that **the product reports and never judges** — it is
1239	already how FR-51 works, and it should be how everything works.
1240	
1241	- **Voice: plain, specific, unexcited.** Numbers and facts. "£140 left in Groceries." Not "You're
1242	  doing great!" and not "Careful — you're close to your limit."
1243	- **Never scold, never congratulate.** No streaks, no badges, no scores, no celebration animations,
1244	  no red. A product that gamifies a couple's money becomes a third voice in the argument.
1245	- **Never editorialise between Partners.** Ledgerleaf states what was spent and who paid. It does
1246	  not characterise anyone's spending, flag one Partner's habits to the other, or imply fault. At
1247	  Settle-Up it presents arithmetic, not a case.
1248	- **Say what is being disclosed, where it is being disclosed.** The §4 opening at Settle-Up is
1249	  stated in plain language on that screen (FR-39). Privacy copy belongs at the moment of exposure,
1250	  not in a policy nobody opens.
1251	- **Silence is a feature.** Notifications are rare by construction, and the complete list is: a
1252	  Settlement proposal (FR-40); at most one batched proposal-change notice per day (FR-42); two
1253	  settle-up reminders, at 7 and 14 days (FR-48); a question asked about a line (FR-43); a
1254	  Transaction marked shared (FR-12) or declined (FR-13); a new device or browser session added to
1255	  one's own account (FR-21, FR-56); a periodic export prompt for a single-device Partner (FR-54);
1256	  and dissolution (FR-23). Nothing else may notify, and anything added to this list is a product
1257	  decision, not an implementation detail.
1258	
1259	**Anti-references:** budgeting apps that shame; aggregators that congratulate you on your own money;

1296	## 10. Constraints and Guardrails
1297	
1298	### 10.1 Safety
1299	
1300	The product is used by two people in a relationship, and relationships are not uniformly safe.
1301	
1302	- **Unilateral exit, always.** Either Partner can dissolve the Household alone and immediately
1303	  (FR-23). No consent, notice period, or cooling-off stands between a person and leaving.
1304	- **No location data anywhere in the product.** Not collected, not derived, not stored, not
1305	  transmitted, not shown. There is no feature for which it is a permitted input.
1306	- **No reason, no attribution on dissolution.** The remaining Partner learns only that the Household
1307	  ended (FR-23).
1308	- **No activity surveillance.** Nothing exposes when a Partner opened the app, what they looked at,
1309	  where they were, or what they checked. The affordability check records nothing (FR-51).
1310	- **Disclosure is never retroactive.** Nothing a Partner did privately becomes visible later because
1311	  of a change in Household state — not on joining (FR-18), not on dissolution (FR-24).
1312	
1313	### 10.2 Privacy
1314	
1315	- **No bank credential is ever requested, stored, or transmitted.** Permanent, not a v1 scope line.
1316	- **No readable server-side copy of Household content** (NFR-5).
1317	- **No sale, brokerage, or sharing of user data, in any form, ever.** No advertising.
1318	- **No third-party analytics with access to financial content.** `[ASSUMPTION: product analytics, if
1319	  any, are limited to non-content signals. See Open Questions — this collides with §14.]`
1320	- **Privacy is stated where it is exercised**, not only in a policy document (§8).
1321	
1322	### 10.3 Cost
1323	
1324	Ledgerleaf is run by one person, so its economics have to survive that.
1325	
1326	- **Marginal server cost per Household must be near zero.** Content is opaque to the operator, so the
1327	  service relays and stores ciphertext; it does not compute over user data.
1328	- **No per-Household server-side computation.** Settle-Up, budgeting, and import all run on-device.

1346	## 12. Non-Goals (Explicit)
1347	
1348	Ledgerleaf is not becoming these things, and v1 does not partially build toward them.
1349	
1350	- **Not a bank aggregator.** No credential linking, ever — this is the product's identity, not a

1353	  balances beyond the Ledgers themselves.
1354	- **Not a payment rail.** Ledgerleaf states who owes whom and records what the Partners did about it.

# Ledgerleaf — Addendum

Depth the user supplied that belongs downstream — architecture, solution design, UX spec — rather
than in the PRD's main narrative. Captured as it arises; not a dumping ground for audit or override
information.

## For Architecture / Solution Design

Each section below names a commitment the PRD already carries and the mechanism work that commitment
implies. The PRD holds the promise; the design has to make it true.

### Storage and sync mechanism

The local-first, end-to-end encrypted posture is a product commitment; the machinery that delivers
it is not.

- **Local-first storage.** The device holds the authoritative copy of household data; the app is
  expected to be fully usable with no network.
- **End-to-end encrypted sync between the two partners' devices.** Stated by the user as a product
  commitment. The PRD carries the *promise* (the operator cannot read household financial data); the
  *mechanism* — key exchange, pairing, conflict resolution, relay vs. peer-to-peer transport, key
  recovery on device loss — is an architecture decision and belongs here.
  - **Open:** device-loss / key-recovery story. It has real product surface (what the user is told,
    what they must do), so the user-visible half may be pulled back into the PRD once decided.
  - **Open:** concurrent-edit conflict semantics between two partners editing the same ledger.

### Sync partitioning and metadata

§4 requires that a Partner's Personal Ledger reaches only their own devices while the Shared Ledger
reaches both. That is a partitioning requirement on the sync layer, not an application-level filter:

- Separate key scopes per Ledger, so the other Partner's device cannot decrypt personal data it may
  relay.
- Metadata leakage: message sizes, timing, and counts can reveal personal-ledger activity even when
  contents cannot be read. §4 claims nothing about a Personal Ledger is inferable; the sync design
  has to make that true.
- Conflict semantics for concurrent edits to the Shared Ledger by both Partners.

### Pairing and session key transport

The PRD carries the user-visible flow (QR, one-time link, matching verification code, per-session
browser authorisation, revocation). The mechanism is architecture's:

- Device-to-device key exchange protocol, and what, if anything, transits a relay.
- The verification code's construction, and what attack it actually defeats.
- How a browser session receives key material "encrypted" from the phone, and where that material
  lives for the session's lifetime (memory only? what survives a refresh?).
- Session expiry enforcement — client-side, server-assisted, or both — and how revocation reaches a
  live session.

### Settle-Up determinism

FR-45 requires both devices to compute an identical settlement figure and an identical content hash.
That makes the arithmetic a consensus problem, not just a calculation:

- Fixed-point money representation, and a single rounding rule applied in a defined order.
- The Sealed-Settlement content hash: what it covers — the input transactions, the split rules as
  applied, the output figure, or all three — how it is computed, and what it is meant to prove to
  whom. The PRD promises the hash is displayed; it does not specify it.
- How two devices that have not fully synced avoid proposing different statements.

### Import pipeline

The PRD fixes what Ledgerleaf will and will not do to get data in; everything below that line is
design work.

- **CSV/OFX import only — no bank credential aggregation, ever.** The *constraint* is a PRD-level
  product principle. The *implementation* — per-bank CSV column mapping, OFX parsing, duplicate
  detection across re-imported statement overlaps, category inference — is design work.

### Telemetry (unresolved, blocks §14)

Nine of eleven success metrics describe behaviour inside encrypted data. If opt-in client-side
aggregate telemetry is adopted, its design is a privacy-critical component: what is aggregated, on
device or off, with what anonymity guarantee, and how a user sees and revokes it.
EOF

content.content:
**Description.** The moment the product earns its keep. From the 1st of a Period onward, either
Partner can open the close for the Period just ended. Ledgerleaf presents a single statement: every
Shared Ledger Transaction, who paid it, the Split Rule applied, the funded-from-personal ones marked
as such, and one number at the bottom — *"Alex owes Sam 137.00"*. This is the surface where the
privacy boundary deliberately opens, and per §4 it says so in plain words, where the user is looking.

Settle-Up is two-sided by design, because a number one person computed alone is exactly the
spreadsheet problem Ledgerleaf exists to retire. This is a deliberate departure from the §1 pitch's
"one tap": the close costs each Partner a tap rather than costing the Household one, and that second
tap is the whole guarantee. It should still take five minutes, not an evening. The initiator **Proposes**; the other Partner is
notified, reviews the same statement, and **Accepts**. Acceptance is always of the exact list on
screen — if anything underneath changes, the proposal is withdrawn and re-proposed automatically,
so nobody ever accepts a number that has since moved. On both accepts the Settlement is **sealed**:
immutable, retained in Settlement History with a hash of its contents.

Ledgerleaf does not move money, and does not want to. It says who owes whom and then gets out of
the way; the Partners pay each other however they already do. When that happens, the app offers to
record it as a Transfer. **The Settlement closes on both accepts, not on payment** — the agreement
and the money are separate acts, and conflating them would let an unpaid debt hold the next month
hostage.

There is no dispute mechanism in v1, deliberately. Disagreement is a conversation between two people
who live together, not a workflow. Tapping any line offers **ask about this**, which attaches a note
to that Transaction for the other Partner; whoever entered it then edits it while the Period is
still open, and the proposal re-forms around the corrected figure. The product carries the question;
the couple settles it.

Settled Periods are never reopened. A Transaction dated inside a sealed Period but entered after it
closed lands in the current Period, flagged with its true date, and settles there.

Realizes UJ-6, UJ-7.

**Functional Requirements:**

#### FR-37: Configure Split Rules
=== 1055 ===
### 5.6 Can We Afford It

*Drafted. `[ASSUMPTION]` tags mark inferences — correct them.*

**Description.** This feature is the whole of the secondary Partner's relationship with Ledgerleaf.
They are standing in a shop. They have a number in their head. They want to know whether it fits,
and they want to know in ten seconds without being lectured.

So it is one tap from opening the app, it takes an amount and a category, and it answers from the
relevant envelope's remaining balance. It is reachable from the app's default screen.

It reports rather than rules. Ledgerleaf shows what the envelope has left and what would remain after
the purchase; it does not render a verdict. No yes/no judgement is displayed: a product built to retire the household
accountant should not install a new one. The decision stays with the person holding the card.

Visibility follows §4 without exception: checking against a Shared envelope is available to both
Partners, checking against a Personal envelope only to its owner. `[ASSUMPTION: the check reads only
envelope balances and ignores both the Unallocated Pool and any outstanding Settlement debt, which
would otherwise leak settle-up state into a glance.]`

Realizes UJ-2.

content.content:
## 1. Vision

> *"Your money, your partner's money, and the money you share — finally three separate piles, with
> the month-end argument done for you in one tap, and no bank password ever leaving your phone."*
> — the product owner's pitch, and the sentence the rest of this document is accountable to.

Ledgerleaf is a budgeting app for two-person households that treats **mine**, **yours**, and
**ours** as three genuinely separate piles of money rather than one merged pot with labels on it.
Each partner keeps a personal ledger; the household keeps a shared one; money moves between them by
explicit transfer. At the end of each month Ledgerleaf computes who owes whom on shared spending —
under whatever split the couple agreed to, whether that is even, scaled to income, or set per
category — so the month closes with a single transfer instead of an argument. Every closed month is
kept as a record, so a disagreement about what was agreed is settled by looking it up rather than by
memory.

It is privacy-first by construction, not by policy. Ledgerleaf never asks for a bank credential and
never will. Transactions are entered by hand or imported from CSV/OFX files the user already has.
Data lives on the partners' own devices and syncs between them end-to-end encrypted, so there is no
readable server-side copy for anyone — the operator included — to mine or sell. Everything exports
to CSV at any time, because a product that asks for trust should be easy to leave.

The point is to retire the household accountant. Today one partner owns the spreadsheet, maintains
it, and resents it, while the other never opens it; bank-linked apps solve the effort problem by
exposing every transaction to both partners and monetising the data behind their backs. Ledgerleaf
takes the opposite trade — a little manual effort in exchange for fairness and privacy. Six months
in, a Ledgerleaf household has no accountant: the partner who never opened the spreadsheet checks
"can we afford this" on their own before a big purchase, settle-up takes five minutes, and neither
person feels surveilled by the other.

content.text:
Finalize is complete bar one step. Here's where it landed.

## What the reviewers found

Five reviewers, ~180 findings, and they independently converged on the same thing: **the prose was finished, the spine wasn't.** The rubric walker called it "strong" on vision and scope honesty; the other three called it not buildable. Both were right.

**Applied — the convergent criticals:**

- **The Floor leaked income under every split rule.** We'd spent a whole turn making the income-proportional split honest about revealing relative income — and then a shared Floor "derived from the lowest of the last six months of combined income" leaked the same thing under *even* and *custom* splits too. Three reviewers caught it independently. Fixed by reframing it as a per-partner **Contribution Floor** — what you commit to Ours, not what you earn. A freelancer on £5,000 can commit £900, and the number is now shareable because it's an agreement rather than a disclosure.
- **The shared Unallocated Pool published Alex's income to the penny.** UJ-4 literally narrated it: the £4,100 invoice surplus landing in a pool Sam can see. Above-Floor income now lands in the partner's *own* private pool.
- **Settle-Up had no arithmetic.** The product's central feature, unspecified. Now written out in five steps — shared spending, each partner's share by per-category rule, contributions, residue attributed to neither, deterministic rounding so both devices compute an identical hash.
- **"Remaining balance" was undefined** across two incompatible accounting models, which made FR-47 — the secondary persona's entire product — unimplementable. Now: planned ≠ assigned ≠ available, and the check answers from available.
- **Three capabilities were depended on but defined nowhere:** recording income, viewing a ledger, and *sync itself* — the product's defining technical claim had no FR and wasn't in MVP scope.
- **Safety gaps the privacy reviewer found and §10.1 had missed:** creating a category announced it to the household, so a partner preparing to leave couldn't track solicitor costs privately (now: private personal categories). And a second device paired from a briefly-unlocked phone mirrored the victim's entire personal ledger silently — device additions now notify unsuppressibly.
- Plus: cross-ledger writes blocked, Current vs Open Period disambiguated, §7 no longer contradicts SM-3b, §8's notification allowlist completed (it was missing 5 of 9), back-dating widened to match your own worked example, FRs reordered and renumbered **FR-1→FR-56** with zero dangling references.

Your verbatim pitch is now the epigraph to §1 — the reconciler pointed out we'd paraphrased away the one sample of the product's voice you'd actually supplied, then labelled §8 "inferred."

---

## Six decisions I did not make for you

**1. Is the Settle-Up arithmetic right?** *(phase-blocker)* I drafted it because three reviewers said nothing could proceed without it. Two choices inside it are mine, not yours: **do Transfers into Ours count as contributions**, and **is unspent residue in Ours owed to neither partner, split by the default rule**? I said yes to both. Everything in §5.5 rests on it.

**2. What breaks a permanent stall?** *(phase-blocker)* FR-44/45/46 together let one partner block *every future settlement forever* by simply never tapping Accept — carry-forward needs both too. It's a dead end, and §10.1 doesn't see that it's also a coercion lever. Options: a one-sided close marked as such in history, or a proposal that expires into a one-sided record.

**3. Telemetry, or give up the metrics.** *(phase-blocker)* **Eight of your ten success metrics are unmeasurable as specified.** Only SM-1 and SM-2 survive, because they're billing facts. Everything else — activation, settlement completion, rubber-stamping, notification volume — describes behaviour inside encrypted data on a device you can't read. Opt-in client-side aggregate telemetry is the obvious answer and has its own trust cost. There's no FR for it and it's now an explicit MVP exclusion.

**4. Ratify the Contribution Floor.** I changed substance, not wording, to keep §4's promise. Worth your explicit yes.

**5. Does dissolution leak its timing?** §10.1 forbids location but not time. A real-time notice tells the remaining partner the exact moment the other left.

**6. How do 1,000 households find this?** No acquisition channel appears anywhere. A privacy-first product that can't advertise on the usual networks, sold by one person — SM-1 assumes that away.

---

**Artifacts** in `_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01/`:

`prd.md` (1,545 lines) · `addendum.md` · `.memlog.md` (113 entries) · four `review-*.md` · `reconcile-memlog.md`

I've left `status: draft` rather than closing it out — three of those are phase-blockers, and marking it final would tell `bmad-architecture` and `bmad-create-epics-and-stories` it's safe to build from when the settle-up arithmetic is still a guess of mine. **Answer 1, 2 and 3 and I'll fold them in and close it.** Next in the chain after that: `bmad-ux`, `bmad-architecture`, then `bmad-create-epics-and-stories`.

content.text:
All six folded in. **`prd.md` is `status: final`.**

## What changed in this last pass

**Settle-Up (FR-38)** — the `[ASSUMPTION]` block is gone; the computation now reads as confirmed, naming both choices you ratified so a future reader knows they were decided rather than defaulted.

**FR-53, Close a stalled proposal one-sidedly** — new. Thirty days, proposer only, sealed as **closed without acceptance** and presented differently from an accepted Settlement *wherever Settlements appear*. Your dissent note is in there as a first-class thing: attachable at any time, visible to both, retained in history, changes no figure. The `[NOTE FOR PM]` on the deadlock is replaced with the reasoning — *"deliberately slow and deliberately visible: 30 days, and the result is never dressed up as agreement."*

**FR-56, Share anonymous usage counts, by choice** — new, and written tightly because this is the one FR where vagueness would cost you the privacy claim. Counts only, with an explicit never-list: no ledger, transaction, merchant, category name, amount, balance, income, Contribution Floor, or settlement figure. Aggregated on device. **Per partner, not per household** — one partner opting in neither opts in nor discloses anything about the other, which your phrasing implied but didn't say.

§14 no longer carries a `[NOTE FOR PM]` about unmeasurability. It now states how each metric is measured and accepts the two consequences honestly:

> Every metric except SM-1 and SM-2 is measured on a self-selected sample [...] **Opt-in rate is itself the limiting factor.** If few Partners consent, the product is flying blind on eight of ten metrics. That is the accepted price of §10.2, and raising the opt-in rate by pressing people is a violation of §8, not a growth tactic.

That last clause closes a loophole: without it, "improve telemetry opt-in" is an obvious growth lever that would have eaten your notification discipline.

**Dissolution timing** — FR-23 and §10.1 both updated. Next app open, date only, no push, no badge, no time of day. §10.1's bullet is now *"No reason, no attribution, no timing"* with the reason attached: *the moment someone leaves can itself be dangerous information.*

**Acquisition** sits under §15 as **Carried out of scope — go-to-market**, recorded explicitly so a reviewer reads it as your decision rather than a gap.

**§15 rewritten** — 8 live questions, resolved ones folded into the body. **§16 split** into *decided by the product owner* (five, with traceability) and *still inferred* (four — the FRs I wrote to fill absences: Record Income, View a Ledger, Sync, private categories, deletion).

**FR-1 → FR-58**, sequential, every cross-reference resolving, no dangling FR or UJ references.

---

**`_bmad/planning-artifacts/prds/prd-bmad-harness-2026-10-01/`**

| | |
|---|---|
| `prd.md` | 1,605 lines · 17 sections · 58 FRs · 8 journeys · **final** |
| `addendum.md` | architecture carry-over: sync partitioning and metadata leakage, key exchange, settle-up determinism, hash semantics, import internals, telemetry design |
| `.memlog.md` | 122 entries |
| `review-*.md` ×4, `reconcile-memlog.md` | the full reviews, if you want to drill into anything I summarised |

Four things remain genuinely inferred rather than decided — flagged in §16, worth a glance before architecture starts. The eight open questions are ordinary follow-ups, not blockers.

Next in the chain: **`bmad-ux`** (§7 and §8 are deliberately thin and tagged as inferred — they're a starting position for a designer, not a design), then **`bmad-architecture`**, then **`bmad-create-epics-and-stories`**. One flag for that last step: §13 carries a note that 58 FRs including hand-rolled E2EE sync has no release sequencing, which is exactly what epic planning is for.
